title: Multi-Modal Anomaly Detection: A Survey
comment: Accepted for publication in IEEE Transactions on Big Data
summary: Multi-Modal Anomaly Detection (MMAD) detects rare abnormal events from heterogeneous data sources and is increasingly used in safety- and reliability-critical applications such as industrial inspection and cybersecurity. Yet the literature is fragmented across domains and modality combinations, and existing surveys usually group methods by architecture rather than by how abnormality is defined and separated in multi-modal settings. We survey MMAD from an assumption-driven perspective. We formalize the problem, identify five intrinsic characteristics underlying its core challenges, and organize prior work into two complementary paradigms. The first, normality-assumption methods, models regularity via representation learning, cross-modal alignment, and knowledge enhancement. The second, anomaly-assumption methods, sharpens decision boundaries through coarse-grained, structural, and semantic anomaly injection. We also investigate how foundation models are reshaping MMAD through scalable pretraining, flexible cross-modal transfer, and emerging reasoning capabilities. Finally, we compile representative benchmarks and evaluation protocols across domains and highlight open problems and future directions for robust, adaptive, and interpretable MMAD systems.

AI.tldr: A comprehensive survey of Multi-Modal Anomaly Detection (MMAD) that proposes an assumption-driven perspective, organizing methods into normality-assumption and anomaly-assumption paradigms, while investigating foundation models' impact and compiling benchmarks.
AI.motivation: The literature on MMAD is fragmented across domains and modality combinations, and existing surveys group methods by architecture rather than by how abnormality is defined and separated. This fragmentation hinders progress and understanding in the field.
AI.method: The paper formalizes the MMAD problem, identifies five intrinsic characteristics underlying its core challenges, and organizes prior work into two complementary paradigms: (1) normality-assumption methods that model regularity via representation learning, cross-modal alignment, and knowledge enhancement; and (2) anomaly-assumption methods that sharpen decision boundaries through coarse-grained, structural, and semantic anomaly injection. The survey also investigates how foundation models are reshaping MMAD.
AI.result: The survey compiles representative benchmarks and evaluation protocols across domains and highlights open problems and future directions for robust, adaptive, and interpretable MMAD systems.
AI.conclusion: This assumption-driven survey provides a structured framework for understanding MMAD, offering insights for developing more effective anomaly detection systems in safety- and reliability-critical applications.

title: Combining Self-Embedding Audio Watermarking with Ultra-Low-Bitrate Neural Codecs
comment: 6 pages; 1 figure; 2 tables; submitted to WIFS 2026
summary: Partial manipulation of speech recordings, where only localized segments of an utterance are altered, poses a significant challenge for content integrity verification, as reliable detection and localization of such edits becomes harder as the manipulated proportion decreases. Watermarking offers a proactive defense alternative by embedding auxiliary information prior to distribution; classical hash-based schemes achieve near-perfect detection and localization under ideal conditions, but the original content cannot be recovered once a segment is manipulated. Building on a prior self-embedding audio steganography framework, this work presents an initial exploration of proactive defense performance under ideal conditions, extending the investigation along three axes: frame-level localization, multi-bit least significant bit variants, and evaluation across multiple ultra-low-bitrate neural codec representations. By embedding a compact neural codec representation rather than a cryptographic hash, the framework additionally enables recovery of the manipulated regions, while supporting training-free detection and localization without spoofed examples. Experiments across four controlled manipulation types under ideal channel conditions show that the embedded payload, and hence an approximate reconstruction of the authentic content, is always fully recovered without bit errors. The results also indicate that the choice of neural codec is the dominant factor for detection and localization performance.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a proactive defense framework for audio content integrity verification using self-embedding audio steganography. By embedding a compact neural codec representation rather than a cryptographic hash, the system enables both detection/localization of manipulated segments and recovery of authentic content. The approach is evaluated across multiple neural codecs under ultra-low-bitrate conditions.
AI.motivation: The challenge of detecting localized speech manipulations becomes increasingly difficult as the manipulated proportion decreases. Traditional hash-based watermarking schemes cannot recover original content once manipulated. This work aims to address both detection/localization and content recovery under ultra-low-bitrate neural codec representations.
AI.method: The framework extends a prior self-embedding audio steganography approach with three key extensions: (1) frame-level localization capability, (2) multi-bit least significant bit (LSB) variants, and (3) evaluation across multiple neural codec representations. Instead of cryptographic hashes, a compact neural codec representation is embedded, enabling content recovery.
AI.result: Under ideal channel conditions across four controlled manipulation types, the embedded payload is always fully recovered without bit errors, enabling approximate reconstruction of authentic content. The neural codec choice emerges as the dominant factor affecting detection and localization performance.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework successfully achieves training-free detection and localization of speech manipulations while enabling recovery of manipulated regions. The choice of neural codec is critical for performance, suggesting future work should focus on optimizing codec selection for specific manipulation scenarios.

title: Learning Continuous Regional Temperature Fields with Lead-Time and Resolution Queries
summary: Accurate regional near-surface temperature forecasting is fundamental to short-range weather services and downstream risk assessment. Existing deep learning-based regional forecasters commonly produce a fixed set of future frames on a prescribed grid, limiting their use when forecast products must be evaluated at query-dependent lead times or display resolutions. To overcome these fixed-output constraints, we formulate regional T2M forecasting as query-conditioned continuous spatiotemporal temperature field evaluation and propose the Continuous Spatiotemporal Temperature Forecaster (CSTF), a neural field that turns forecast lead time and output resolution into explicit queries when evaluating 2-m temperature (T2M). Specifically, CSTF first encodes multivariable ERA5 histories into latent meteorological states and then decodes T2M as a coordinate-based field. Accordingly, spatial location, forecast lead time, and output resolution are introduced as queries, enabling standard hourly forecasts, intermediate lead-time diagnostics, and resolution-controllable outputs within a unified field-evaluation framework. Furthermore, to maintain coherence across flexible field queries, we design spatial-gradient, temporal-difference, and scale-consistency objectives that regularize regional thermal structures, lead-wise evolution, and cross-resolution agreement. Experiments on the Southeast China 0-6 h ERA5-Land benchmark demonstrate that CSTF achieves the best aggregate deterministic skill, including a 17.0 percent reduction in Bias, with global-scope diagnostics further illustrating flexible lead-time and resolution-controllable inference.

AI.tldr: CSTF is a neural field model for regional 2-m temperature (T2M) forecasting that enables query-conditioned continuous spatiotemporal evaluation, allowing flexible forecast lead times and output resolutions within a unified framework.
AI.motivation: Existing deep learning-based regional forecasters produce fixed outputs on prescribed grids, limiting their use when forecasts must be evaluated at query-dependent lead times or display resolutions. There was a need for a more flexible approach.
AI.method: CSTF encodes multivariable ERA5 histories into latent meteorological states and decodes T2M as a coordinate-based field. It introduces spatial location, forecast lead time, and output resolution as explicit queries. The model uses spatial-gradient, temporal-difference, and scale-consistency objectives to maintain coherence across flexible field queries.
AI.result: On the Southeast China 0-6 h ERA5-Land benchmark, CSTF achieves the best aggregate deterministic skill with a 17.0 percent reduction in Bias compared to baseline methods.
AI.conclusion: CSTF successfully enables flexible lead-time and resolution-controllable inference through its continuous spatiotemporal field evaluation framework, demonstrating the feasibility of query-conditioned weather forecasting.

title: ARISMA: Guidelines for AI- and LLM-Assisted Systematic Reviews, Scoping Reviews, and Mapping Studies
comment: Accepted to be presented at AGENTICS 2026, to be published by Springer
summary: Systematic reviews, scoping reviews, mapping studies, and related evidence syntheses are increasingly difficult to conduct with fully manual workflows as search volumes, update cycles, and synthesis requirements continue to expand. At the same time, artificial intelligence, machine learning, and large language models are rapidly entering review practice across query formulation, screening, extraction, categorization, appraisal support, and reporting. Yet the empirical evidence remains uneven, task-dependent, and insufficient to justify unconstrained automation. Existing standards such as PRISMA 2020, PRISMA-S, PRISMA-ScR, PRISMA-P, PRESS, and SWiM remain essential, but none provides an end-to-end operational standard for when AI use is methodologically appropriate, how it should be validated, which review decisions must remain human-led, and how AI involvement should be reported so that readers can audit it. This paper proposes ARISMA, an AI Reporting and Integration standard for Systematic Methods and Analysis. ARISMA treats AI as an inspected, benchmarked, logged, and reversible assistant rather than an autonomous reviewer. It is built around one governing principle: every consequential scientific decision must remain human-interpretable, human-auditable, and human-accountable. The paper contributes a lifecycle taxonomy, process guidance, stepwise recommendations across the review pipeline, a governance and provenance model, a tool-support framework, an AI-integrated reporting checklist, and a validation matrix. It also addresses legal, privacy, infrastructure, and sustainability considerations. The framework was iteratively refined through structured expert consultation. The result is a practical and auditable guideline for responsible AI-assisted evidence synthesis.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes ARISMA, a new reporting standard for AI-assisted systematic reviews. It addresses the gap in existing guidelines (PRISMA, PRISMA-S, etc.) regarding when AI can be used, how it should be validated, and how AI involvement should be reported. The framework treats AI as an assisted tool rather than autonomous reviewer, with the core principle that all consequential decisions must remain human-interpretable, auditable, and accountable.
AI.motivation: Systematic reviews are becoming increasingly difficult to conduct manually due to expanding search volumes and update cycles. While AI/ML/LLMs are rapidly entering review practice, the empirical evidence remains uneven and insufficient to justify full automation. Existing standards (PRISMA 2020, PRISMA-S, PRISMA-ScR, PRISMA-P, PRESS, SWiM) lack operational guidance on appropriate AI use, validation requirements, human-led decisions, and AI reporting for transparency.
AI.method: The framework was iteratively refined through structured expert consultation. The paper contributes: (1) a lifecycle taxonomy, (2) process guidance, (3) stepwise recommendations across the review pipeline, (4) a governance and provenance model, (5) a tool-support framework, (6) an AI-integrated reporting checklist, and (7) a validation matrix.
AI.result: ARISMA treats AI as an inspected, benchmarked, logged, and reversible assistant rather than an autonomous reviewer. It provides practical and auditable guidelines for responsible AI-assisted evidence synthesis, addressing legal, privacy, infrastructure, and sustainability considerations.
AI.conclusion: ARISMA offers a comprehensive operational standard for AI integration in systematic reviews, ensuring methodological appropriateness, proper validation, human accountability for key decisions, and transparent reporting to enable reader auditing.

title: AI-Powered Mental Health Chatbots in Africa: A Systematic Review and Culturally Adaptive Framework
summary: Mental health challenges in Africa remain under-addressed due to inadequate infrastructure, stigma, and a chronic shortage of professionals. Artificial Intelligence (AI)-powered chatbots are emerging globally as low-cost, accessible tools that can offer psychological support. This paper presents a systematic review of 52 empirical studies published between 2017 and 2025, critically analysing their cultural, linguistic, and infrastructural relevance to African contexts. The findings demonstrate the potential of AI chatbots to improve accessibility, reduce symptoms of anxiety and depression, and expand psychosocial support, yet reveal limited African-specific adaptation. Most systems remain rooted in Western models and English-language designs, leaving critical gaps in local relevance, inclusivity, and sustainability. Based on the findings, the authors develop a Culturally Adaptive Digital Mental Health (CADMH) framework that integrates African cultural values, multilingual design, mobile-first optimisation, and ethical safeguards. The study highlights opportunities and barriers for integrating AI chatbots into African healthcare, offering guidance for research, practice, and policy.

AI.tldr: This systematic review examines 52 empirical studies on AI-powered chatbots for mental health in Africa (2017-2025), finding that while these tools show potential for improving accessibility and reducing anxiety/depression, they remain largely based on Western models with limited African-specific adaptation. The authors propose a Culturally Adaptive Digital Mental Health (CADMH) framework to address these gaps.
AI.motivation: Mental health challenges in Africa are under-addressed due to inadequate infrastructure, stigma, and professional shortages. AI chatbots emerge as potential low-cost, accessible solutions, but their cultural and linguistic relevance to African contexts remains unclear.
AI.method: Systematic review of 52 empirical studies published between 2017 and 2025, analyzing cultural, linguistic, and infrastructural relevance to African contexts.
AI.result: AI chatbots demonstrate potential to improve accessibility, reduce anxiety/depression symptoms, and expand psychosocial support. However, most systems remain rooted in Western models and English-language designs, with limited local relevance, inclusivity, and sustainability.
AI.conclusion: The study proposes a Culturally Adaptive Digital Mental Health (CADMH) framework integrating African cultural values, multilingual design, mobile-first optimization, and ethical safeguards. This provides guidance for research, practice, and policy on integrating AI chatbots into African healthcare systems.

title: Targeting the Attention Heads Behind Object Hallucination in LLaVA
comment: 10 pages, 5 figures, 3 tables. Accepted at the Actionable Interpretability Workshop, COLM 2026
summary: Vision-language models such as LLaVA-1.5-7B often hallucinate objects absent from the image when generating captions. We ask whether an interpretability diagnosis of this failure can guide a targeted fix, and we measure what that fix actually changes. We rank attention heads by how much their image attention drops around hallucinated object words, then screen the shortlist by ablating candidate heads and measuring the change in hallucination-token log probability, yielding a 32-head set. We restrict two interventions to these heads: a head-sliced LoRA adapter and an inference-time grounding controller. On 400 held-out COCO images, the combined method lowers CHAIRs (the fraction of captions with a hallucinated object) from 0.370 to 0.230 and CHAIRi (the fraction of hallucinated object mentions) from 0.156 to 0.096 (p < 0.001, paired sign-flip tests). Two controls sharpen attribution. A random-head LoRA control, matched layer-for-layer and trained identically, performs no better than the matched baseline on a separate 200-image control split, supporting the role of head selection rather than LoRA capacity. Under fixed decoding budgets, the CHAIR reduction persists and grows with budget (23% at 64 tokens to 58% at 128), arguing against a pure max-token or truncation artifact, although the method remains shorter and more conservative. The resulting behavior reduces unsupported object mentions while also lowering object recall (0.78 to 0.70). We present a diagnosis-to-intervention pipeline for object hallucination, and, more importantly, a controlled account of what acting on the diagnostic signal actually does: it localizes intervention sites with real, non-random leverage, reported as a behavioral profile rather than a single score.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a diagnosis-to-intervention pipeline for reducing object hallucination in vision-language models like LLaVA-1.5-7B. The method identifies 32 attention heads responsible for hallucination by measuring attention drops around hallucinated object words, then applies two interventions: a head-sliced LoRA adapter and an inference-time grounding controller. The combined approach significantly reduces hallucination rates (CHAIRs from 0.370 to 0.230, CHAIRi from 0.156 to 0.096) while controlling for confounds through random-head baselines.
AI.motivation: Vision-language models often hallucinate objects absent from images during caption generation. The authors investigate whether interpretability-based diagnosis of this failure can guide targeted fixes, and more importantly, measure what those fixes actually change behaviorally.
AI.method: The approach involves: (1) Ranking attention heads by image attention drops around hallucinated object words, (2) Screening candidates via ablation to measure hallucination-token log probability changes, yielding 32 identified heads, (3) Applying two interventions: a head-sliced LoRA adapter and an inference-time grounding controller, (4) Using random-head LoRA controls matched layer-for-layer to isolate the effect of head selection.
AI.result: On 400 held-out COCO images, the combined method reduces CHAIRs from 0.370 to 0.230 and CHAIRi from 0.156 to 0.096 (p < 0.001). The reduction persists across decoding budgets (23% at 64 tokens to 58% at 128 tokens). However, object recall also decreases from 0.78 to 0.70. The random-head control performs no better than baseline, supporting that head selection provides real, non-random leverage.
AI.conclusion: The diagnosis-to-intervention pipeline successfully reduces object hallucination in VLMs through targeted attention head intervention. The controlled experiments demonstrate that the identified heads have genuine causal leverage rather than being artifacts. The method trades off hallucination reduction for some loss in object recall, producing more conservative outputs. The key contribution is providing a behavioral profile of intervention effects rather than single-score metrics.

title: ExFold: Unified Expert Folding for Training-Free MoE Prefill-Decode Acceleration
summary: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models scale capacity for strong quality while keeping per-token compute bounded through sparse expert activation. Yet low-latency MoE serving is increasingly challenging, because it spans two inference phases with fundamentally different bottlenecks: prefill is dominated by token-wise expert computation, whereas decode is constrained by memory traffic from the batch-wise activated expert set. However, existing training-free acceleration methods optimize only a single resource proxy, either the experts each token executes or the experts a batch activates, and either discard the excluded experts' contribution or leave it only implicitly approximated. In this paper, we propose ExFold, a unified training-free expert-folding framework for jointly accelerating MoE prefill and decode. ExFold casts both prefill and decode as one budgeted output-approximation problem: execute only a phase-specific constrained expert set while projecting the contribution of budget-excluded experts onto retained experts using calibrated scalar projectors. Motivated by the observation that many expert outputs are directionally aligned but differ in magnitude, ExFold calibrates a pairwise scalar-projector matrix on unlabeled data and uses it at inference time to fold excluded expert contributions into retained experts. Under this view, prefill acceleration becomes token-level Top-K folding, and decode acceleration becomes batch-level expert-pool folding. The two phases differ only in how retained experts are selected, while excluded contributions are recovered by one shared folding mechanism. We implement ExFold as a plug-and-play plugin in vLLM, with a lightweight expert-folding CUDA kernel, delivering up to 1.41x TTFT and 2.45x TPOT speedups while retaining about 99% of the original average quality.

AI.tldr: ExFold is a training-free acceleration framework for Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models that jointly optimizes both prefill and decode inference phases by folding excluded expert contributions onto retained experts using calibrated scalar projectors.
AI.motivation: MoE serving faces two distinct bottlenecks: prefill is dominated by token-wise expert computation, while decode is constrained by memory traffic from batch-wise activated experts. Existing training-free methods only optimize a single resource proxy, either per-token or per-batch expert selection, discarding or only implicitly approximating the excluded experts' contribution.
AI.method: ExFold casts both prefill and decode as a budgeted output-approximation problem: execute only a phase-specific constrained expert set while projecting excluded expert contributions onto retained experts using calibrated scalar projectors. The method calibrates a pairwise scalar-projector matrix on unlabeled data, where prefill becomes token-level Top-K folding and decode becomes batch-level expert-pool folding. Implemented as a plug-and-play plugin in vLLM with a lightweight expert-folding CUDA kernel.
AI.result: Delivers up to 1.41x Time-to-First-Token (TTFT) and 2.45x Time-per-Output-Token (TPOT) speedups while retaining approximately 99% of the original average quality.
AI.conclusion: ExFold provides a unified framework that effectively accelerates both MoE inference phases through a shared folding mechanism, achieving significant speedups with minimal quality degradation.

title: Dissonance Spectrum explicitly models perceptual frequency interactions for better music understanding
summary: Conventional music representations describe acoustic energy over time and frequency but do not explicitly expose relations among simultaneous frequency components. We introduce the \emph{Dissonance Spectrum} (DS), a nonnegative time--frequency representation that applies a tolerance-based rational pitch-relation kernel with logarithmic harmonic distance to a constant-Q spectrum and attributes aggregate pairwise interactions back to individual frequency bins. Controlled music-theory tests show strong ordinal agreement for intervals, harmonic-function connections, and church modes, and weaker but significant agreement across diverse chord voicings. DS is then encoded by a lightweight parallel branch whose zero-initialized residual projection preserves the baseline function at initialization. Across six paired training seeds in open-ended music question answering and categorical and dimensional music emotion recognition, DS obtains the highest mean on every reported endpoint relative to the unchanged baseline, a parameter-matched Gaussian-input branch, and an architecture-matched magnitude-CQT branch. These results support DS as an interpretable, complementary representation, while listener-specific perception and broader task coverage remain open problems.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces the Dissonance Spectrum (DS), a novel nonnegative time-frequency music representation that exposes relations among simultaneous frequency components using a tolerance-based rational pitch-relation kernel with logarithmic harmonic distance applied to a constant-Q spectrum. When integrated into a neural network as a lightweight parallel branch, DS achieves state-of-the-art performance across multiple music understanding tasks including question answering and emotion recognition.
AI.motivation: Conventional music representations describe acoustic energy over time and frequency but do not explicitly expose relations among simultaneous frequency components. This limits their ability to capture harmonic and dissonant interactions that are fundamental to music perception.
AI.method: The Dissonance Spectrum applies a tolerance-based rational pitch-relation kernel with logarithmic harmonic distance to a constant-Q spectrum, then attributes aggregate pairwise interactions back to individual frequency bins. This representation is encoded by a lightweight parallel branch with zero-initialized residual projection that preserves baseline function at initialization.
AI.result: Controlled music-theory tests show strong ordinal agreement for intervals, harmonic-function connections, and church modes, and weaker but significant agreement across diverse chord voicings. In six paired training seeds across open-ended music question answering and categorical/dimensional music emotion recognition, DS achieves the highest mean on every reported endpoint relative to baseline, Gaussian-input branch, and magnitude-CQT branch.
AI.conclusion: DS serves as an interpretable, complementary music representation. Open problems remain including listener-specific perception and broader task coverage.

title: VBVR-Pro: A Scalable and Verifiable Suite for Native Visual Reasoning
summary: Native visual reasoning treats visual generation as the medium of reasoning itself: visual states (i.e. images and videos) are not merely inputs to be understood or outputs to be rendered, but first-class substrates for problem solving beyond language. Yet progress remains bottlenecked by the lack of scalable training tasks, reliable feedback, and controlled comparisons across generative substrates. In this work, we introduce VBVR-Pro, a closed-loop testbed that makes native visual reasoning through generation trainable, verifiable, optimizable, and experimentally controllable. 1) Task scaling. VBVR-Pro turns visual reasoning into a controlled task space of 300 procedurally generated tasks. Models trained on VBVR-Pro show strong transfer beyond the proposed suite across seven external visual reasoning benchmarks such as RISE-Video, MME-CoF-Pro, and BabyVision. 2) Verifiable rewards. VBVR-Pro provides verifiable reward scorers for task-grounded evaluation. Through a systematic study of leading MLLMs as judges, we identify recurring failure modes of the prevalent VLM-as-a-judge paradigm. In contrast, the proposed scorers are grounded in deterministic, task-specific rules, achieve fine-grained alignment with human judgments. Importantly, they serve as reliable reward signals for large-scale multi-task reinforcement learning and demonstrate stronger post-RL performance across visual reasoning tasks. 3) Mechanism study. VBVR-Pro enables controlled modality studies across more than 30 image, video, and interleaved generators. Our analysis shows that video generation remains strongest for tasks requiring persistent spatiotemporal state tracking, while interleaved generation provides a compute-efficient alternative. Critically, ablations and probing suggest the presence of vision-native trajectories that are crucial to visual reasoning. We release all data, models, scorers, and code.

AI.tldr: VBVR-Pro is a closed-loop testbed for training, verifying, and optimizing native visual reasoning through generation. It provides 300 procedurally generated tasks with verifiable rewards, enabling scalable training and evaluation across image, video, and interleaved generators. The framework demonstrates strong transfer to 7 external benchmarks and reveals that video generation excels at spatiotemporal tracking while interleaved generation offers compute efficiency.
AI.motivation: Native visual reasoning treats visual generation as a first-class reasoning medium beyond language. However, progress is bottlenecked by lack of scalable training tasks, reliable feedback mechanisms, and controlled comparisons across generative substrates.
AI.method: VBVR-Pro introduces: (1) 300 procedurally generated tasks enabling task scaling; (2) Verifiable reward scorers grounded in deterministic, task-specific rules (avoiding VLM-as-a-judge failure modes); (3) Controlled modality studies across 30+ image, video, and interleaved generators.
AI.result: Models trained on VBVR-Pro show strong transfer to 7 external benchmarks (RISE-Video, MME-CoF-Pro, BabyVision). The verifiable scorers achieve fine-grained human alignment and serve as reliable RL reward signals. Video generation excels at persistent spatiotemporal state tracking; interleaved generation provides compute-efficient alternatives. Ablations confirm vision-native trajectories are crucial.
AI.conclusion: VBVR-Pro enables trainable, verifiable, and optimizable native visual reasoning. It provides the first scalable testbed with deterministic rewards for multi-task RL, reveals modality-specific strengths, and demonstrates that vision-native reasoning trajectories are essential for visual problem-solving. All data, models, scorers, and code are released.

title: Model-Based Agentic Software Engineering
summary:
Coding agents increase implementation capacity without automatically making project intent, system structure, or acceptance evidence explicit. As implementation becomes abundant relative to engineering judgment, the scarce work shifts toward choosing useful abstractions, producing evidence, and determining which obligations govern acceptance. Existing workflows address parts of this gap through larger prompts, repository retrieval, or perchange review, but still require agents and engineers to reconstruct consequential properties.
  As an alternative, we present Model-Based Agentic Software Engineering (MAGE). MAGE is a framework and a theory for building trustworthy autonomy from commodity intelligence. MAGE addresses a representation problem and an authority problem: it externalizes the smallest purposeful representation needed to answer an engineering question, then gives settled obligations proportionate authority through constraints, sensors, validators, and gates. It keeps uncertain intent open and turns recurring reconstruction and judgment into durable engineering structure that later work can inherit. We developed MAGE from a longitudinal case and refined it through six independently reported industrial accounts. Across these sources, MAGE explains how externalized knowledge, bounded action, independent evaluation, and retained human authority can compose into a governed engineering environment, and proposes tests of when that environment turns commodity intelligence into durable engineering progress.

AI.tldr: MAGE (Model-Based Agentic Software Engineering) is a framework that addresses the gap between coding agents' implementation capacity and the need for explicit project intent, system structure, and acceptance evidence. It solves a representation problem (externalizing minimal purposeful representations) and an authority problem (giving settled obligations proportionate authority through constraints, sensors, validators, and gates). Developed from a longitudinal case and refined through six industrial accounts.
AI.motivation: Coding agents increase implementation capacity but don't make project intent, system structure, or acceptance evidence explicit. As implementation becomes abundant, the scarce work shifts to choosing useful abstractions, producing evidence, and determining acceptance obligations. Existing workflows (larger prompts, repository retrieval, per-change review) still require agents and engineers to reconstruct consequential properties.
AI.method: MAGE was developed from a longitudinal case study and refined through six independently reported industrial accounts. It proposes externalizing the smallest purposeful representation needed to answer engineering questions, then giving settled obligations proportionate authority through constraints, sensors, validators, and gates.
AI.result: MAGE explains how externalized knowledge, bounded action, independent evaluation, and retained human authority can compose into a governed engineering environment. It proposes tests for when commodity intelligence turns into durable engineering progress.
AI.conclusion: MAGE offers a framework and theory for building trustworthy autonomy from commodity intelligence by addressing representation and authority problems, keeping uncertain intent open, and turning recurring reconstruction into durable engineering structure that later work can inherit.

title: Measurement-Budget Allocation in Quantum Learning with Finite-Shot Generalization Guarantees
summary: On near-term quantum hardware, estimating a Born probability requires repeated circuit executions. A quantum learning experiment with a fixed measurement budget $B$ must therefore decide how many distinct training states $n$ to use and how many shots $S$ to allocate to each state. We study this tradeoff for binary quantum classifiers with fixed or independently selected measurement operators $M$, where the ideal score is $\Tr(Mρ)$. We prove a distribution-free generalization bound that separates the finite-sample and finite-shot contributions. The sample term scales as $\sqrt{d/n}$, while the shot term scales as $\sqrt{(\log n)/S}$; under the constraint $B=nS$, these two terms move in opposite directions. Minimising a conservative closed-form surrogate of the bound gives the allocation rule $\nstar = 2\sqrt{2dB/\log(2B/δ)}$ and $\Sstar = B/\nstar$. This surrogate has the same asymptotic scaling as the exact minimizer and yields a worst-case rate of $B^{-1/4}$. The guarantee is intentionally conservative, since it applies to the full class of binary quantum measurements. We complement the theory with PennyLane simulations using 2-qubit and 4-qubit variational quantum circuits on nine synthetic binary classification benchmarks. In all tested configurations, the one-sided empirical generalization gap remains below the theoretical bound. The result provides a conservative statistical guideline for allocating measurement budgets in finite-shot evaluation and pre-experimental planning for near-term quantum learning systems, complementing hardware-level scheduling and circuit-design considerations. Extending the guarantee to fully adaptive shot-noisy training remains an open problem.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses the measurement budget allocation problem in near-term quantum learning, where estimating Born probabilities requires repeated circuit executions. The authors derive a distribution-free generalization bound that separates finite-sample and finite-shot contributions, leading to an optimal allocation rule n* = 2√(2dB/log(2B/δ)) and S* = B/n*, with a worst-case convergence rate of B^(-1/4).
AI.motivation: On near-term quantum hardware, estimating Born probabilities requires repeated circuit executions. A quantum learning experiment with fixed measurement budget B must decide how many distinct training states n to use and how many shots S to allocate to each state. This fundamental tradeoff between sample complexity (n) and shot noise (S) was not well understood theoretically.
AI.method: The authors prove a distribution-free generalization bound that separates the finite-sample and finite-shot contributions. The sample term scales as √(d/n) while the shot term scales as √((log n)/S). Under the constraint B = nS, they minimize a conservative closed-form surrogate of the bound to derive the optimal allocation rule. The theoretical results are validated with PennyLane simulations using 2-qubit and 4-qubit variational quantum circuits on nine synthetic binary classification benchmarks.
AI.result: The derived allocation rule is n* = 2√(2dB/log(2B/δ)) and S* = B/n*, achieving a worst-case rate of B^(-1/4). In all tested configurations (2-qubit and 4-qubit circuits on nine benchmarks), the one-sided empirical generalization gap remains below the theoretical bound, confirming the validity of the conservative guarantee.
AI.conclusion: This work provides a conservative statistical guideline for allocating measurement budgets in finite-shot evaluation and pre-experimental planning for near-term quantum learning systems. It complements hardware-level scheduling and circuit-design considerations. The guarantee applies to the full class of binary quantum measurements. Extending the guarantee to fully adaptive shot-noisy training remains an open problem.

title: SHIFT-LLM: Distribution Shift Correction in Depth-Pruned LLMs
summary: Depth pruning removes entire Transformer blocks to reduce the inference cost of large language models, but disrupts the hidden-state distributions expected by downstream layers, leading to significant accuracy loss. We introduce SHIFT-LLM, a training-free post-pruning correction framework that inserts a Linear Residual Adapter (LRA) at each pruning site. Each LRA preserves the identity pathway of the original residual block and adds a lightweight affine residual correction. This correction is calibrated via closed-form least-squares regression on a small held-out set, without gradient computation, to approximate the missing residual update produced by the pruned block. Together with the preserved identity pathway, the resulting LRA output approximates the hidden state produced by the original block, thereby mitigating the distributional mismatch introduced by layer removal while avoiding the expensive attention and feed-forward computations of the removed blocks. The resulting LRAs support low-rank factorization and exact merging across consecutive pruned layers for additional compression, and combine naturally with parameter-efficient fine-tuning for further recovery beyond fine-tuning the pruned model alone. Experiments on five model families, six layer-selection criteria, and seven zero-shot benchmarks show that SHIFT-LLM consistently recovers accuracy lost to depth pruning across most configurations, achieving gains up to +15.7 points on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct while requiring only a few hundred calibration samples and no gradient computation.

AI.tldr: SHIFT-LLM is a training-free post-pruning correction framework that inserts Linear Residual Adapters (LRAs) at each pruning site to recover accuracy lost from depth pruning in large language models. It uses closed-form least-squares regression on a small calibration set to approximate the missing residual update, achieving up to +15.7 points accuracy recovery on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct without gradient computation.
AI.motivation: Depth pruning removes entire Transformer blocks to reduce inference cost, but this disrupts the hidden-state distributions expected by downstream layers, leading to significant accuracy loss. Existing methods either require expensive retraining or fail to address the distributional mismatch caused by layer removal.
AI.method: SHIFT-LLM inserts a Linear Residual Adapter (LRA) at each pruning site, consisting of (1) a preserved identity pathway maintaining the original residual connection, and (2) a lightweight affine residual correction. The correction is calibrated via closed-form least-squares regression on a small held-out set (few hundred samples) without gradient computation. The method supports low-rank factorization and exact merging across consecutive pruned layers, and can combine with parameter-efficient fine-tuning.
AI.result: Experiments across five model families, six layer-selection criteria, and seven zero-shot benchmarks show consistent accuracy recovery. SHIFT-LLM achieves gains up to +15.7 points on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct while requiring only a few hundred calibration samples and no gradient computation.
AI.conclusion: SHIFT-LLM provides an effective training-free solution for recovering accuracy lost to depth pruning in LLMs. By approximating the missing residual updates through lightweight LRAs calibrated via closed-form regression, it successfully mitigates distributional mismatch with minimal computational overhead. The method is versatile, supporting additional compression techniques and combination with parameter-efficient fine-tuning.

title: When Does Frequency Decomposition Benefit Physics-Informed Neural Networks? A Preliminary Ablation Study
summary: Partial differential equations (PDEs) often have high-frequency and multi-scale features that neural networks struggle to approximate. Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) build the governing equations directly into training, but suffer from spectral bias: they learn low-frequency components faster than high-frequency ones. Techniques such as Fourier feature embeddings and sinusoidal activations address this, but most studies assume they help across the board without checking which spectral regimes actually benefit. We introduce a dual-branch, spectrally-gated architecture (DBSG-PINN) that splits low- and high-frequency components into separate subnetworks joined by an adaptive gate, and use it to run a partially controlled ablation of frequency decomposition and spectral routing. We test this on five one-dimensional benchmark PDEs, ranging from smooth, single-scale problems to oscillatory, multi-scale ones. Frequency decomposition helps most on the spectrally complex benchmarks, cutting relative $L_2$ error by up to $59.2\%$ on a multimodal wave problem, but gives little benefit on smoother PDEs. On one benchmark (1D Wave), it performs substantially worse than a simpler fixed-combination variant. The gate's benefit scales with how spectrally rich the target solution is: the full model's advantage over the ablations is largest on multi-scale benchmarks and smallest (or negative) on single-scale ones, consistent with the gate exploiting frequency structure rather than acting as noise,though we do not directly visualize or quantify its spatial activations in this study. All results come from a single training seed across five 1D benchmarks, so we present this as an exploratory study meant to raise questions rather than answer them, and outline the additional seeds and benchmarks needed to test whether the pattern holds.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces DBSG-PINN, a dual-branch spectrally-gated architecture that splits low- and high-frequency components into separate subnetworks with an adaptive gate to address spectral bias in Physics-Informed Neural Networks. Testing on 5 1D benchmark PDEs shows frequency decomposition reduces error by up to 59.2% on multi-scale problems but provides little benefit on smoother PDEs, with the gate's advantage scaling with spectral complexity.
AI.motivation: PINNs suffer from spectral bias - they learn low-frequency components faster than high-frequency ones. While Fourier feature embeddings and sinusoidal activations exist, there hasn't been systematic analysis of which spectral regimes actually benefit from these techniques. The authors aimed to develop an architecture that can adaptively handle different frequency components and quantify when frequency decomposition actually helps.
AI.method: The proposed DBSG-PINN architecture splits the network into two subnetworks: one for low-frequency and one for high-frequency components, joined by an adaptive gate mechanism. The authors conducted a partially controlled ablation study varying frequency decomposition and spectral routing across five 1D benchmark PDEs ranging from smooth, single-scale to oscillatory, multi-scale problems.
AI.result: Frequency decomposition provides the largest benefit on spectrally complex benchmarks, reducing relative L2 error by up to 59.2% on a multimodal wave problem. However, it provides minimal benefit on smoother PDEs. On the 1D Wave benchmark specifically, the full model performs substantially worse than a simpler fixed-combination variant. The gate's benefit scales with spectral richness - the advantage is largest on multi-scale benchmarks and smallest/negative on single-scale ones.
AI.conclusion: The study concludes that frequency decomposition is most beneficial for spectrally complex PDEs but may hurt performance on simpler problems. The adaptive gate exploits frequency structure rather than acting as noise. Limitations include using only a single training seed across five benchmarks, making this an exploratory study meant to raise questions rather than provide definitive answers. The authors outline needed follow-up work including additional seeds and benchmarks.

title: SPECMINE: A Large-Scale Corpus of Spec-Driven Development Artifacts
summary: Spec-Driven Development (SDD) is a fast-emerging practice in which a structured natural-language specification, written by a developer, or (more often) drafted by an AI tool and then curated by the developer, drives an AI coding agent's implementation. A wave of tooling (GitHub Spec Kit [3], OpenSpec [4], AWS Kiro [5], and dozens of others) has appeared since 2025, yet the artifacts these tools produce have never been studied at scale. We present SPECMINE, a corpus that captures SDD in public GitHub repositories through two censuses: a broad census of spec.md/specs.md files covering most tools (470,795 files across 73,030 repositories, attributed to 17 named tools), and a Kiro census of its distinct requirements/design/tasks layout (98,574 files across 12,910 repositories). Each spec is enriched with full repository metadata, complete commit history, and parsed document structure. How a spec becomes code is itself an open question, so for 11 tools we sweep every pull request that touches a spec in their repositories with at least ten stars, capturing 5,992 such PRs across 581 repositories with their changesets. That makes the simplest workflow, spec and implementation changing together in one PR, directly observable, and a census-wide index of 2,421,323 typed references (1.28M to code files, 863k to sibling documents, 152k to PRs, 62k refs, 43k branches, 22k issues) gives a second, independent link from spec to code. SPECMINE lets the community study, for the first time, how software is specified in the age of AI agents.

AI.tldr: SPECMINE is the first large-scale corpus studying Spec-Driven Development (SDD) in public GitHub repositories, capturing 470,795 spec files across 73,030 repositories attributed to 17 tools, along with PR data and 2.4M+ typed references linking specifications to code.
AI.motivation: Spec-Driven Development (SDD) is a fast-emerging practice where natural-language specifications drive AI coding agents, but the artifacts produced by SDD tools have never been studied at scale. The research addresses the open question of how specs become code.
AI.method: Two-pronged approach: (1) Broad census of spec.md/specs.md files (470,795 files, 73,030 repos, 17 tools) plus Kiro-specific census (98,574 files, 12,910 repos); (2) Analysis of 5,992 PRs across 581 repos with at least 10 stars, plus a census-wide index of 2,421,323 typed references linking specs to code files, documents, PRs, branches, and issues.
AI.result: Created SPECMINE corpus with enriched data: full repository metadata, complete commit history, parsed document structure, and comprehensive reference linking. Captured the simplest SDD workflow (spec + implementation in one PR) for direct observation.
AI.conclusion: SPECMINE enables the first systematic study of how software is specified in the AI agent era, providing a foundational resource for understanding SDD practices at scale.

title: Natural Language Input, Semantic Track Representation, and LLM Inference: Making the Maritime Information Exchange Model Tractable
summary: We describe a practical architecture for making the Maritime Information Exchange Model (MIEM) and the broader Rich Semantic Track model tractable using current large language model (LLM) technology. The barrier to adoption of semantic track models in defense and law enforcement has been the requirement that operators learn formal ontology languages and manually encode observations as typed logical assertions. We propose eliminating this barrier entirely: operators contribute observations in natural language; an LLM translates these into typed Semantic Assertion Records (SARs), which are named case frames that capture n-ary relations in a single compact structure; a knowledge graph accumulates the SARs; and a second LLM pass performs inference, anomaly detection, and hypothesis ranking over the graph. We work through two detailed examples (a 9/11-era pre-attack indicator scenario and a maritime cargo inspection scenario) showing the full pipeline from natural language input to SAR representation to inference output. We argue that this architecture makes the Track Model and MIEM immediately deployable with current technology, establishes prior art against proprietary enclosure of the approach, and grounds the method in a theoretical framework connecting semantic track representations to neural manifold geometry.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a practical LLM-based architecture to make semantic track models (MIEM) tractable for defense and law enforcement by eliminating the need for operators to learn formal ontology languages, using natural language input converted to Semantic Assertion Records (SARs) with dual LLM passes for translation and inference.
AI.motivation: The barrier to adoption of semantic track models in defense and law enforcement is the requirement that operators learn formal ontology languages and manually encode observations as typed logical assertions, making such systems impractical for real-world deployment.
AI.method: Operators contribute observations in natural language; an LLM translates these into typed Semantic Assertion Records (SARs) which capture n-ary relations in a compact structure; a knowledge graph accumulates the SARs; a second LLM pass performs inference, anomaly detection, and hypothesis ranking over the graph.
AI.result: Two detailed examples demonstrate the full pipeline: a 9/11-era pre-attack indicator scenario and a maritime cargo inspection scenario, showing the progression from natural language input to SAR representation to inference output.
AI.conclusion: This architecture makes the Track Model and MIEM immediately deployable with current technology, establishes prior art against proprietary enclosure, and grounds the method in a theoretical framework connecting semantic track representations to neural manifold geometry.

title: RefLAM: A Reference-Grounded Line Annotation Pipeline for Historical Arabic Manuscripts
summary: Existing approaches to building line-level Arabic handwritten-text-recognition (HTR) training data either rely on fully manual annotation, which does not scale, or on automatic OCR-to-reference alignment methods not yet extended to multi-script, two-zone (main-plus-margin) manuscript layouts with a provable correctness guarantee. We present RefLAM (Reference-grounded Line Annotation for Manuscripts), a pipeline converting manuscript page images and clean transcriptions into validated, line-level ground truth without sacrificing human oversight. RefLAM couples a deep-learning page-segmentation model with a multimodal large language model (MLLM) for structured OCR and a diacritic-agnostic fuzzy alignment engine that grounds each OCR line in a contiguous span of the reference text, with a character-level confidence score in $[0,100]$. A perfect score is provably equivalent to character-for-character identity of the normalised strings (the Confidence-100 rule), verified with no counterexample across the released corpus. A reviewer can thus trust a perfect score, confirming most lines at a glance rather than retyping them, so annotation becomes triaged, with attention concentrated on uncertain alignments. Across 7 fully page-validated books we measured a 75$\times$ throughput gain over manual annotation (3,000 vs. 40 lines/hr); applying the same guarantee to 7 further books, we retained 16,533 confidence-100 main-text lines within one week, excluding sub-100 lines rather than manually correcting them. Using RefLAM, we release AraMS-28k: 14 historical Arabic manuscript books, 3,043 pages, and 27,971 main-text and 629 margin-line annotations with bounding boxes, layout labels, and insertion anchors for 191 margin entries (30.4%). We also finetune Muharaf-pretrained baselines (including HATFormer) on AraMS-28k and report CER results confirming its practical utility for downstream HTR training.

AI.tldr: RefLAM is a pipeline for creating validated line-level Arabic handwritten text recognition (HTR) training data from manuscript page images and clean transcriptions, achieving 75× speedup over manual annotation while providing provable correctness guarantees through a confidence scoring system.
AI.motivation: Existing approaches to building Arabic HTR training data either rely on time-consuming manual annotation or automatic OCR-to-reference alignment methods that cannot handle multi-script, two-zone (main-plus-margin) manuscript layouts with correctness guarantees.
AI.method: RefLAM combines three components: (1) a deep-learning page-segmentation model, (2) a multimodal large language model (MLLM) for structured OCR, and (3) a diacritic-agnostic fuzzy alignment engine that assigns character-level confidence scores [0,100]. The Confidence-100 rule guarantees that a perfect score equals character-for-character identity of normalized strings, verified across the released corpus.
AI.result: 75× throughput gain over manual annotation (3,000 vs. 40 lines/hr); retained 16,533 confidence-100 main-text lines from 7 additional books within one week. Released AraMS-28k: 14 historical Arabic manuscript books, 3,043 pages, 27,971 main-text and 629 margin-line annotations with bounding boxes, layout labels, and insertion anchors for 191 margin entries (30.4%). Fine-tuned Muharaf-pretrained baselines (including HATFormer) on AraMS-28k confirmed practical utility for downstream HTR training.
AI.conclusion: RefLAM enables efficient, validated line-level annotation of Arabic manuscripts with provable correctness guarantees, releasing the largest dataset AraMS-28k for Arabic HTR training and demonstrating significant throughput improvements while maintaining quality through automated triage of uncertain alignments.

title: FAMPWQ: Fisher Information-based Adaptive Mixed Precision Weight Quantization for Effective LLM Inference
summary: Recent years have witnessed remarkable achievements of Large Language Models (LLMs) in multiple domains, while the excessive resource requirements of LLMs hinder the deployment on resource-constrained devices. Although model quantization stands out as an effective approach, conventional quantization approaches typically incur severe performance degradation due to uniform bit-width or simple heuristic sensitivity evaluation. In this paper, we propose a novel Fisher information-based Adaptive Mixed Precision Weight Quantization approach, i.e., FAMPWQ, which performs layer-adaptive weight quantization for effective LLM inference on commodity GPUs. First, we propose a system model with a novel Fisher information metric to measure the layer-wise sensitivity to quantization. Second, we propose a reinforcement learning-based bit-width allocator in FAMPWQ, which generates an adaptive bit-width allocation strategy based on the Fisher information sensitivity metric. Extensive experiments on 7 models and 5 benchmarks demonstrate that FAMPWQ significantly outperforms 7 baseline approaches in terms of PPL (up to 3.39 smaller), accuracy (up to 6.87% higher), and LLM-as-a-judge comparison (up to 76% win rate).

AI.tldr: FAMPWQ is a novel Fisher information-based adaptive mixed precision weight quantization method for efficient LLM inference. It uses Fisher information to measure layer-wise quantization sensitivity and employs reinforcement learning for adaptive bit-width allocation, significantly outperforming 7 baseline approaches across 7 models and 5 benchmarks.
AI.motivation: The motivation stems from the challenge that LLMs require excessive computational resources, hindering deployment on resource-constrained devices. Existing quantization methods suffer from severe performance degradation due to uniform bit-width allocation or simplistic sensitivity evaluation approaches.
AI.method: The paper proposes two key components: (1) A system model with a novel Fisher information metric to measure layer-wise sensitivity to quantization, and (2) A reinforcement learning-based bit-width allocator that generates adaptive bit-width allocation strategies based on the Fisher information sensitivity metric.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on 7 models and 5 benchmarks demonstrate significant improvements: PPL reduced by up to 3.39x, accuracy improved by up to 6.87%, and LLM-as-a-judge comparison achieved up to 76% win rate compared to 7 baseline approaches.
AI.conclusion: The proposed FAMPWQ approach effectively performs layer-adaptive weight quantization for LLM inference on commodity GPUs, achieving superior performance through Fisher information-based sensitivity measurement and reinforcement learning-based bit-width allocation.

title: Cooperative Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Adaptive Aggregation in Semi-Supervised Federated Learning with non-IID Data
comment: 5 pages, 4 figures, ICASSP 2026 - 2026 IEEE International Conference on Acoustics, Speech and Signal Processing (ICASSP)
summary: Federated Learning (FL) enables distributed training of machine learning models while preserving data privacy. However, FL struggles with heterogeneous, non-IID client data distributions, resulting in sub-optimal and biased global models. In this paper, we propose pFedMARL, a novel approach leveraging Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) with Twin Delayed Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (TD3) to dynamically adapt aggregation strategies in FL settings. Our method employs a server-side agent adjusting client contributions to optimize global model robustness and client-side agents balancing global and local updates to personalize models effectively without pre-training. We demonstrate superior performance of pFedMARL for training a semi-supervised audio spectrogram transformer, matching or outperforming FedAvg, Ditto, and local training approaches across multiple non-IID scenarios and in the presence of adversarial clients. Our results indicate that pFedMARL actively improves accuracy, robustness, and fairness, making it suitable for real-world deployments.

AI.tldr: pFedMARL uses Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning with TD3 to dynamically adapt federated learning aggregation strategies, addressing non-IID data heterogeneity and adversarial clients for training a semi-supervised audio spectrogram transformer.
AI.motivation: Federated Learning struggles with heterogeneous, non-IID client data distributions, resulting in sub-optimal and biased global models. Existing methods fail to effectively handle varying data distributions across clients.
AI.method: pFedMARL employs a server-side agent using Twin Delayed Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (TD3) to dynamically adjust client contributions for optimizing global model robustness, while client-side agents balance global and local updates to personalize models without pre-training.
AI.result: pFedMARL demonstrates superior performance, matching or outperforming FedAvg, Ditto, and local training approaches across multiple non-IID scenarios and in the presence of adversarial clients, actively improving accuracy, robustness, and fairness.
AI.conclusion: pFedMARL effectively addresses non-IID data heterogeneity in federated learning through dynamic MARL-based aggregation, making it suitable for real-world deployments requiring robust and fair model training.

title: A Few Pages of Markdown: Committed AI Configuration and Lower Quality Cost after Coding-Agent Adoption
summary: Coding agents increase development velocity but also technical debt. Prior work reports only average effects across adopters, hiding wide differences between teams. We introduce RAMP (Repository AI Maturity Profile), a four-level cumulative maturity model grounded in version-controlled artifacts that teams commit to configure AI tools. RAMP runs from behavioral rules and coding standards through named agent definitions to multi-agent orchestration, with observed practice concentrated in the first three levels. Across 441 repositories the levels behave as a cumulative scale, and independent human annotation reproduces RAMP's repository-level labels on 97% of a held-out sample. Adoption is cumulative, forward-only, and set-and-forget: 73.8% of artifacts are committed once and never modified. Re-estimating an existing agent-adoption panel within each stratum, agents accelerate development regardless of maturity (28-38% more commits), but quality diverges: among agent-first repositories, where the contrast is identified, those without committed AI configuration show roughly twice the increase in cognitive complexity (+53% versus +27%) and 1.7x the increase in static-analysis warnings. Because maturity is observational, correlated engineering discipline or model capability may explain part of the gap; we present these findings as hypothesis-generating and release RAMP as a reusable instrument.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces RAMP, a four-level maturity model for AI coding tool adoption in software repositories. The study analyzes 441 repositories to show that agents increase development velocity (28-38% more commits) across all maturity levels, but quality outcomes diverge significantly: repositories without committed AI configuration show roughly twice the increase in cognitive complexity (+53% vs +27%) and 1.7x more static-analysis warnings compared to those with mature configurations.
AI.motivation: Prior research on AI coding agents reports only average effects across adopters, which masks substantial variation between teams. The authors seek to understand why some teams benefit more than others and identify factors that distinguish high-performing adopters from those accumulating technical debt.
AI.method: The authors developed RAMP (Repository AI Maturity Profile), a cumulative four-level maturity model based on version-controlled artifacts that teams commit to configure AI tools. They analyzed 441 repositories, validated the model through independent human annotation (97% agreement on held-out sample), and used a panel study design to re-estimate agent adoption effects within each maturity stratum.
AI.result: Key findings: (1) RAMP levels behave as a cumulative scale across 441 repositories; (2) 73.8% of AI configuration artifacts are committed once and never modified (set-and-forget pattern); (3) Agents accelerate development regardless of maturity level (28-38% more commits); (4) Quality diverges: agent-first repositories without committed AI configuration show ~2x the cognitive complexity increase (+53% vs +27%) and 1.7x more static-analysis warnings.
AI.conclusion: The study presents a reusable instrument (RAMP) for measuring AI coding tool adoption maturity. The findings suggest that committed AI configuration—reflecting engineering discipline—may help mitigate quality degradation from agent adoption. The authors acknowledge that correlated engineering discipline or model capability may partially explain the gap, presenting these results as hypothesis-generating rather than causal.

title: Same-Player Verification for Account Consistency in Counter-Strike 2
comment: 10 pages, 2 figures, 8 tables. Submitted to IEEE for possible publication
summary: In competitive first-person shooter (FPS) games such as Counter-Strike 2 (CS2), account-integrity review often asks whether an account's recent behavior remains consistent with its historical operator. This consistency question arises in cases such as temporary substitution, rank boosting, and high-skill players using lower-ranked accounts, where manual review requires comparing a current match against multiple historical matches. We formulate this review task as same-player verification: we encode the behavioral trajectory of a single player in a match replay (demo) as a demo-player behavioral fingerprint, and train a model to judge whether two behavioral observations come from the same real player. Grounded in CS2 game understanding, the fingerprints cover crosshair control, movement-stop-fire coordination, economy/buy, combat/engagement, and temporal rhythm. From 1,330 CS2 demos we extract 13,300 demo-player observations, and sample 663,590 same/different pairs from an 88.4M candidate-pair space for supervised training and evaluation. The final pairwise model reaches an average ROC AUC of 0.931 and achieves 0.722 different-player recall at 95% precision. Feature analysis shows that the strongest identity signals come from low-level operations, especially crosshair control, firing rhythm, and movement-stop-fire coordination, indicating that stable low-level mechanical habits are more informative for this verification task than single-match performance outcomes. In the account-history aggregation evaluation, increasing history depth raises AUC from the K=1 single-pair baseline of 0.931 to 0.986 at K=10. These results show that CS2 demo behavior can support supervised same-player verification and account-level identity-consistency modeling through multi-demo history aggregation.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses same-player verification in CS2 by training a model to compare behavioral fingerprints extracted from match replays. The model achieves 0.931 ROC AUC for pairwise verification and 0.986 AUC when aggregating 10 historical matches, demonstrating that low-level mechanical habits (crosshair control, firing rhythm) are stronger identity signals than high-level performance outcomes.
AI.motivation: In competitive FPS games like CS2, account integrity review needs to verify whether an account's recent behavior matches its historical operator. This arises in cases of temporary substitution, rank boosting, or high-skill players using lower-ranked accounts. Manual review is labor-intensive, requiring comparison of current matches against multiple historical matches.
AI.method: The authors formulate this as a same-player verification task. They extract behavioral fingerprints from CS2 match replays (demos) covering five dimensions: crosshair control, movement-stop-fire coordination, economy/buy, combat/engagement, and temporal rhythm. From 1,330 CS2 demos, they extract 13,300 demo-player observations and sample 663,590 same/different pairs for supervised training. A pairwise model is trained to judge whether two behavioral observations come from the same real player.
AI.result: The final pairwise model achieves: (1) ROC AUC of 0.931; (2) 0.722 different-player recall at 95% precision. Feature analysis reveals that low-level operations (crosshair control, firing rhythm, movement-stop-fire coordination) are the strongest identity signals. In account-history aggregation, increasing history depth raises AUC from 0.931 (K=1) to 0.986 (K=10).
AI.conclusion: CS2 demo behavior can support supervised same-player verification and account-level identity-consistency modeling through multi-demo history aggregation. Stable low-level mechanical habits are more informative for player verification than single-match performance outcomes.

title: Can You Trust Frozen Hematology Foundation Models under Acquisition Shift?
comment: Accepted at the HemaRAI 2026 workshop (MICCAI 2026 satellite event), oral presentation; to appear in MICCAI 2026 Satellite Events, LNCS, Springer. 25 pages (10 main incl. references + 15 supplementary), 4 figures. Project page: https://jaishrm07.github.io/hematology-fm-robustness/
summary: Frozen hematology foundation-model (FM) embeddings reach near-saturated in-domain white-blood-cell (WBC) accuracy, but clinical deployment demands reliability across scanners, sites, stains and preparation pipelines. We audit 15 frozen encoders (hematology, pathology, and general vision) across four public single-cell acquisition domains along two axes: accuracy robustness and calibration. In-domain linear-probe macro-F1 is saturated (0.98-0.997), yet cross-dataset macro-F1 drops 34-72% and rankings re-order: DinoBloom-L, the in-domain best, falls to 10th of 15 on the most-shifted target (MLL23) at the benchmark's shared 224-px input, behind RedDino and several general and pathology encoders. Rank transfer is probe-dependent: 1-NN retrieval is more stable on average than a source-fitted linear head (median $ρ$ 0.65 vs 0.45), but neither probe universally predicts target robustness. Calibration also collapses: source-trained probes are nearly calibrated in-domain (expected calibration error, ECE, 0.004) but confidently wrong off-domain (ECE 0.35), and source-fitted temperature scaling transfers poorly. We further audit pretraining exposure and identify MLL23 as DinoBloom's internal cohort; because DinoBloom's only held-out dataset is also our source domain, this benchmark cannot isolate exposure from scanner-associated shift. Label-free adaptation and marginal-entropy-based model selection appear safe under balanced evaluation but fail under realistic WBC class-prior shift. Class-Balanced Re-standardization (CBR), a training-free pseudo-label-balanced feature normalization, improves all evaluated target-prior scenario means and partially improves calibration, although encoder-level exceptions and residual miscalibration remain. Hematology FM benchmarks must therefore jointly audit accuracy, calibration, exposure, and class-prior robustness.

AI.tldr: This paper audits 15 frozen hematology, pathology, and general vision foundation models across four public single-cell acquisition domains, finding that while in-domain accuracy is saturated (0.98-0.997), cross-dataset accuracy drops 34-72% and calibration collapses off-domain (ECE 0.004 to 0.35). The study identifies issues with pretraining exposure (MLL23 appears in DinoBloom's training data) and shows that Class-Balanced Re-standardization (CBR) partially improves results but doesn't fully solve robustness issues.
AI.motivation: While frozen hematology foundation-model embeddings achieve near-saturated in-domain WBC accuracy, clinical deployment requires reliability across scanners, sites, stains, and preparation pipelines. The authors aimed to audit accuracy robustness and calibration across different acquisition domains.
AI.method: The study evaluated 15 frozen encoders (hematology, pathology, and general vision) across four public single-cell acquisition domains using two evaluation axes: accuracy robustness and calibration. Methods included linear-probe and 1-NN retrieval evaluation, assessment of source-fitted temperature scaling, auditing of pretraining exposure, and evaluation of label-free adaptation, marginal-entropy-based model selection, and Class-Balanced Re-standardization (CBR).
AI.result: In-domain linear-probe macro-F1 reached 0.98-0.997, but cross-dataset macro-F1 dropped 34-72% with reordered rankings. DinoBloom-L fell from 1st to 10th on MLL23. 1-NN retrieval was more stable than linear heads (median ρ 0.65 vs 0.45). Calibration collapsed off-domain (ECE 0.004 in-domain to 0.35 off-domain). MLL23 was identified as DinoBloom's internal cohort, creating exposure bias. CBR improved most target-prior scenarios but encoder-level exceptions and residual miscalibration remained.
AI.conclusion: Hematology FM benchmarks must jointly audit accuracy, calibration, exposure, and class-prior robustness. Current benchmarks cannot isolate exposure from scanner-associated shift when the only held-out dataset is also the source domain. While CBR helps, it doesn't fully resolve robustness issues.

title: MacroAgent: Regularity-Aware Macro Legalization with LLM-Agent-Designed Contour Algorithms
summary: Macros constitute a large part of the core area in modern very large-scale integration (VLSI) designs. Moreover, macro positions have a significant impact on the final quality of result (QoR), and macro legalization is typically the final step in determining the macro positions. However, existing approaches related to macro legalization either lack robustness or incur substantial computational costs or neglect the regularity between macros. To address these limitations, we introduce MacroAgent. The novel framework is a four-stage approach: clustering, contour generation, template matching, and inter-cluster refinement. We propose leveraging Large Language Models (LLMs) to discover multiple, effective heuristic regularity-aware contour algorithms. This framework successfully generates robust and effective algorithmic solutions for macro legalization. Compared with state-of-the-art macro legalization works, experimental results on TILOS and Chipyard benchmarks demonstrate a 2 to 8 fold improvement in layout regularity, a 3% to 5% reduction in routed wirelength with comparable congestion after global routing, and significantly better robustness with an acceptable runtime. Furthermore, end-to-end evaluation through Cadence Innovus place-and-route confirms that the regularity improvements translate into tangible PPA gains, including 2.9% lower routed wirelength and 68.3% TNS improvement over the DREAMPlace macro legalization baseline; it also achieves 1.8% lower routed wirelength when integrated into the Innovus macro placement flow.
