title: Lowering the Barrier to AI-Driven Inspection: A No-Code Workflow for Automated Structural Defect Detection
comment: 11 pages, 7 figures. Accepted to ASME SMASIS 2026 (paper SMASIS2026-190654). Software available at https://github.com/michaelholm6/YOLOEZ
summary:
Structural health monitoring (SHM) is essential in modern engineering, providing data for condition-based maintenance, lifecycle assessment, and predictive decision-making. Traditionally, SHM relied on visual inspection to detect defects such as cracks and deformations. Early computer vision (CV) methods, including thresholding, edge detection, and handcrafted features, aimed to automate this process but were highly sensitive to noise, imaging variations, and multiscale defects, limiting their reliability.
  Recent advances in machine learning, particularly convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and You Only Look Once (YOLO), have improved defect detection accuracy and enabled real-time analysis. However, adoption in SHM remains limited due to technical barriers such as data labeling, model training, and deployment, which typically require programming expertise.
  To address this gap, we introduce YOLOEZ, an open-source, GUI-based tool for end-to-end YOLO model application. YOLOEZ integrates data labeling, training, and inference into a single interface, enabling high-performance model development without code while supporting reproducible workflows.
  Evaluation against existing software and classical image processing demonstrates that YOLOEZ not only outperforms traditional methods across most detection metrics, but also lowers adoption barriers present in other modern CV tools. By combining accuracy with accessibility, YOLOEZ facilitates wider use of AI-driven monitoring for predictive maintenance, digital twins, and intelligent structural systems.

AI.tldr: YOLOEZ is an open-source, GUI-based tool that integrates data labeling, training, and inference for YOLO-based defect detection in structural health monitoring, enabling code-free high-performance model development while outperforming traditional methods and lowering adoption barriers.
AI.motivation: Traditional SHM relied on visual inspection, while early computer vision methods were highly sensitive to noise and imaging variations. Although CNNs and YOLO have improved defect detection, adoption remains limited due to technical barriers requiring programming expertise in data labeling, model training, and deployment.
AI.method: YOLOEZ integrates data labeling, training, and inference into a single GUI interface, enabling end-to-end YOLO model application without code while supporting reproducible workflows.
AI.result: YOLOEZ outperforms traditional methods across most detection metrics and lowers adoption barriers present in other modern CV tools.
AI.conclusion: YOLOEZ facilitates wider use of AI-driven monitoring for predictive maintenance, digital twins, and intelligent structural systems by combining accuracy with accessibility.

title: AFDBench: A Reasoning-First AI Scientist for NationalWeather Service Forecast Discussions
summary: Large language models (LLMs) hallucinate numerical values when generating high-stakes meteorological text, posing risks for weather communication. We present AFDBench, an AI meteorologist that generates professional Area Forecast Discussions (AFDs) by reasoning through structured AI weather forecast data from Google's WeatherNext 2. We introduce AFDBench, the first benchmark for evaluating generative meteorological reasoning, comprising 7,732 expert written discussions from 13 National Weather Service (NWS) offices paired with real AI weather forecast inputs, and three complementary metrics: Met-Align (numerical accuracy), Style-Align (professional dialect adherence), and Input-Grounding (fidelity to source weather data). Zero-shot evaluations reveal that open-source LLMs achieve low Style-Align (~0.33) and moderate Input-Grounding (~0.88), failing to write in the professional NWS register or faithfully use their input data. We apply Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with domain-specific rewards targeting temperature accuracy, synoptic correctness, and format compliance. On 1,033 held-out samples from two unseen NWS offices, GRPO nearly doubles Style-Align from 0.318 to 0.619 and improves Input-Grounding from 0.881 to 0.940, demonstrating that reinforcement learning teaches a 7B-parameter model to write like a professional meteorologist and faithfully interpret AI weather data.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses hallucination problems in LLMs when generating high-stakes meteorological forecasts. The authors present AFDBench, a benchmark and AI system for generating professional Area Forecast Discussions (AFDs) using Google's WeatherNext 2 data. They introduce three evaluation metrics (Met-Align, Style-Align, Input-Grounding) and use Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) to train a 7B-parameter model, achieving near-doubling of Style-Align (0.318 to 0.619) and improved Input-Grounding (0.881 to 0.940).
AI.motivation: Large language models hallucinate numerical values when generating high-stakes meteorological text, posing significant risks for weather communication and public safety. Existing LLMs fail to write in the professional NWS register or faithfully use their input weather data.
AI.method: The authors developed AFDBench, the first benchmark for evaluating generative meteorological reasoning, comprising 7,732 expert-written discussions from 13 NWS offices paired with AI weather forecast inputs. They applied Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with domain-specific rewards targeting temperature accuracy, synoptic correctness, and format compliance. Zero-shot evaluations were conducted on open-source LLMs, followed by fine-tuning on 1,033 held-out samples from two unseen NWS offices.
AI.result: Zero-shot evaluations revealed that open-source LLMs achieve low Style-Align (~0.33) and moderate Input-Grounding (~0.88). After GRPO training, Style-Align nearly doubled from 0.318 to 0.619 and Input-Grounding improved from 0.881 to 0.940, demonstrating that reinforcement learning can teach a 7B-parameter model to write like a professional meteorologist and faithfully interpret AI weather data.
AI.conclusion: Reinforcement learning through GRPO with domain-specific rewards effectively trains LLMs to generate professional meteorological text that adheres to NWS register and accurately grounds predictions in source weather data, significantly reducing hallucination risks in high-stakes weather communication.

title: RotDroid: Cross-Orientation State Equivalence Testing for Detecting GUI Rotation Bugs in Android Apps
summary: Screen rotation is a fundamental interaction in Android applications, but it often introduces non-crashing functional failures (NCFs), such as layout inconsistencies and state loss, which are difficult to detect automatically. A key challenge is the lack of effective test oracles for checking cross-orientation state equivalence between portrait and landscape views. We propose RotDroid, a testing framework for detecting GUI rotation bugs via cross-orientation state equivalence. RotDroid generates and mutates State-Preserving action Sequences (SPS) to construct semantically equivalent GUI states across orientations. To support reliable oracle checking, we build RotBench, a dataset of paired portrait-landscape GUI states, and develop RotVL, a vision-language model fine-tuned for equivalence checking. Experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets show that RotVL outperforms state-of-the-art models, and RotDroid detects more rotation-induced failures than existing techniques under equal budgets. In large-scale studies on open- and closed-source apps, RotDroid reports 94 previously unknown bugs, with 47 confirmed or fixed by developers, demonstrating its practical effectiveness.

AI.tldr: RotDroid is a testing framework that detects GUI rotation bugs in Android apps by checking cross-orientation state equivalence between portrait and landscape views, using generated State-Preserving action Sequences (SPS) and a fine-tuned vision-language model (RotVL).
AI.motivation: Screen rotation in Android apps frequently causes non-crashing functional failures (NCFs) like layout inconsistencies and state loss, yet these bugs are difficult to detect automatically due to the lack of effective test oracles for verifying cross-orientation state equivalence.
AI.method: RotDroid generates and mutates State-Preserving action Sequences (SPS) to construct semantically equivalent GUI states across portrait and landscape orientations. It leverages RotBench, a curated dataset of paired portrait-landscape GUI states, to fine-tune RotVL—a vision-language model specifically designed for equivalence checking.
AI.result: RotVL outperforms state-of-the-art models on equivalence checking tasks. RotDroid detects more rotation-induced failures than existing techniques under equal budgets. In large-scale studies on both open- and closed-source apps, RotDroid identified 94 previously unknown bugs, with 47 confirmed or fixed by developers.
AI.conclusion: The combination of SPS-based test generation and the RotVL oracle effectively addresses the challenge of detecting rotation-induced NCFs in Android applications, demonstrating practical effectiveness through real-world bug discovery and developer confirmation.

title: Solving Robust POMDPs with Omega-regular Objectives via Partially Observable Stochastic Games
summary: Robust POMDPs (RPOMDPs) generalize classical POMDPs to the setting where exact transition probabilities are not known -- rather, they are only known to belong to some uncertainty set of values. In this work, we study the problem of solving RPOMDPs with general omega-regular objectives, which subsume a broad class of objectives such as reachability, safety, and linear temporal logic (LTL) objectives. We show that, for (s,a)-rectangular RPOMDPs with polytopic uncertainty sets, the problem of solving RPOMDPs under omega-regular objectives can be reduced to solving partially observable stochastic games (POSGs) under omega-regular objectives. Moreover, we show for the first time that reductions can be constructed in both directions, establishing the semantic equivalence between (s,a)-rectangular RPOMDPs with polytopic uncertainty sets and POSGs. This allows us to derive a range of new computational complexity results, including both upper and lower complexity bounds, on solving RPOMDPs with different omega-regular objectives. As a corollary, we also derive new computational complexity results for RMDPs.

AI.tldr: This paper establishes the computational complexity of solving Robust POMDPs (RPOMDPs) with omega-regular objectives by showing equivalence to Partially Observable Stochastic Games (POSGs), enabling derivation of both upper and lower complexity bounds.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to address the problem of solving RPOMDPs where transition probabilities are uncertain (known only to belong to some uncertainty set), which generalizes classical POMDPs. The goal is to handle general omega-regular objectives (including reachability, safety, and LTL) which subsume many practical specifications.
AI.method: The method involves constructing reductions in both directions between (s,a)-rectangular RPOMDPs with polytopic uncertainty sets and POSGs under omega-regular objectives. This establishes semantic equivalence between these two problem classes.
AI.result: The key results include: (1) reduction of RPOMDPs with omega-regular objectives to POSGs under omega-regular objectives for (s,a)-rectangular RPOMDPs with polytopic uncertainty sets; (2) bidirectional reductions establishing semantic equivalence; (3) derivation of new computational complexity bounds (both upper and lower) for solving RPOMDPs with different omega-regular objectives; (4) new complexity results for RMDPs as a corollary.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that (s,a)-rectangular RPOMDPs with polytopic uncertainty sets are semantically equivalent to POSGs, enabling the derivation of a comprehensive range of computational complexity results for RPOMDPs with omega-regular objectives, with implications for RMDPs as well.

title: Lightweight Machine Learning-Driven Monocular Sidewalk Path Extraction for Embedded Micromobility Navigation
summary: Sidewalk-scale path extraction demands perception and planning that run reliably on compact, low-power hardware in cluttered, map-sparse environments. We present a monocular vision pipeline for sidewalk path extraction in micromobility systems that progresses through three design iterations, from a skeleton-graph baseline through distance-transform corridor planning to a lightweight image-space architecture, and provides a systematic comparison of five path-planning methods across both bird's-eye-view (BEV) and image-space domains. A compact SegFormer-B0 student model, trained with a semi-supervised teacher-student framework using OneFormer Swin-L pseudo-labels, achieves a hand-annotated IoU of 0.946 at 11.7 ms per frame, improving over the baseline checkpoint (IoU 0.758, 18.9 ms). In a controlled planner comparison on 32 hand-labeled frames, image-space midpoint planning achieves the lowest lateral center error (14.3 px) at 2.2 ms, a 421x speedup over BEV distance-transform planning (926.8 ms, 65.0 px center error), while maintaining comparable mask-path alignment (98.5% versus 98.6%). A full-video replay across six campus sequences (22,679 frames) confirms that the improved segmentation reduces temporal instability from 1.46% to 0.33% and increases template-path availability from 73.7% to 79.3%. We further show that BEV-only path extraction is fragile in monocular settings: in one profiled run, 99.3% of frames produced no valid BEV path. The final recommended architecture, image-space midpoint primary, image-space distance-transform fallback, and BEV reserved for visualization, runs the full perception-to-path stack in under 50 ms per frame on CPU, making it suitable for embedded pedestrian-speed micromobility systems.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a monocular vision pipeline for sidewalk path extraction in micromobility systems, progressing through three design iterations. The final architecture uses a SegFormer-B0 model achieving 0.946 IoU at 11.7ms, with image-space path planning providing 421x speedup over BEV methods while maintaining comparable accuracy. The recommended system runs under 50ms per frame on CPU, suitable for embedded micromobility applications.
AI.motivation: Sidewalk-scale path extraction for micromobility systems requires perception and planning that can run reliably on compact, low-power hardware in cluttered, map-sparse environments. The research addresses the challenge of enabling autonomous navigation for pedestrian-speed vehicles (e.g., e-scooters) using only monocular vision.
AI.method: The study developed three design iterations: (1) skeleton-graph baseline, (2) distance-transform corridor planning, and (3) lightweight image-space architecture. A compact SegFormer-B0 student model was trained using a semi-supervised teacher-student framework with OneFormer Swin-L pseudo-labels. Five path-planning methods were systematically compared across both bird's-eye-view (BEV) and image-space domains, using 32 hand-labeled frames for controlled comparison and six campus sequences (22,679 frames) for full-video replay.
AI.result: The SegFormer-B0 achieved 0.946 IoU at 11.7 ms/frame, improving over the baseline (0.758 IoU, 18.9 ms). Image-space midpoint planning achieved the lowest lateral center error (14.3 px) at 2.2 ms, representing a 421x speedup over BEV distance-transform planning (926.8 ms, 65.0 px error), while maintaining comparable mask-path alignment (98.5% vs 98.6%). Segmentation improvements reduced temporal instability from 1.46% to 0.33% and increased template-path availability from 73.7% to 79.3%. A critical finding: BEV-only path extraction proved fragile in monocular settings, with 99.3% of frames producing no valid BEV path.
AI.conclusion: The recommended architecture combines image-space midpoint planning as primary, image-space distance-transform as fallback, and BEV reserved for visualization only. This approach runs the full perception-to-path stack in under 50 ms per frame on CPU, making it suitable for embedded pedestrian-speed micromobility systems. The study demonstrates that image-space methods significantly outperform BEV approaches in monocular settings while requiring far less computational resources.

title: Why and When Neural Networks Improve Local Approximation in Optimization
comment: 30 pages, 3 figures, 3 tables. Supplementary material (6 pages) included as an ancillary file. Code and raw results: https://github.com/chengkuobian/neural-surrogates-dfo
summary: Published experience with neural surrogates in derivative-free optimisation is contradictory: the same family of models that cuts the evaluation count of one solver leaves another unchanged, or makes it worse. We show that the contradiction dissolves once three factors are stated, and that these, rather than the fit accuracy a training curve reports, are what delimit when a learned local model pays. Role: a surrogate that proposes candidates the true objective must still approve helps, while one that replaces a gradient the solver depends on hurts. Radius: a model fitted to an optimisation path is reliable only inside a bounded neighbourhood, and its error neither vanishes as that neighbourhood shrinks nor survives its growth. Room: a surrogate can only accelerate progress the base method is still able to make. We formalise radius-aware local generalisation, relate it to the classical fully linear condition, and test each factor with the surrogate class, training pipeline and base method held fixed. Over 117 benchmark instances safeguarded assistance raises the instances solved to high accuracy from 67 to 84 while gradient replacement lowers them to 65; removing the gradient term from the training loss cuts surrogate acceptance from 0.703 to 0.148; and 1000 paired comparisons over ten noise levels show no noise threshold, only a base method that stops early. The same factors bound the gain: a model-based trust-region solver, which leaves little room, drops from 88 to 86 when the identical surrogate is attached, and released interpolation software stays ahead at 103, and on a Monte-Carlo inventory model repairing the acceptance interface is worth 10.40 cost units against 0.00 for the surrogate.

AI.tldr: This paper resolves the contradictory published results on neural surrogates in derivative-free optimisation by identifying three key factors—Role (proposal vs gradient replacement), Radius (bounded local reliability), and Room (base method progress capacity)—that determine when learned models help versus hurt. Experiments over 117 benchmarks show safeguarded assistance increases solved instances from 67 to 84, while gradient replacement decreases them to 65.
AI.motivation: Published experiences with neural surrogates in derivative-free optimisation are contradictory: identical surrogate models can help one solver, leave another unchanged, or make another worse. This contradiction needed resolution to understand when learned models truly benefit optimisation.
AI.method: The authors formalize three factors: (1) Role—distinguishing surrogates that propose candidates for approval versus those replacing gradients the solver depends on; (2) Radius—formalizing radius-aware local generalisation and relating it to the classical fully linear condition; (3) Room—recognizing surrogates can only accelerate when base methods can still make progress. Experiments held surrogate class, training pipeline, and base method fixed while testing each factor.
AI.result: Over 117 benchmark instances: safeguarded assistance raised high-accuracy solutions from 67 to 84 while gradient replacement lowered them to 65. Removing the gradient term from training loss cut surrogate acceptance from 0.703 to 0.148. 1000 paired comparisons over 10 noise levels showed no noise threshold, only base method early stopping. A model-based trust-region solver with little room dropped from 88 to 86 with the identical surrogate. Released interpolation software remained ahead at 103. On a Monte-Carlo inventory model, repairing the acceptance interface yielded 10.40 cost units versus 0.00 for the surrogate alone.
AI.conclusion: The three factors—Role, Radius, and Room—rather than training curve fit accuracy, delimit when neural surrogates benefit derivative-free optimisation. Surrogates should propose candidates for the true objective to approve (not replace gradients), must operate within their reliable neighborhood, and require the base method to still have room for progress. These factors bound the potential gain from learned models in optimisation.

title: A Hybrid Usability Approach for Rating Evaluation of M-Commerce Applications
summary: The success of any mobile application relies on its usefulness and rating is considered as an important measure in this regard. This research work focuses on identifying usability factors, which contribute significantly towards the rating of M-commerce apps. This work intends to explore existing usability models consisting of different factors along with a set of criteria and evaluate in terms of rating estimation by considering 5 well-known mobile applications, namely (i) daraz, (ii) shophive, (iii) home shopping, (iv) Symbios. (v) yayvo. Then, this work provides a hybrid usability model for rating prediction of M-commerce applications. The initial hybrid usability model comprises of (i) learnability, (ii) consistency, (iii) human factors,(iv)communicativeness,(v)effectiveness, (vi) Operability, (vii) efficiency, (viii) satisfaction. Each factor consists of some criteria. Keeping in view the factors of hybrid usability model, the data was collected from 40 users for each application. Furthermore, Forward Stepwise Multiple Linear Regression based rating prediction model is suggested by analyzing each criterion of all factors of hybrid usability model. Finally, the model is assessed and validated by using PRED(x) and K-fold techniques.

AI.tldr: This research identifies usability factors contributing to M-commerce app ratings by evaluating 5 apps (daraz, shophive, home shopping, Symbios, yayvo) against a hybrid usability model with 8 factors, using Forward Stepwise Multiple Linear Regression for rating prediction, validated via PRED(x) and K-fold techniques with data from 40 users per app.
AI.motivation: The success of mobile applications depends on their usefulness, with app ratings serving as a critical measure. This study aims to identify which usability factors significantly contribute to M-commerce app ratings to help developers improve their applications.
AI.method: The researchers (1) explored existing usability models with various factors and criteria, (2) evaluated 5 M-commerce applications using these criteria, (3) developed a hybrid usability model with 8 factors (learnability, consistency, human factors, communicativeness, effectiveness, operability, efficiency, satisfaction), (4) collected data from 40 users per application, (5) applied Forward Stepwise Multiple Linear Regression for rating prediction, and (6) validated the model using PRED(x) and K-fold cross-validation techniques.
AI.result: The study produced a hybrid usability model for rating prediction of M-commerce applications, with each of the 8 factors consisting of specific criteria. The Forward Stepwise Multiple Linear Regression model was built by analyzing each criterion of all factors.
AI.conclusion: The proposed hybrid usability model effectively predicts M-commerce app ratings, validated through PRED(x) and K-fold techniques, providing developers with actionable insights into which usability factors most significantly impact user ratings.

title: CVE-SAI: Counterfactual Visual Evidence-Guided Selective Attribute Indexing for Risk-Controlled E-commerce Search
summary: Multimodal product models can complete missing e-commerce attributes, yet current methods still optimize attribute-answer accuracy without verifying visual support, conflate transient prediction with persistent index admission, and lack explicit risk control over factually incorrect or visually unsupported values. We address these gaps with Counterfactual Visual Evidence-Guided Selective Attribute Indexing (CVE-SAI), which first infers and freezes an ontology-constrained candidate from the primary image and attribute question without catalog text, and then decides whether that candidate should enter the index. Focus-Zone Distortion (FZD) constructs an attribute-specific visual-dependence proxy through a controlled counterfactual intervention, and Evidence-Guided Attention Redistribution (EGAR) uses the proxy to refine ontology-constrained scoring. The canonical candidate is frozen before evidence necessity, evidence retention, nuisance-transformation stability, and candidate-specific catalog-text conflict audits; catalog text can only tighten admission and cannot revise the candidate. Independent family-level calibration selects one policy with a simultaneous one-sided finite-sample bound under a 5% unsafe-admission budget. Experiments on five visual attributes derived from Amazon Berkeley Objects show that CVE-SAI improves attribute inference and evidence localization, achieves the highest certified admission coverage under the shared risk protocol, and yields the strongest controlled retrieval performance with the lowest unsafe auto-induced exposure among automatic-admission systems. Separating inference from admission therefore enables visually supported attribute completion to improve retrieval while limiting persistent index contamination.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces CVE-SAI, a novel framework for visually supported attribute completion in e-commerce product indexing. It addresses critical gaps in current multimodal models by separating inference from admission, using counterfactual visual evidence to verify attribute predictions before index entry, and implementing risk control to prevent persistent index contamination.
AI.motivation: Current multimodal product models for e-commerce have three fundamental limitations: (1) they optimize attribute-answer accuracy without verifying visual support, (2) they conflate transient prediction with persistent index admission, and (3) they lack explicit risk control over factually incorrect or visually unsupported values. These issues lead to index contamination and poor retrieval performance.
AI.method: The proposed CVE-SAI framework consists of several key components: (1) Focus-Zone Distortion (FZD) constructs attribute-specific visual-dependence proxies through controlled counterfactual interventions; (2) Evidence-Guided Attention Redistribution (EGAR) uses these proxies to refine ontology-constrained scoring; (3) The canonical candidate is frozen before evidence necessity, evidence retention, nuisance-transformation stability, and candidate-specific catalog-text conflict audits; (4) Catalog text can only tighten admission criteria, not revise the candidate; (5) Independent family-level calibration selects one policy with simultaneous one-sided finite-sample bound under a 5% unsafe-admission budget.
AI.result: Experiments on five visual attributes from Amazon Berkeley Objects dataset show that CVE-SAI: (1) improves attribute inference and evidence localization; (2) achieves the highest certified admission coverage under the shared risk protocol; (3) yields the strongest controlled retrieval performance with the lowest unsafe auto-induced exposure among automatic-admission systems.
AI.conclusion: Separating inference from admission enables visually supported attribute completion to improve retrieval while limiting persistent index contamination. The key insight is that by freezing the candidate before evidence verification and allowing catalog text only to tighten (not revise) admission criteria, the system can maintain visual grounding while preventing index pollution.

title: What Do Medical Vision-Language Models Learn in Radiology? Transfer, Alignment, and Source-Proxy Leakage Under Distribution Shift
summary: Medical vision-language models (VLMs) can appear reliable in-domain while failing when acquisition domain, paired supervision, or evaluation protocol changes. We study this failure mode as a representation-level blind spot relevant to epistemic intelligence, without claiming a formal estimator of epistemic uncertainty. Using NIH ChestXray14 and CheXpert, we first isolate source-only cross-dataset visual transfer from unsupervised domain-adaptation diagnostics. Using PadChest and OpenI, we then evaluate multimodal alignment under strict pair-index retrieval and quantify metadata-derived source-proxy information retained in frozen embeddings. Self-supervised visual initialization improves NIH-to-CheXpert transfer over supervised ImageNet initialization in matched ResNet-18 comparisons, whereas adversarial adaptation is useful only in a narrow regime and becomes unstable as adversarial pressure increases. Multimodal exact-pair retrieval remains low under external OpenI stress testing, and source-proxy information remains recoverable from learned representations. Qualitative nearest-neighbor and Grad-CAM analyses show clinically plausible cross-dataset structure and thoracic attention patterns in many cases, while device-heavy and false-positive cases remain ambiguous. Auxiliary architecture checks are task-dependent and do not support a universal backbone ranking. Overall, the study shows that apparent competence under a single protocol can conceal transfer, alignment, and shortcut-related failure modes, motivating stress-tested evaluation of medical VLMs under distribution shift.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates failure modes of medical vision-language models (VLMs) under distribution shift, showing that models appearing reliable in-domain can fail when acquisition domain, paired supervision, or evaluation protocol changes. The study identifies representation-level blind spots relevant to epistemic intelligence through cross-dataset experiments.
AI.motivation: Medical VLMs can appear reliable in controlled settings but fail when deployed in different domains or under different evaluation protocols. The researchers aim to understand these failure modes as representation-level blind spots relevant to epistemic intelligence, without claiming a formal estimator of epistemic uncertainty.
AI.method: The study uses multiple datasets (NIH ChestXray14, CheXpert, PadChest, OpenI) to: (1) isolate source-only cross-dataset visual transfer from unsupervised domain-adaptation diagnostics; (2) evaluate multimodal alignment under strict pair-index retrieval; (3) quantify metadata-derived source-proxy information retained in frozen embeddings. Methods include matched ResNet-18 comparisons, adversarial adaptation, exact-pair retrieval, nearest-neighbor analysis, and Grad-CAM analysis.
AI.result: Self-supervised visual initialization improves NIH-to-CheXpert transfer over supervised ImageNet initialization, while adversarial adaptation is useful only in narrow regimes and becomes unstable under increased pressure. Multimodal exact-pair retrieval remains low under external OpenI stress testing, and source-proxy information remains recoverable from learned representations. Qualitative analyses show clinically plausible cross-dataset structure and thoracic attention patterns, though device-heavy and false-positive cases remain ambiguous. Auxiliary architecture checks are task-dependent and do not support universal backbone ranking.
AI.conclusion: Apparent competence under a single evaluation protocol can conceal transfer, alignment, and shortcut-related failure modes in medical VLMs. This motivates the need for stress-tested evaluation of medical VLMs under distribution shift to uncover hidden failure modes before clinical deployment.

title: Physics-Informed Error Field Learning: A Post-Training Optimization Framework for Physics-Informed Neural Networks
summary: Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) have emerged as an important class of numerical methods for solving partial differential equations (PDEs). However, during the late-stage optimization process, further parameter updates often yield diminishing accuracy improvements while increasing computational costs. To address this issue, this paper proposes a Physics-Informed Error Field Learning (PIEFL) framework for PINNs. Unlike conventional approaches that continuously approximate the solution field using a single network, PIEFL introduces an auxiliary error network after the primary network achieves satisfactory accuracy and shifts the learning objective from the solution field to the error field. By deriving error control equations under physical constraints, the error network learns the discrepancy between the current approximation and the exact solution, and the learned error correction is combined with the primary prediction to improve solution accuracy. The proposed framework avoids continuous optimization of the entire solution space and focuses computational resources on correcting existing prediction errors. Moreover, PIEFL requires no modification to the primary network architecture, making it compatible with existing PINN models and applicable as a general post-training optimization strategy. Numerical experiments on representative PDEs demonstrate that PIEFL achieves higher solution accuracy under the same computational budget, validating its effectiveness in improving the performance of PINNs.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes Physics-Informed Error Field Learning (PIEFL), a framework that introduces an auxiliary error network after a primary PINN achieves initial accuracy, shifting the learning objective from the solution field to the error field to improve computational efficiency and accuracy.
AI.motivation: To address the limitation that during late-stage optimization of PINNs, further parameter updates yield diminishing accuracy improvements while increasing computational costs.
AI.method: PIEFL introduces an auxiliary error network after the primary network achieves satisfactory accuracy. Error control equations are derived under physical constraints, and the error network learns the discrepancy between the current approximation and the exact solution. The learned error correction is combined with the primary prediction to improve accuracy.
AI.result: PIEFL achieves higher solution accuracy under the same computational budget. It avoids continuous optimization of the entire solution space and focuses computational resources on correcting existing prediction errors.
AI.conclusion: PIEFL is a general post-training optimization strategy that requires no modification to the primary network architecture, making it compatible with existing PINN models.

title: From General Agents to RCA Experts: A Self-Evolving Harness for Root Cause Analysis
summary: Automated root cause analysis (RCA) with large language models (LLMs) has drawn growing attention. Today, SREs typically automate RCA with LLMs in one of two ways: directly using a general-purpose agent (e.g., Codex or Claude Code) for diagnosis, or building a specialized RCA agent from scratch. As mainstream general agents grow more capable and iterate quickly, our quantitative study finds that the former now often surpasses the latter. Its accuracy, however, still falls short of production needs, and this gap stems mainly from the external adaptation layer outside the agent's general capabilities, namely the harness. We therefore argue that LLM-based RCA should focus on this external harness, reusing the strong general capabilities of a modern agent rather than rebuilding an agent from scratch. A key capability of such a harness is to self-evolve, accumulating system-specific experience from past diagnoses so that it gets better the more it is used. We introduce OpsHarness, a self-evolving RCA harness that turns diagnosis experience into reusable expertise. Its data plane combines layered operational knowledge with an idea-card tool library, while its control plane coordinates setup, diagnosis, evolution, and verification. During evolution, OpsHarness contrasts successful and failed trajectories, converts their evidence into atomic proposals, and admits updates only through a dual-gate verification process designed to prevent overfitting and regression. Across two public benchmarks and an industrial deployment, OpsHarness achieves 59.0\% top-1 accuracy, improving over a bare general agent by 63.4\% and over baseline RCA agents by 4.02$\times$.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces OpsHarness, a self-evolving RCA (Root Cause Analysis) harness that leverages general-purpose LLM agents rather than building specialized agents from scratch. It achieves 59.0% top-1 accuracy by accumulating system-specific experience through a dual-gate verification process that contrasts successful and failed trajectories.
AI.motivation: SREs typically automate RCA with LLMs in two ways: using general-purpose agents or building specialized RCA agents from scratch. While general agents now often surpass specialized ones, their accuracy still falls short of production needs. The authors argue the gap stems from the external adaptation layer (harness) rather than the agent itself, suggesting focus should be on building a strong harness that reuses strong general capabilities.
AI.method: OpsHarness consists of two main components: (1) Data plane combining layered operational knowledge with an idea-card tool library, and (2) Control plane coordinating setup, diagnosis, evolution, and verification. During evolution, it contrasts successful and failed trajectories, converts evidence into atomic proposals, and admits updates only through a dual-gate verification process designed to prevent overfitting and regression.
AI.result: OpsHarness achieves 59.0% top-1 accuracy across two public benchmarks and an industrial deployment, improving over a bare general agent by 63.4% and over baseline RCA agents by 4.02×.
AI.conclusion: LLM-based RCA should focus on the external harness rather than rebuilding agents from scratch. The key capability is self-evolution, accumulating system-specific experience from past diagnoses so the system gets better with use.

title: Retrieve, Match, Escalate: Accurate and Scalable Product Linking with VLM-Distilled Cross-Encoders and Agentic VLMs
summary: Product linking, the entity-resolution task of mapping merchant product records to canonical catalog products, consolidates fragmented listings so downstream search, recommendation, and advertising see one clean entry per product. At marketplace scale, billions of noisy, multi-category records must be resolved against tens of millions of canonical products, where scoring every candidate with a single model is either too weak for the hard cases or too costly for the easy ones. We present a production retrieve-then-match cascade that spends computation in proportion to difficulty: retrieval surfaces plausible matches, a lightweight text cross-encoder auto-resolves the high-confidence majority, and an agentic multimodal vision-language model settles the ambiguous remainder by inspecting product images and issuing web searches for evidence that is in neither record. The cross-encoder is distilled from millions of dual-VLM-consensus labels, retiring human annotation from the training set, and is calibrated to auto-accept links at a 98% precision bar validated against a smaller operator-certified audit. The agent is a self-hosted open-weight model that reaches a closed frontier VLM's precision at a four-point recall cost (88% versus 92%) for roughly one-seventh the per-pair cost, with no fine-tuning. Per-pair cost spans nearly five orders of magnitude from the cheap cross-encoder to the frontier VLM, so escalating only the hard tail to the agent raises end-to-end link coverage from the cheap stage's 68% to 77%.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a production retrieve-then-match cascade for product linking in e-commerce marketplaces, using a three-stage approach: retrieval, lightweight cross-encoder, and agentic multimodal VLM. The system achieves 98% precision with auto-acceptance, increasing end-to-end coverage from 68% to 77% while managing computational costs across five orders of magnitude.
AI.motivation: At marketplace scale, resolving billions of noisy product records against tens of millions of canonical products is computationally prohibitive if every candidate is scored with a single powerful model. There's a fundamental trade-off between accuracy (needed for hard cases) and cost (preferable for easy cases).
AI.method: The system uses a three-stage cascade: (1) retrieval to surface plausible matches, (2) a lightweight text cross-encoder auto-resolving high-confidence matches at 98% precision, and (3) an agentic multimodal VLM that inspects product images and issues web searches to resolve ambiguous cases. The cross-encoder is trained via distillation from dual-VLM-consensus labels (eliminating human annotation), while the agent uses a self-hosted open-weight model without fine-tuning.
AI.result: The cross-encoder achieves 98% precision and auto-accepts the high-confidence majority. The agentic VLM reaches 88% recall versus the closed frontier VLM's 92%, at roughly one-seventh the per-pair cost. End-to-end link coverage increases from 68% (cheap stage alone) to 77% when escalating hard cases to the agent. Costs span nearly five orders of magnitude from cross-encoder to frontier VLM.
AI.conclusion: The cascade architecture successfully balances accuracy and computational cost by spending computation proportional to difficulty. Using VLM-consensus for training data generation eliminates human annotation burden, and self-hosted open-weight models provide cost-effective alternatives to frontier VLMs for ambiguous product matching.

title: OpenCVL: An Open, Diverse, and Large-Scale Dataset for Fine-Grained Cross-View Localization
summary: Fine-grained Cross-View Localization (CVL) estimates the precise position and orientation of a ground-level image by aligning it with geo-referenced aerial imagery, offering a scalable alternative to Global Navigation Satellite Systems (GNSS) in challenging urban environments. Existing datasets rely on data collected with high-end sensor suites, which inherently limit image diversity and scalability. While in-the-wild images are abundant, their noisy geo-tags make them unsuitable for reliable evaluation. To bridge this gap, we introduce OpenCVL, a large-scale, diverse, and open dataset containing 617,388 ground-aerial image pairs spanning 41 cities across four European countries. All images are sourced from permissive platforms, ensuring long-term accessibility and supporting open and reproducible research. The training set combines images captured with high-end sensors with diverse in-the-wild imagery. We further develop a data curation framework that filters and corrects pose annotations to construct reliable in-the-wild evaluation data. In addition, OpenCVL includes dedicated cross-area and snowy test sets to assess generalization and robustness. Experiments with a state-of-the-art CVL model on OpenCVL show that incorporating noisy in-the-wild data consistently improves performance on clean test sets, suggesting a promising direction for scaling CVL with diverse real-world imagery.

AI.tldr: OpenCVL is a large-scale cross-view localization dataset containing 617,388 ground-aerial image pairs from 41 cities across 4 European countries, combining high-end sensor data with diverse in-the-wild imagery and including a data curation framework for reliable evaluation.
AI.motivation: Existing CVL datasets rely on high-end sensor suites, limiting image diversity and scalability. In-the-wild images are abundant but have noisy geo-tags unsuitable for reliable evaluation, creating a need for a diverse, accessible dataset that supports open research in urban navigation.
AI.method: The authors created OpenCVL by sourcing images from permissive platforms and developed a data curation framework that filters and corrects pose annotations to construct reliable in-the-wild evaluation data. The dataset includes dedicated cross-area and snowy test sets for assessing generalization and robustness.
AI.result: Experiments with a state-of-the-art CVL model demonstrate that incorporating noisy in-the-wild data consistently improves performance on clean test sets, suggesting that scaling CVL with diverse real-world imagery is effective.
AI.conclusion: OpenCVL provides a scalable solution for cross-view localization research by enabling the use of diverse real-world imagery while maintaining evaluation reliability, offering a promising direction for practical deployment in urban environments.

title: Resource-Efficient Pruning for Transformer via Low-Rank Importance Estimation
summary: With the rapid development of large-scale pre-trained language models based on Transformer architectures, their high computational and memory costs have become a major obstacle to deployment, especially in resource-constrained environments. Traditional pruning methods typically depend on full gradient-based importance estimation, and they necessitate prior finetuning of the model to achieve satisfactory performance. This process often results in intolerable resource consumption. This paper proposes REP-LIE, a new approach to enable resource-efficient pruning during the process of finetuning. REP-LIE leverages the gradients of LoRA low-rank matrices to estimate the importance of weights without requiring full gradient computation. To address the inherent randomness in importance estimation, a stability score is introduced, serving as the basis for iterative pruning of unimportant model parameters. The pruned model is further finetuned through lightweight updates, eliminating the need for full-parameter optimization in the process of finetuning. Extensive experiments on both medium-scale encoder models and large-scale generative models (LLaMA-7B and Mistral-7B) demonstrate that REP-LIE still achieves competitive performance compared to existing approaches.

AI.tldr: REP-LIE is a resource-efficient pruning method that leverages LoRA low-rank matrix gradients to estimate weight importance during finetuning, eliminating the need for full gradient computation. It uses a stability score for iterative pruning and achieves competitive performance on large models like LLaMA-7B and Mistral-7B.
AI.motivation: The rapid development of large-scale pre-trained language models based on Transformers faces a major deployment obstacle due to high computational and memory costs, especially in resource-constrained environments. Traditional pruning methods require full gradient-based importance estimation and prior finetuning, resulting in intolerable resource consumption.
AI.method: REP-LIE leverages the gradients of LoRA low-rank matrices to estimate the importance of weights without requiring full gradient computation. To address randomness in importance estimation, a stability score is introduced as the basis for iterative pruning of unimportant model parameters. The pruned model is further finetuned through lightweight updates, eliminating the need for full-parameter optimization during finetuning.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on both medium-scale encoder models and large-scale generative models (LLaMA-7B and Mistral-7B) demonstrate that REP-LIE still achieves competitive performance compared to existing approaches.
AI.conclusion: REP-LIE provides a resource-efficient pruning approach that can maintain competitive performance while significantly reducing the computational and memory costs of large language models, making them more suitable for deployment in resource-constrained environments.

title: Predicting Struggling Students in CS1 Programming Using Keystroke-Level Editing Features
comment: 6 pages, 3 figures, 1 table, Accepted to the 34th IEEE/ACIS International Conference on Software Engineering, Artificial Intelligence, Networking and Parallel/Distributed Computing (SNPD 2026)
summary: This paper investigates the feasibility of early detection of struggling students during CS1 programming exercises using keystroke-level logs. Some students fail to reach a correct solution before the exercise ends, and by the time this becomes apparent from grades or final outcomes, the opportunity for timely instructor support aimed at helping them recover may have passed. We use data from the CodeBench platform, which records real-time code editing events at the keystroke level, alongside execution and submission logs. We define two outcome groups: Breakthrough (BT) students, whose prior submissions all receive 0% and whose final submission achieves full credit, and Fully Stuck (FS) students, whose submissions all receive 0% without reaching a correct solution. To examine this feasibility, we focus on two questions: (RQ1) whether adding keystroke-level editing features improves the prediction of FS students over execution-log features alone, and (RQ2) at which stage BT and FS students can be predicted most accurately. Experiments on the 2019-1 semester of the CodeBench dataset, comprising 507 students, compare three feature configurations: execution-based features (ExecOnly), CodeMirror-based features (CMOnly), and their combination (Combined). We evaluate prediction across successive submission-based stages during each exercise. In the earliest stage, CMOnly outperforms ExecOnly (AUROC 0.654 vs. 0.575), and Combined further improves over ExecOnly by +0.098 (AUROC 0.674). Across all configurations, the earliest stage yielded the strongest predictive signal. These findings indicate that behavioral signals present at the very start of an exercise contain useful clues about whether a student will ultimately solve the problem, and that keystroke-level editing logs provide additional value for early prioritization beyond execution logs alone.

AI.tldr: This paper explores using keystroke-level logs to early detect struggling CS1 students during programming exercises. Using CodeBench data from 507 students, researchers compared execution-based features vs. keystroke-level editing features (CodeMirror) for predicting 'Fully Stuck' students who never solve the problem. Results show keystroke features improve early prediction (AUROC 0.654 vs 0.575), with combined features achieving 0.674 AUROC, indicating behavioral signals at exercise start are predictive of student outcomes.
AI.motivation: The problem is that instructor support often comes too late - after grades reveal a student is struggling, the opportunity for timely intervention has passed. The authors aim to enable early detection so instructors can provide proactive support before students fall too far behind.
AI.method: The study used CodeBench platform data recording keystroke-level editing events, execution logs, and submissions. They defined two outcome groups: Breakthrough (BT) students who eventually solve the problem, and Fully Stuck (FS) students who never achieve a correct solution. Three feature configurations were compared across successive submission stages: execution-based (ExecOnly), CodeMirror-based (CMOnly), and their combination (Combined).
AI.result: At the earliest stage, CodeMirror-only features (CMOnly) outperformed execution-only features (AUROC 0.654 vs 0.575). The Combined approach improved over ExecOnly by +0.098 (AUROC 0.674). The earliest stage provided the strongest predictive signal across all configurations.
AI.conclusion: Keystroke-level editing logs provide additional value for early identification of struggling students beyond execution logs alone. Behavioral signals present at the very start of programming exercises contain useful predictive information about whether students will ultimately solve the problem, enabling earlier instructor intervention.

title: LifePlanner: Evaluating LLM Agents for Geo-spatial Planning with Social Media Data
summary: Geo-spatial planning, like trip design, is a realistic testbed for LLM agents because it requires grounded tool use, noisy evidence retrieval, and multi-constraint reasoning. Most benchmarks, however, only provide clean geospatial data and tools, missing the open-ended social signals that people use in daily planning. We introduce LifePlanner, a benchmark that enriches map data with large-scale local social media posts and provides access through an MCP toolset. LifePlanner provides an evaluation suite spanning four task categories and three difficulty levels. Experiments show frontier LLMs perform well on simple retrieval but degrade sharply on complex planning, with the Pass Rate dropping to 40.2%. Results show that failures mainly stem from incomplete evidence acquisition from such a large multimodal database, imprecise tool use, and weak constraint integration rather than model size or reasoning length, suggesting that future progress requires effective grounded planning instead of scaling alone.

AI.tldr: LifePlanner is a benchmark for evaluating LLM agents on geo-spatial planning tasks, enriched with large-scale local social media posts to simulate real-world social signals missing in existing benchmarks. Frontier LLMs perform well on simple tasks but show sharp performance degradation (40.2% pass rate) on complex planning, with failures stemming from incomplete evidence acquisition, imprecise tool use, and weak constraint integration rather than model scale or reasoning length.
AI.motivation: Current geo-spatial planning benchmarks only provide clean data and tools, missing the open-ended social signals that people use in daily planning. This creates a gap between benchmark evaluation and real-world task performance, as real planning involves noisy evidence retrieval and multi-constraint reasoning grounded in social context.
AI.method: LifePlanner enriches map data with large-scale local social media posts and provides access through an MCP (Model Context Protocol) toolset. The benchmark includes an evaluation suite with four task categories and three difficulty levels designed to test grounded tool use, noisy evidence retrieval, and multi-constraint reasoning.
AI.result: Experiments reveal frontier LLMs perform well on simple retrieval tasks but degrade sharply on complex planning, with Pass Rate dropping to 40.2%. Key failure modes include: (1) incomplete evidence acquisition from large multimodal databases, (2) imprecise tool use, and (3) weak constraint integration. Notably, failures are not primarily caused by model size or reasoning length.
AI.conclusion: Future progress in LLM agents for geo-spatial planning requires effective grounded planning approaches rather than simply scaling model size. The benchmark highlights the need for better evidence acquisition, tool use precision, and constraint integration capabilities in LLM agents.

title: PointRL: Learning Point-Level Vision-Language Grounding from Verifiable Annotation Evidence
summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) increasingly rely on point coordinates as a compact and executable interface for visual grounding in GUI interaction, robotic manipulation, and interactive visual systems. However, learning reliable pointing behavior remains difficult because the supervision space is inherently non-unique: many coordinates may be valid within the same target region, while multi-instance instructions require target coverage, count consistency, and duplicate suppression. This work presents PointRL, a verifiable reinforcement learning framework that learns point-level grounding from existing heterogeneous annotation evidence. PointRL converts bounding boxes, masks, and instance labels into pointing instructions, while retaining their target supports, instance membership, and set constraints as hidden verifier evidence, i.e., annotations kept outside the prompt and used by a deterministic checker to score predictions. The proposed reward evaluates parseability, point validity, instance coverage, cardinality consistency, and redundant or missing predictions. On PointArena, PointRL improves the overall accuracy of Qwen3.5-4B from 56.11% to 65.58%. Further evaluations on RoboSpatial, BLINK, and Ref-Adv show same-backbone gains on the evaluated external benchmarks, suggesting that verifiable point-level feedback may benefit spatial grounding in these settings.

title: Clearing the Underbrush: AI-Enhanced RF Interference Suppression
comment: 7 pages, 10 figures, Accepted to the 2026 IEEE Military Communications Conference (MILCOM)
summary: AI-based structured interference rejection has grown more popular because deep learning approaches can outperform traditional methods by jointly considering the signal of interest (SOI) and the signal mixture (SOI plus interference). This work builds on a previous AI-enabled approach utilizing autoregressive transformer-based models by adding a Finite Scalar Quantization (FSQ) tokenizer layer which aims to improve the interference rejection performance while keeping overall latency to a minimum. Additionally, we experiment with other inference optimization techniques with the goal of speeding up inference without much accuracy loss. We explore this space with an experiment where the SOI is a digitally modulated radio frequency (RF) signal and the structured interference is a digital television signal, an extremely common type of Orthogonal Frequency-Division Multiplexing (OFDM) transmission. Our results achieve low latency and increased interference rejection over traditional techniques and prior work with other AI-enabled methods. We demonstrate the benefits of the AI-enabled approaches via audio metrics such as Perceptual Evaluation of Speech Quality (PESQ). Additionally, we explore a variety of applications and detail how our interference rejection algorithm may be used in operationally-relevant scenarios.

AI.tldr: This paper presents an AI-based structured interference rejection method using autoregressive transformer models with Finite Scalar Quantization (FSQ) tokenizer layer. The approach aims to improve interference rejection performance while minimizing latency for RF signal processing applications.
AI.motivation: Deep learning approaches can outperform traditional interference rejection methods by jointly considering the signal of interest (SOI) and the signal mixture (SOI plus interference). The authors seek to improve upon previous AI-enabled approaches while keeping latency minimal.
AI.method: The approach builds on autoregressive transformer-based models by adding a Finite Scalar Quantization (FSQ) tokenizer layer. Additional inference optimization techniques are explored to speed up inference without significant accuracy loss. The experiment uses digitally modulated RF signals as SOI and digital TV (OFDM) signals as structured interference.
AI.result: The method achieves low latency and increased interference rejection over traditional techniques and prior AI-enabled methods. Performance is evaluated using audio metrics such as Perceptual Evaluation of Speech Quality (PESQ).
AI.conclusion: AI-enabled approaches demonstrate benefits for interference rejection in operationally-relevant scenarios. The FSQ tokenizer layer combined with inference optimization techniques provides an effective solution for practical RF signal processing applications.

title: Beyond the Editing Canvas: Evidence Divergence in OOXML-to-LLM Ingestion
summary:
LLM pipelines increasingly ingest Office Open XML (OOXML) documents (Word, Excel, and PowerPoint files) as first-class evidence in financial, compliance, and retrieval-augmented workflows, implicitly assuming semantic integrity: that the evidence consumed by the model matches the content shown in the Microsoft Office suite editing canvas. We show that this assumption can fail in OOXML-to-LLM pipelines. The same specification-valid OOXML file can yield one evidentiary view in Microsoft Office and another when extracted for an LLM. Each view is treated as authoritative by its consumer, a condition we call plural ground truth. The ingestion contract rarely states which view and semantic roles become model evidence or preserves how that evidence was derived. We call the specification-grounded OOXML constructions that induce such divergence evidence forks.
  We systematically traverse and mine the OOXML specification and confirm 21 evidence forks across Excel, Word, and PowerPoint, spanning six dimensions of view construction. All 13 tools in our extraction panel emit evidence from at least one fork. We test four native-ingestion LLM APIs and seven web chatbots. Each test document carries a trap: a task-relevant fact exposed by extraction but not shown in Office. Across this 21-mechanism evaluation, the four APIs return the trap in 48--76% of trials. For 20 of 21 mechanisms, at least one of the eleven interfaces returns the trap. Our measurements further show that exposure is shaped upstream of the model by the ingestion path and extractor configuration. A source-level survey of sixteen popular open-source LLM projects further shows that default OOXML ingestion paths concentrate on affected extractor families.

title: SimVerity: When Does Simulated Agent Success Survive Physical Deployment?
comment: Submitted to the Main Technical Track of AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence (AAAI-27); currently under review
summary: Simulated evaluation is widely used to benchmark AI agents, yet how much evidence a simulated pass provides about physical deployment has not been systematically quantified. We present SimVerity, a verdict-transfer assurance framework: it replays matched scenarios on target smart home deployments and cross-validates agent execution against independently qualified physical witnesses. Our evaluation highlights that deployment success is a real-world process, not a static property in simulation: completion, reported state, observable effect, and settled outcome diverged within the same execution. Although an advanced simulator cleared all 240 light trials, a camera caught 42 sub-second failures invisible to settled-state checks. False clearance was predictable: a risk profile learned from measured trials and locked before evaluation predicted failures on a path it never physically measured, beating a property-blind baseline in all eleven held-out sessions across two cohorts. Agent auditability was also measurable: switching one agent loop's model-client/serving configuration raised its scenario-matching share from 52-88% to 100%. Finally, a second qualified simulator added no independent cross-check: it never disagreed on any overlapping case, and only physical measurement exposed their shared blind spots. SimVerity turns verdict transfer into an explicit decision: clear, abstain, or escalate before deployment.

AI.tldr: SimVerity is a verdict-transfer assurance framework that bridges simulated AI agent evaluation with physical smart home deployment by replaying matched scenarios and cross-validating against physical witnesses. It addresses the critical gap in quantifying how much evidence a simulated pass provides about real-world deployment success.
AI.motivation: Simulated evaluation is widely used to benchmark AI agents, but there has been no systematic quantification of how much evidence a simulated pass actually provides about physical deployment. The key question is: can we trust simulation results to predict real-world performance?
AI.method: SimVerity replays matched scenarios on target smart home deployments and cross-validates agent execution against independently qualified physical witnesses (e.g., cameras). The framework uses risk profiles learned from measured trials to predict failures and evaluates agent auditability by testing different model-client/serving configurations.
AI.result: 1) Deployment success is a process, not a static property: completion, reported state, observable effect, and settled outcome diverged within the same execution. 2) Advanced simulator cleared all 240 light trials, but physical cameras caught 42 sub-second failures invisible to settled-state checks. 3) False clearance was predictable: a risk profile learned from measured trials predicted failures on paths never physically measured, beating a property-blind baseline in all 11 held-out sessions across two cohorts. 4) Agent auditability was measurable: switching one agent loop's model-client/serving configuration raised scenario-matching share from 52-88% to 100%. 5) Second qualified simulator provided no independent cross-check: it never disagreed on overlapping cases; only physical measurement exposed their shared blind spots.
AI.conclusion: SimVerity transforms verdict transfer into an explicit decision framework with three outcomes: clear (pass), abstain (insufficient evidence), or escalate (requires further investigation) before deployment. Physical validation remains essential as simulators share blind spots that only real-world measurement can detect.

title: WAVE: Reversing the Guidance Hierarchy for Coarse-to-Fine Guided Depth Super-Resolution
summary: Guided depth super-resolution (GDSR) typically extracts RGB guidance features through convolutional hierarchies, inheriting their fine-to-coarse bias. Thus, low-level spatial cues surface in early layers, leaving the deeper layers to suppress those that do not correspond to true depth boundaries, which risks artifacts and blurred edges. The same fine-to-coarse bias persists in semantics-based methods that consume low-level tokens early and global tokens late. We present WAVE, which introduces a multi-level discrete wavelet transform (ML-DWT) as an explicit and interpretable feature-control mechanism, enabling a coarse-to-fine reconstruction by consuming sub-bands and semantic tokens in reverse of their generation order. WAVE further exploits these sub-bands to treat high- and low-frequency content separately, filtering at its source the misleading RGB color and texture cues that often lead to blurred boundaries and artifacts, offering an intuitive alternative to the suppression learned implicitly by an opaque network. WAVE separates structure and detail reconstruction into dedicated modules that: i) model interactions within and across wavelet sub-bands, depth features, and semantic priors, ii) apply semantic gating to the high-frequency bands, and iii) fuse modalities through an invertible coupling mechanism that prevents collapse onto a single modality. Extensive experiments across multiple benchmarks demonstrate that WAVE matches or outperforms existing methods, with the largest gains at high upsampling factors, where low-resolution depth contains the least structure.
