title: Understanding the Energy Scaling of Large Language Model Inference Across Context Lengths and Attention Architectures
summary: The growing adoption of large language models (LLMs) has raised increasing concerns about the energy consumption and environmental impact of inference. This paper presents a systematic empirical study of decode-phase energy consumption across representative open-source LLMs employing Multi-Head Attention (MHA), Grouped Query Attention (GQA), and Grouped Query Attention with Sliding Window Attention (SWA) to characterize how attention architecture influences decode-phase energy consumption under varying inference workloads. We evaluate four models across different context lengths, batch sizes, and generation workloads while measuring GPU energy using NVIDIA hardware counters. We examine the effects of context length, attention mechanism, Key-Value (KV) cache growth, and batching on decode-phase energy consumption. Results show that attention mechanism is the primary factor governing how decode energy scales with context length. MHA models exhibit substantially steeper energy growth than GQA models, whereas GQA with SWA maintains nearly constant energy consumption. We further show that model size primarily determines absolute energy consumption, while batching reduces both energy per generated token and request latency by up to 87%. These findings provide practical guidance for selecting energy-efficient LLM architectures and inference configurations.

AI.tldr: This paper empirically studies how different attention architectures (MHA, GQA, SWA) affect decode-phase energy consumption in LLMs, finding that attention mechanism is the primary factor determining how energy scales with context length, with SWA maintaining constant energy and batching reducing energy per token by up to 87%.
AI.motivation: The growing adoption of LLMs has raised concerns about energy consumption and environmental impact of inference, necessitating systematic empirical studies on decode-phase energy consumption across different attention architectures.
AI.method: The authors evaluate four models across different context lengths, batch sizes, and generation workloads using NVIDIA hardware counters to measure GPU energy. They examine effects of attention mechanism, KV cache growth, and batching on decode-phase energy consumption.
AI.result: MHA models exhibit substantially steeper energy growth with context length than GQA models; GQA with SWA maintains nearly constant energy consumption. Model size determines absolute energy consumption. Batching reduces both energy per generated token and request latency by up to 87%.
AI.conclusion: Attention mechanism is the primary factor governing how decode energy scales with context length. These findings provide practical guidance for selecting energy-efficient LLM architectures and inference configurations.

title: Hierarchical MoE for Multi-Modal ILD Diagnosis
summary: Mixture-of-experts (MoE) models combine specialized predictors under learned routing, offering a principled mechanism for leveraging heterogeneity in medical data. We present a hierarchical multimodal MoE for interstitial lung disease (ILD) classification that integrates a frozen, pre-trained imaging expert with structured electronic health records (EHR) via two-stage gating. A modality-level gate assigns patient-specific weights to imaging and EHR predictions, while a sub-gating module decomposes the EHR branch into clinically defined feature groups with learned, group-specific contributions. This design preserves stable imaging representations while enabling input-dependent clinical weighting and explicit EHR specialization. Under strict patient-level cross-validation, the model achieved the highest mean AUC among the evaluated methods (0.8750 +- 0.0443), compared with 0.8646 for imaging-only REN and 0.7685 for SwinUNETR. The framework extends interpretability across anatomical regions, imaging--EHR utilization, and clinically defined EHR feature groups.

AI.tldr: A hierarchical multimodal mixture-of-experts (MoE) model for interstitial lung disease (ILD) classification that integrates a frozen pre-trained imaging expert with structured electronic health records (EHR) through two-stage gating: modality-level gate for patient-specific weighting and sub-gating module for clinically defined EHR feature groups. The model achieved the highest mean AUC of 0.8750 ± 0.0443 under strict patient-level cross-validation.
AI.motivation: Medical data exhibits heterogeneity that standard models fail to leverage effectively. Mixture-of-experts (MoE) models offer a principled mechanism to combine specialized predictors through learned routing, but existing approaches lack proper integration of imaging and clinical data while maintaining interpretability. The motivation is to develop a framework that preserves stable imaging representations while enabling input-dependent clinical weighting and explicit EHR specialization for improved ILD classification.
AI.method: The proposed hierarchical multimodal MoE architecture uses two-stage gating: (1) A modality-level gate assigns patient-specific weights to imaging and EHR predictions, and (2) A sub-gating module decomposes the EHR branch into clinically defined feature groups with learned, group-specific contributions. The imaging expert is frozen (pre-trained), preserving stable imaging representations. The model was evaluated under strict patient-level cross-validation.
AI.result: The model achieved the highest mean AUC of 0.8750 ± 0.0443 among evaluated methods. This outperformed imaging-only REN (0.8646) and SwinUNETR (0.7685). The framework provides interpretability across three dimensions: anatomical regions, imaging-EHR utilization, and clinically defined EHR feature groups.
AI.conclusion: The hierarchical multimodal MoE approach effectively combines imaging and EHR data for ILD classification, outperforming single-modality and baseline multimodal methods. The two-stage gating mechanism enables patient-specific weighting and explicit EHR specialization while maintaining interpretability across anatomical regions, modality utilization, and clinical feature groups. This demonstrates the potential of MoE frameworks for leveraging heterogeneity in multimodal medical data.

title: Capacity Overflow: A Blind Spot for Backdoor Attacks in Vision MoE
summary: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) has become a prevalent paradigm for scaling Vision Transformers efficiently. To ensure computational scalability and prevent expert overload, Vision MoE architectures employ a capacity-bounded token dispatch mechanism, where each expert's processing budget depends on the inference batch size. This work identifies this batch-dependent behavior as an overlooked attack surface, and proposes a stealthy supply-chain backdoor attack that exploits this property through a three-phase framework. First, we inject a backdoor into an early MoE layer. Second, we train a neutralizer in a deeper MoE layer that suppresses the backdoor under normal capacity. Third, we configure a batch-adaptive capacity factor that preserves high capacity for small batches while reducing it for large batches, naturally disabling the neutralizer via token overflow at deployment-scale batch sizes. The attack remains in dormant mode during small-batch security audits and enters activation mode during large-batch deployment. Experiments on V-MoE and Swin-MoE across ImageNet-100 and GTSRB demonstrate activation-mode attack success rates of 76-87% with dormant-mode ASR below 9%, while evading Neural Cleanse, STRIP, Fine-Pruning, and Activation Clustering. Our findings reveal a fundamental security risk arising from batch-dependent execution in scalable Vision MoE architectures.

AI.tldr: This paper discovers a novel security vulnerability in Vision MoE architectures where the batch-dependent capacity mechanism creates an attack surface. It proposes a three-phase supply-chain backdoor attack that remains dormant during small-batch audits but activates during large-batch deployment, achieving 76-87% attack success rates while evading multiple detection methods.
AI.motivation: The authors identify that existing Vision MoE architectures employ batch-dependent token dispatch mechanisms where expert processing budget scales with inference batch size. This batch-dependent behavior has not been previously explored as a security vulnerability, creating an overlooked attack surface for stealthy backdoor attacks.
AI.method: The proposed attack uses a three-phase framework: (1) Inject a backdoor trigger into an early MoE layer; (2) Train a neutralizer in a deeper MoE layer that suppresses the backdoor under normal (small batch) capacity conditions; (3) Configure a batch-adaptive capacity factor that maintains high capacity for small batches but reduces capacity for large batches, causing token overflow that disables the neutralizer at deployment scale.
AI.result: Experiments on V-MoE and Swin-MoE across ImageNet-100 and GTSRB datasets demonstrate: activation-mode attack success rates of 76-87%, while maintaining dormant-mode attack success rate below 9%. The attack successfully evades detection by four defensive methods: Neural Cleanse, STRIP, Fine-Pruning, and Activation Clustering.
AI.conclusion: This work reveals a fundamental security risk inherent to batch-dependent execution in scalable Vision MoE architectures. The batch-adaptive capacity mechanism, designed for computational efficiency, inadvertently creates a condition where backdoor attacks can remain hidden during security audits (small batches) but activate during actual deployment (large batches), representing a significant supply-chain security threat.

title: Flower Hub: A Reproducible Benchmarking Platform for Federated Learning in Simulation and Deployment
summary: Federated learning (FL) has emerged as a key approach for training models across decentralized data, yet benchmarking in FL remains difficult to reproduce, compare, and extend. Existing evaluations are often tied to custom infrastructure, released as incomplete research code, and conducted primarily in simulation, which limits portability and practical relevance. We present Flower Hub, a platform for publishing, discovering, and executing decentralized and federated applications. We show how it enables reproducible benchmarking by packaging benchmarks as executable, versioned applications with standardized metadata, pinned dependencies, and explicit evaluation workflows. We instantiate this approach with a multi-domain benchmark suite spanning cross-silo and cross-device settings, and including tasks in medical imaging, financial tabular learning, legal instruction tuning, phishing URL detection, and audio tagging. We further demonstrate that the same benchmarking application can run across both simulation and deployment runtimes without changing the application code, enabling unified evaluation across varying learning environments. Beyond model quality, our benchmark design supports system-aware reporting, including runtime and communication metrics. This work advances benchmarking in FL settings from ad hoc code artifacts towards portable, executable, and reusable benchmark applications.

AI.tldr: Flower Hub is a platform for publishing, discovering, and executing decentralized and federated learning applications. It addresses reproducibility challenges in FL benchmarking by packaging benchmarks as executable, versioned applications with standardized metadata and pinned dependencies.
AI.motivation: Federated learning benchmarking is difficult to reproduce, compare, and extend due to reliance on custom infrastructure, incomplete research code, and simulation-only evaluations, which limits portability and practical relevance.
AI.method: Flower Hub instantiates a multi-domain benchmark suite spanning cross-silo and cross-device settings across five domains: medical imaging, financial tabular learning, legal instruction tuning, phishing URL detection, and audio tagging. The platform enables benchmarks to run across both simulation and deployment runtimes without code changes, supporting system-aware reporting including runtime and communication metrics.
AI.result: The same benchmarking application runs across both simulation and deployment runtimes without changing the application code, enabling unified evaluation across varying learning environments. Beyond model quality, the benchmark design supports system-aware reporting including runtime and communication metrics.
AI.conclusion: Flower Hub advances FL benchmarking from ad hoc code artifacts towards portable, executable, and reusable benchmark applications, facilitating reproducible and comparable evaluations in federated learning settings.

title: PhaseShift: Topology-Aware Data Harmonization and Model Consolidation Across Signalized Intersections
summary: Learned traffic-behavior models are commonly trained separately for each intersection, creating model portfolios that cannot share evidence across sites. We present PhaseShift, a topology-aware framework that harmonizes heterogeneous roadside trajectories into a shared actor-centric representation and trains one reusable backbone. Ego-relative coordinates, trajectory-induced movement paths, normalized signal context, and variable-cardinality interaction tokens remove site conventions while preserving behaviorally relevant topology. The backbone supports pooled operation, zero-shot at a held-out intersection, and low-data adaptation. We evaluate five intersections in two Florida regions on balanced field data, 100k training windows and equal-sized test sets per site under a replay-conditioned, best-of-sampled-trajectory protocol. At 10s, one pooled model lowers both minADE and minFDE relative to trained local models at all five sites, with median reductions of 36.8% and 22.0%. Leave-one-intersection-out deployment, including one cross-region fold, beats local training on both 10-s metrics at four of five sites, although short-horizon performance is less uniform. Fine-tuning with 1,000 target update windows improves on zero-shot at three sites and is the strongest regime at one. At site 7, every cross-site mixture sharply lowers long-horizon error under a fixed 100k-window budget; test-likelihood gains argue against a best-of-sample dispersion-only explanation. Local models fall behind calibrated IDM at the two highest-flow sites after long autoregressive rollouts; pretrained-backbone regimes do not. Within this five-site evaluation, PhaseShift demonstrates consolidation across heterogeneous physical control settings while identifying sites that still require adaptation. The protocol measures conditional single-vehicle generation under replayed context, not closed-loop traffic simulation.

AI.tldr: PhaseShift is a topology-aware framework that harmonizes heterogeneous roadside trajectories into a shared actor-centric representation, enabling a single reusable backbone for traffic-behavior modeling across multiple intersections. It removes site-specific conventions while preserving behaviorally relevant topology, supporting pooled operation, zero-shot deployment, and low-data adaptation.
AI.motivation: Current learned traffic-behavior models are trained separately for each intersection, creating isolated model portfolios that cannot share evidence across sites. This approach lacks generalization capability and requires training from scratch for each new intersection.
AI.method: PhaseShift uses ego-relative coordinates, trajectory-induced movement paths, normalized signal context, and variable-cardinality interaction tokens to create a unified representation. The framework trains one reusable backbone that can be pooled across sites, deployed zero-shot at held-out intersections, or fine-tuned with limited data.
AI.result: At 10s horizon, one pooled model reduced both minADE and minFDE relative to trained local models at all five sites, with median reductions of 36.8% and 22.0%. Leave-one-intersection-out deployment beat local training on both metrics at 4/5 sites. Fine-tuning with 1,000 target update windows improved zero-shot performance at three sites. At the highest-flow sites, pretrained-backbone regimes outperformed both local models and calibrated IDM after long autoregressive rollouts.
AI.conclusion: PhaseShift demonstrates successful consolidation across heterogeneous physical control settings while identifying sites that still require adaptation. The approach enables knowledge sharing across intersections, though performance varies by site and adaptation may be needed for optimal results.

title: Efficient Training with Foresight: Multi-Token Auxiliary Supervision for Autoregressive Image Generation
summary: Autoregressive (AR) image generation has shown strong potential for scalable high-fidelity synthesis by modeling images as discrete token sequences. However, traditional next token prediction (NTP) continues to suffer from sparse and myopic supervision, insufficiently discriminative representations, and high training cost caused by dense computation over the full token sequence. To address these issues, we propose multi-token autoregressive (MTAR), a unified training framework that improves autoregressive image generation from three aspects: prediction objectives, representation regularization, and training efficiency. Specifically, MTAR introduces multi-token prediction (MTP) to alleviate the sparsity and myopia of traditional NTP by imposing joint supervision on multiple future tokens; employs token-level contrastive regularization (TCR) to explicitly enhance the separability of sampled token representations and thereby improve representation discriminability; and incorporates semantic dropping (SD) as a semantics-aware training acceleration strategy to reduce redundant computation on low-information tokens while preserving informative learning signals. All three components are applied only during training and introduce no additional overhead during autoregressive inference. On ImageNet, MTAR achieves a better balance between generation quality and training efficiency. Compared with LlamaGen, MTAR achieves up to 0.95 lower FID and 39\% faster training. Moreover, even with only 1/3 of the training iterations, it still attains performance comparable to or better than the baseline, substantially reducing training time.

AI.tldr: MTAR is a unified training framework that improves autoregressive image generation through three components: multi-token prediction (MTP) for joint supervision on multiple future tokens, token-level contrastive regularization (TCR) for better representation discriminability, and semantic dropping (SD) for efficient training. It achieves 0.95 lower FID and 39% faster training than LlamaGen on ImageNet.
AI.motivation: Traditional next token prediction (NTP) in autoregressive image generation suffers from three critical limitations: (1) sparse and myopic supervision as each token predicts only the next one, (2) insufficiently discriminative token representations, and (3) high training cost due to dense computation over full token sequences. These issues limit both generation quality and training efficiency.
AI.method: MTAR introduces three complementary components: (1) Multi-token prediction (MTP) - predicts multiple future tokens simultaneously to alleviate sparse/myopic supervision; (2) Token-level contrastive regularization (TCR) - uses contrastive learning to enhance separability of sampled token representations; (3) Semantic dropping (SD) - semantics-aware acceleration that reduces computation on low-information tokens while preserving learning signals. All three components are training-only, adding no inference overhead.
AI.result: On ImageNet: MTAR achieves up to 0.95 lower FID (Fréchet Inception Distance) compared with LlamaGen; 39% faster training; with only 1/3 training iterations, still attains comparable or better performance than baseline.
AI.conclusion: MTAR successfully improves the balance between generation quality and training efficiency in autoregressive image generation. The combination of MTP, TCR, and SD addresses the limitations of traditional NTP without adding inference overhead, making it a practical approach for scalable high-fidelity image synthesis.

title: GRAPE: Gradient Refinement and Progress-Aware Exploitation for Query-Efficient High-Dimensional Bayesian Optimization
summary: Optimizing expensive, high-dimensional black-box functions remains a central challenge in modern machine learning and scientific discovery. While local Bayesian optimization mitigates the curse of dimensionality, existing techniques often prioritize the probability of descent over the magnitude of progress. This leads to overly conservative steps that yield negligible improvement, wasting queries on directions that are nearly certain to descend but offer little decrease. We introduce Gradient Refinement and Progress-Aware Exploitation (GRAPE), a two-stage framework that first sharpens the local gradient posterior via a closed-form acquisition function, then selects update directions by maximizing the expected decrease conditional on descent. Theoretical analysis proves that this gradient refinement stage monotonically minimizes local uncertainty and that the progress-aware direction converges to true steepest descent as the posterior sharpens. Empirically, GRAPE demonstrates superior query efficiency across high-dimensional tasks: in black-box adversarial attacks, it achieves an average 5.4$\times$ speedup over baselines, and on large language model prompt optimization tasks, it outperforms the second best method by a reduction of 3.8 log-units in the final average regret.

AI.tldr: GRAPE is a two-stage framework for optimizing expensive, high-dimensional black-box functions that addresses over-conservative steps in local Bayesian optimization by first sharpening gradient posterior via closed-form acquisition, then selecting directions by maximizing expected decrease conditional on descent.
AI.motivation: Existing local Bayesian optimization techniques prioritize probability of descent over magnitude of progress, leading to overly conservative steps with negligible improvement and wasted queries on directions that are nearly certain to descend but offer little decrease.
AI.method: GRAPE employs a two-stage approach: (1) Gradient Refinement - sharpens the local gradient posterior via a closed-form acquisition function, monotonically minimizing local uncertainty; (2) Progress-Aware Exploitation - selects update directions by maximizing expected decrease conditional on descent, converging to true steepest descent as posterior sharpens.
AI.result: Empirically, GRAPE achieves 5.4x speedup in black-box adversarial attacks and reduces final average regret by 3.8 log-units in LLM prompt optimization compared to baselines.
AI.conclusion: The theoretical analysis confirms gradient refinement monotonically minimizes uncertainty while progress-aware direction selection converges to true steepest descent. GRAPE demonstrates superior query efficiency across high-dimensional tasks.

title: BixBench3: Benchmarking AI agents on research-study-scale computational biology tasks
summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) promises to accelerate biological research by automating computational analyses. Yet the ability of AI agents to carry out computational biology at the scale of complete research studies has not been systematically evaluated. Here we introduce BixBench3, a benchmark that measures the capacity of AI agents to process raw biological data through to scientific results. We designed BixBench3 tasks to mirror the delegation of work from a scientist to an agent: the scientist chooses the research question and high-level methods, then delegates implementation of all analyses to the agent. In each task, an agent receives a research objective, methodological guidance, and raw data derived from a published scientific study, and must execute a sequence of analyses to achieve the research objective. The data artifacts resulting from these analyses - such as peak call matrices or differential expression tables - are programmatically graded against the corresponding artifacts generated and reported in the original study. Across 20 BixBench3 tasks encompassing the generation of 138 unique artifacts, we find that 13 frontier models achieve scores ranging from 0.00 for Gemini 3.1 Flash Lite to 0.48 for GPT 5.6 Sol. Agents perform worse on tasks with larger raw datasets (0.36 on tasks with <100 GB versus 0.10 on tasks with >100 GB) and on analyses requiring more sequential steps (0.36 at 1-2 steps vs 0.24 at 3+). On average, agents use 6.8 hours, 102 million tokens, and $43 to complete each task, with the longest attempts consuming 24 hours, 1.07 billion tokens, and $525. Notably, the highest-scoring agents used fewer tokens and were cheaper than less performant options. These results reveal that LLMs vary substantially in their ability to (1) execute multiple sequential analysis steps coherently, (2) manage large quantities of raw data, and (3) work across scientific domains.

AI.tldr: BixBench3 is a benchmark evaluating AI agents' ability to conduct complete computational biology research studies. Testing 13 frontier models across 20 tasks (138 unique artifacts), scores ranged from 0.00 to 0.48, with performance degradation on larger datasets (>100 GB) and more sequential steps (3+).
AI.motivation: To systematically evaluate whether AI agents can carry out computational biology at the scale of complete research studies, automating the full pipeline from raw data to scientific results.
AI.method: Benchmark tasks mirror scientist-to-agent delegation: agents receive research objectives, methodological guidance, and raw data from published studies, then execute analysis sequences. Results are programmatically graded against artifacts from original studies.
AI.result: 13 frontier models achieved scores from 0.00 (Gemini 3.1 Flash Lite) to 0.48 (GPT 5.6 Sol). Performance drops on larger datasets (0.36 for <100 GB vs 0.10 for >100 GB) and more steps (0.36 for 1-2 steps vs 0.24 for 3+). Average resource usage: 6.8 hours, 102M tokens, $43 per task. Highest-scoring agents used fewer tokens and were cheaper.
AI.conclusion: LLMs vary substantially in their ability to execute multiple sequential analysis steps coherently, manage large quantities of raw data, and work across scientific domains. Current AI agents have significant limitations in handling complex, multi-step computational biology workflows at scale.

title: PIVOT: A Multi-Trajectory Dataset and Testbed for Pose, Intrinsics, and Novel Viewpoint Evaluation in Real-World 3D Reconstruction
summary:
Neural radiance fields (NeRFs), 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS), and related novel-view synthesis methods are commonly evaluated under capture and reconstruction conditions cleaner than those encountered by robots, drones, and autonomous systems. Benchmarks often rely on reconstruction-friendly trajectories, optimized camera poses and intrinsics, and held-out views sampled from trajectories represented during training. These assumptions can obscure performance with measured poses, reusable camera calibration, and structurally different camera paths.
  We introduce PIVOT (Pose, Intrinsics and Viewpoint Oriented Testbed), a multi-trajectory dataset, processing pipeline, and evaluation framework for independently studying these factors. PIVOT captures each scene using diverse camera trajectories and retains, where available, both sensor-derived measured poses and COLMAP-optimized poses, together with calibrated and optimized camera intrinsics. It defines three benchmark families: (1) seen versus unseen trajectory novel-view generalization, (2) measured versus optimized pose sensitivity, and (3) calibrated versus optimized intrinsics sensitivity. We also introduce a directed pose-space Chamfer distance to quantify how well training poses cover an evaluation trajectory.
  PIVOT v1 contains five real-world scenes captured with a DJI Mini 4 Pro and provides an open processing and Nerfstudio-based evaluation toolchain. Benchmark results show a consistent quality gap between held-out views on represented trajectories and unseen trajectories, as well as substantial sensitivity to pose source and camera intrinsics.

AI.tldr: PIVOT is a multi-trajectory dataset and evaluation framework for assessing NeRF and 3DGS methods under real-world conditions rather than ideal laboratory settings. It addresses the gap between benchmark evaluation (clean conditions, optimized poses) and practical robot/drone/autonomous system deployment.
AI.motivation: Current novel-view synthesis benchmarks use reconstruction-friendly trajectories, optimized camera poses/intrinsics, and held-out views from training trajectories. These ideal conditions obscure real-world performance when robots, drones, and autonomous systems encounter measured poses, reusable camera calibration, and structurally different camera paths.
AI.method: PIVOT provides: (1) Multi-trajectory dataset with 5 real-world scenes captured by DJI Mini 4 Pro, (2) Processing pipeline with both sensor-derived measured poses and COLMAP-optimized poses, (3) Calibrated and optimized camera intrinsics, (4) Three benchmark families: seen vs unseen trajectory generalization, measured vs optimized pose sensitivity, and calibrated vs optimized intrinsics sensitivity, (5) Directed pose-space Chamfer distance to quantify training pose coverage of evaluation trajectories.
AI.result: Benchmark results reveal: (1) Consistent quality gap between held-out views on represented trajectories and unseen trajectories, (2) Substantial sensitivity to pose source (measured vs optimized), (3) Significant sensitivity to camera intrinsics (calibrated vs optimized). The dataset includes an open processing and Nerfstudio-based evaluation toolchain.
AI.conclusion: PIVOT provides a more realistic evaluation framework for novel-view synthesis methods, demonstrating that current benchmarks may overestimate performance in practical deployment scenarios. The framework enables independent study of trajectory generalization, pose sensitivity, and intrinsics sensitivity - factors critical for robotics and autonomous systems applications.

title: Toward Machine Learning with the Unit as a Primitive: Learning from Unit-Linked Events
summary: Machine learning is usually formalized through samples, while the persistent individual to which multiple observed or possible events refer often remains implicit. We propose the \emph{unit} as an explicit primitive at the level of task semantics. A learning task first declares a population of persistent referents and a sameness criterion; the realized value $u$ denotes the selected referent. Supervised learning is the main formal specialization. Its semantic object is a family of unit-conditioned response laws. Homogeneity is the special case in which those laws coincide; a sample-only conditional is silent as to whether the world is homogeneous or the observed law is only the marginal of a heterogeneous family. What is learned from data is a pair $(T_φ,R_θ)$: a tokenizer that produces a contextual unit token and one shared response-law form that reads it. The structured class takes that form to be a simple relation in the token; a linear predictor is the running instance. The token is the learner-side representation through which the task-side unit affects prediction, while a learner specification that omits unit information is unit-insensitive; homogeneity remains a property of the world-side response family. When identity is unresolved, the world-side law mixes unit-conditioned targets, while the learner composes its shared form with a token. A trusted resolver may fix the unit and supply a lookup token; otherwise \emph{unit abduction} forms a token of the same type from factual evidence. Unlinked single-row observations can fail to distinguish a heterogeneous unit world from a homogeneous pooled world; trusted same-unit pairs separate a restricted witness. The formal results concern this supervised specialization.

title: FinRiskAtlas: Decision-Aligned Evaluation of Large Language Models for Financial Risk Review
summary: Deploying large language models for professional financial review requires more than measuring general financial competence: models must perform the specific review operation required by a workflow and determine whether available evidence is sufficient for a defensible decision. Existing financial benchmarks cover knowledge, reasoning, compliance, and professional tasks, but their evaluation units are often organized around datasets or task formulations rather than the decisions that deployed systems support. We introduce FinRiskAtlas, a Chinese-language benchmark that evaluates financial LLMs along two complementary dimensions: operation execution under fixed evidence states and evidence-state control under evolving review conditions. The static benchmark contains 9,742 instances across 53 task families, including 42 Domain Knowledge families and eleven downstream review operations defined by explicit evaluation contracts. FinRisk-Ask extends this framework through offline replay of 680 pre-action states from 104 de-identified professional trajectories, withholding future evidence during inference and using it only to construct expert-verified evidence targets. Across 33 model configurations, operation-level evaluation yields non-redundant rankings (mean pairwise Spearman correlation 0.42 across downstream operations), and knowledge-based shortlisting can incur up to 18.01 points of regret on individual operations. FinRisk-Ask further shows that entering the Ask branch more frequently does not necessarily improve request targeting or end-to-end evidence acquisition. These results show that broad financial capability scores do not fully capture where models are reliable in professional workflows, motivating evaluation units aligned with the decisions and evidence states that deployed systems must support.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces FinRiskAtlas, a Chinese-language benchmark for evaluating financial LLMs along two dimensions: operation execution under fixed evidence states and evidence-state control under evolving review conditions. The benchmark contains 9,742 instances across 53 task families and evaluates models on both domain knowledge and downstream review operations, with results showing that broad capability scores fail to capture model reliability in professional workflows.
AI.motivation: Existing financial benchmarks evaluate general financial competence but fail to assess whether models can perform specific review operations required by workflows and determine if available evidence is sufficient for defensible decisions. The evaluation units are organized around datasets rather than the decisions that deployed systems must support.
AI.method: FinRiskAtlas contains 9,742 instances across 53 task families (42 Domain Knowledge families + 11 downstream review operations). FinRisk-Ask extends this through offline replay of 680 pre-action states from 104 de-identified professional trajectories, withholding future evidence during inference and using it only to construct expert-verified evidence targets. 33 model configurations were tested.
AI.result: Operation-level evaluation yields non-redundant rankings (mean pairwise Spearman correlation 0.42 across downstream operations). Knowledge-based shortlisting can incur up to 18.01 points of regret on individual operations. Entering the Ask branch more frequently does not necessarily improve request targeting or end-to-end evidence acquisition.
AI.conclusion: Broad financial capability scores do not fully capture where models are reliable in professional workflows. Evaluation should be aligned with the specific decisions and evidence states that deployed systems must support.

title: AdaptiveEmbed: Sample-Adaptive Multi-Vector Representation for Multimodal Retrieval
summary: Multi-vector representations have emerged as an effective paradigm for multimodal retrieval, representing each sample with multiple complementary embeddings to capture fine-grained cross-modal information. However, existing approaches typically employ a fixed representation capacity, assigning the same number of vectors to all samples regardless of their individual retrieval demands. Such a fixed-capacity formulation overlooks the fact that different samples may require different amounts of representation capacity for effective retrieval. In this work, we introduce \emph{Sample-Adaptive Multi-Vector Representation} (SAMVR), a new problem setting for multimodal retrieval that studies how multi-vector representation capacity can be allocated at the sample level. Under SAMVR, each sample is represented by a \emph{content-adaptive embedding set} (CAES), whose capacity is determined according to the sample-specific retrieval utility of additional representation vectors. To instantiate SAMVR, we propose \emph{AdaptiveEmbed}, a unified framework for learning sample-adaptive multi-vector representations. AdaptiveEmbed learns structured multi-vector representations through \emph{Multi-Group Contrastive Learning} (MGCL) with the symmetric \emph{set-to-set similarity} (SetSim), and further employs \emph{Utility Policy Optimization} (UPO) to determine sample-specific representation capacity via \emph{Marginal Utility Allocation} (MUA). Experiments across multimodal retrieval benchmarks involving image, text, video, and audio show that sample-adaptive capacity allocation achieves overall better retrieval performance than fixed-capacity multi-vector representations, validating the effectiveness of SAMVR for multimodal retrieval. These results establish SAMVR as a viable formulation for adaptive capacity allocation in multi-vector multimodal retrieval.

title: Multimodal Injury Risk Prediction in Tennis
comment: 7 pages, 2 figures, 5 tables. Published in the 2025 IEEE 5th International Conference on Human-Machine Systems (ICHMS)
summary: Machine learning has had a significant positive impact on the prediction of athlete performance and injury risk. Most works in this field rely on subjective observations and expert assessments, which restrict their effectiveness. In sports like soccer, basketball, and wrestling, some studies attempt to address this challenge by integrating data from alternative sources, such as readings from wearable devices, alongside traditional subjective observations and expert assessments to enhance accuracy. However, similar research in tennis remains largely unexplored. In this paper, we propose a multimodal Predictive Athlete Readiness framework for Tennis (PART) to assess both performance and injury risk in tennis players. By leveraging machine learning and deep learning techniques, PART processes multiple sources of data collected from nine collegiate tennis players, including physiological metrics, training and match data, sleep data from wearable devices, self-reported information via daily questionnaires, jump assessments, and motion analysis from match play videos. PART captures four characteristics of tennis players: overall wellness, injury risk, physical capability, and playing style. By integrating these four characteristics by supervised learning, it is capable of providing a holistic assessment of the tennis athlete's condition, along with advanced forecasts of specific body areas at risk such as the upper body (e.g., elbows) or lower body (e.g., knees). Our evaluation, conducted with data from nine collegiate tennis players, shows that PART achieves strong performance in predicting both overall wellness and injury risk. Additionally, our framework also shows promise for recreational tennis players, who often suffer from injuries due to incorrect playing techniques.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes PART (Predictive Athlete Readiness framework for Tennis), a multimodal machine learning framework for assessing tennis player performance and injury risk. Using data from nine collegiate tennis players—including physiological metrics, training/match data, sleep data from wearables, self-reported questionnaires, jump assessments, and motion analysis—the framework captures four characteristics: overall wellness, injury risk, physical capability, and playing style. It integrates these through supervised learning to provide holistic athlete assessments and predict injury risk for specific body areas (e.g., elbows, knees).
AI.motivation: While machine learning has improved athlete performance and injury prediction, most approaches rely on subjective observations and expert assessments, limiting their effectiveness. Although some sports (soccer, basketball, wrestling) have integrated alternative data sources like wearable devices, similar research in tennis remains largely unexplored. This work addresses this gap by developing a comprehensive multimodal framework specifically for tennis players.
AI.method: The PART framework employs machine learning and deep learning techniques to process nine types of data collected from nine collegiate tennis players: (1) physiological metrics, (2) training and match data, (3) sleep data from wearable devices, (4) self-reported information via daily questionnaires, (5) jump assessments, and (6) motion analysis from match play videos. The framework captures four key characteristics of tennis players—overall wellness, injury risk, physical capability, and playing style—and integrates them through supervised learning to provide holistic assessments and predict injuries to specific body areas (upper body: elbows; lower body: knees).
AI.result: Evaluation with data from nine collegiate tennis players demonstrates that PART achieves strong performance in predicting both overall wellness and injury risk. Additionally, the framework shows promise for recreational tennis players, who often suffer injuries due to incorrect playing techniques.
AI.conclusion: The PART framework successfully integrates multimodal data sources to provide comprehensive assessment of tennis athletes and predict injury risk. Its effectiveness for both collegiate and recreational tennis players suggests potential for broader application in tennis performance and injury prevention.

title: Learning What to Share and What to Personalize: Hierarchical Strategy Co-Evolution for Agent Memory
summary: Memory-augmented agents maintain compact user profiles throughout extended conversations, enabling personalized and consistent responses without the need to process the entire dialogue history. The quality of these user profiles relies on the underlying memory management strategy: at each step, the agent must determine what to retain, compress, or discard. However, existing methods typically employ a static, one-size-fits-all strategy established before training. In practice, the optimal memory decision is inherently user-specific and dynamically evolves alongside policy optimization. To address this, we propose \textbf{HiPS} (\textbf{Hi}erarchical \textbf{P}ersonalized \textbf{S}trategy), a framework that decouples memory management into a globally shared foundation and a user-specific adaptive tier. Specifically, HiPS employs \textbf{Universal Strategy} to extract shared principles from cross-persona trajectories, alongside \textbf{Persona Delta Distillation} to generate tailored rules for users whose behaviors diverge from general patterns. \textbf{Cross-Level Rule Flow} dynamically calibrates their boundary by promoting broadly validated personal rules and demoting contradicted global ones. The architecture establishes a co-evolution loop where a mechanism guarantees that all strategy refinements are anchored to task outcomes. Extensive experiments demonstrate consistent improvements over memory-augmented baselines.
