title: Bootstrapping a 4D LiDAR Annotation Tool from Video Foundation Models
summary: Progress in 4D LiDAR segmentation is bottlenecked by data. Assigning temporally consistent labels across sparse point cloud sequences is costly and hard to scale, and every new task or domain tends to demand fresh dense annotation. This motivates a simple question of whether high-quality LiDAR training data can be produced automatically, without any human labeling. To this end, we introduce LiDAR-SAM2, a framework that turns a 2D video foundation model, SAM2, into a scalable source of supervision for the 4D LiDAR domain. On the data side, it automatically generates temporally coherent LiDAR-level labels from SAM2 video masks through multi-view projection and spatio-temporal aggregation. On the modeling side, a tailored modality interface and a two-stage learning objective adapt SAM2's video segmentation kernel to spatio-temporal LiDAR structure, so that a single click per object yields a consistent mask track across the sequence. Trained with no human LiDAR annotation, LiDAR-SAM2 produces semantic and panoptic labels on SemanticKITTI that approach the quality of full human annotation from only a few points, and models trained on these labels approach the performance of full ground-truth supervision. This positions LiDAR-SAM2 as a scalable labeling tool that substantially reduces the annotation burden for 3D and 4D scene understanding.

AI.tldr: LiDAR-SAM2 automatically generates 4D LiDAR segmentation labels using a 2D video foundation model (SAM2), eliminating the need for human annotation. It produces temporally coherent labels through multi-view projection and spatio-temporal aggregation, achieving near-human annotation quality on SemanticKITTI.
AI.motivation: Progress in 4D LiDAR segmentation is bottlenecked by data - manual labeling is costly, hard to scale, and new tasks/domains require fresh dense annotations. The paper seeks to produce high-quality LiDAR training data automatically without human labeling.
AI.method: LiDAR-SAM2 has two main components: (1) Data side - automatically generates temporally coherent LiDAR-level labels from SAM2 video masks through multi-view projection and spatio-temporal aggregation; (2) Modeling side - a tailored modality interface and two-stage learning objective adapt SAM2's video segmentation kernel to spatio-temporal LiDAR structure, enabling single-click per object to yield consistent mask tracks across sequences.
AI.result: LiDAR-SAM2 produces semantic and panoptic labels on SemanticKITTI that approach the quality of full human annotation from only a few points. Models trained on these auto-generated labels approach the performance of models trained on full ground-truth supervision.
AI.conclusion: LiDAR-SAM2 positions itself as a scalable labeling tool that substantially reduces the annotation burden for 3D and 4D scene understanding, with potential to democratize LiDAR segmentation research by eliminating manual annotation bottlenecks.

title: When Does Context Routing Help? A Systematic Study of Multi-Modal Fusion in Time Series Forecasting
summary:
Multi-modal time series forecasting methods integrate auxiliary context into temporal predictions through increasingly sophisticated fusion mechanisms. A growing body of work reports substantial gains, yet it is often unclear whether they reflect genuine use of the context or incidental architectural effects. We ask a narrower, checkable question: when can auxiliary context help a forecaster at all?
  We identify two dataset-level conditions that must both hold: (1) the target is not dominated by a last-value shortcut (low autocorrelation rho_h), and (2) the context carries information about the target beyond history (non-zero conditional mutual information delta; when delta=0 no predictor can benefit---a distribution-free result). Through controlled experiments on MoME (a 14.3B-parameter mixture-of-experts model, 6 datasets, 10 seeds) and four additional fusion mechanisms implemented within a single-backbone testbed (5 datasets), we find that when both conditions hold, text-conditioned expert modulation contributes a sizeable MSE reduction; when either fails, the contribution collapses to the capacity floor of the modulation pathway and carries no context-attributable signal.
  We establish causality through two interventions: adding a shortcut to MoME suppresses routing contribution by 77-93% across 3 datasets; progressively corrupting context quality drives the context-specific benefit from +44% to negative. We validate the autocorrelation component of our diagnostic on 27 Monash Archive datasets. We provide a calibrated pre-training diagnostic that, on the datasets we test, yields no false positives in well-powered settings. We are explicit about the asymmetry of our evidence: the negative arm is broadly reliable, while the large positive magnitudes come from a single model family (MoME) and are corroborated only in direction by the testbed.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates when auxiliary context (e.g., text) can genuinely improve time series forecasting. It identifies two necessary conditions: (1) low autocorrelation (target not dominated by last-value shortcut) and (2) non-zero conditional mutual information (context carries beyond-history information). Through experiments on a 14.3B-parameter MoME model and additional fusion mechanisms, the authors find substantial MSE reduction only when both conditions hold. They establish causality through interventions showing that shortcuts suppress routing contribution by 77-93% and context corruption drives benefit from +44% to negative.
AI.motivation: Multi-modal time series forecasting methods report substantial gains from integrating auxiliary context, but it's unclear whether these gains reflect genuine use of context or incidental architectural effects. The authors seek to determine when context can actually help a forecaster.
AI.method: The authors identify two dataset-level conditions required for context to help: (1) low autocorrelation (rho_h) indicating target is not dominated by last-value shortcut, and (2) non-zero conditional mutual information (delta) meaning context carries information beyond history. They conduct controlled experiments on MoME (14.3B-parameter mixture-of-experts, 6 datasets, 10 seeds) and four additional fusion mechanisms in a single-backbone testbed (5 datasets). They establish causality through two interventions: adding a shortcut to MoME and progressively corrupting context quality.
AI.result: When both conditions hold, text-conditioned expert modulation yields sizeable MSE reduction. When either condition fails, contribution collapses to the capacity floor. Adding a shortcut suppresses routing contribution by 77-93% across 3 datasets; corrupting context quality drives context-specific benefit from +44% to negative. The autocorrelation diagnostic validated on 27 Monash Archive datasets shows no false positives in well-powered settings.
AI.conclusion: Auxiliary context can only help time series forecasting when the target has low autocorrelation (not dominated by last-value persistence) AND the context carries non-zero predictive information beyond historical data. The authors provide a calibrated pre-training diagnostic that reliably predicts when context will help, though they acknowledge the asymmetry of evidence: the negative findings are broadly reliable while large positive magnitudes come primarily from a single model family (MoME).

title: Where vs What: Decomposing Structural and Content Failures in LLM-Generated Structured Outputs
summary: Structured outputs such as JSON and tables are central to modern LLM-based systems, yet generation failures are evaluated monolithically, conflating two distinct error modes: placement errors (correct values at wrong positions) and value errors (wrong values at intended positions). We introduce Structure-Content Decomposition (SCD), a framework that independently measures structural fidelity and content accuracy. Applying SCD to nested JSON and table tasks across six models (7B to frontier), we uncover a consistent phenomenon: structural fidelity degrades earlier and more sharply than content accuracy as complexity increases. At the highest complexity, even DeepSeek-V4-Flash (with reasoning) misplaces 35% of recalled values, while Qwen2.5-7B misplaces 74%. Controlled ablations suggest that this pattern is associated with reliance on semantic shortcuts rather than topological understanding of output structure. Based on these findings, we propose SA-RLVR, converting SCD metrics into verifiable rewards for reinforcement learning via GRPO. SA-RLVR successfully optimizes structural addressing across distinct topologies: it lifts JSON Value Placement Accuracy (VPA) from 26% to 63% while generalizing to held-out schemas; moreover, it consistently drives VPA improvements in the table domain, demonstrating that structure-aware rewards can directly enhance multi-domain structural positioning.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Structure-Content Decomposition (SCD), a framework that separately measures structural fidelity and content accuracy in LLM-generated structured outputs (JSON/tables). The authors discover that structural fidelity degrades faster than content accuracy as complexity increases, and propose SA-RLVR, a reinforcement learning approach using SCD metrics as rewards, which improved JSON Value Placement Accuracy from 26% to 63%.
AI.motivation: Current evaluation of structured output generation fails monolithically, conflating placement errors (correct values at wrong positions) with value errors (wrong values at intended positions). This prevents understanding the root causes of generation failures and developing targeted improvements.
AI.method: The authors propose (1) Structure-Content Decomposition (SCD) framework to independently measure structural fidelity and content accuracy; (2) SA-RLVR, converting SCD metrics into verifiable rewards for reinforcement learning via GRPO to optimize structural addressing across different topologies.
AI.result: Across six models (7B to frontier) on nested JSON and table tasks: structural fidelity degrades earlier and more sharply than content accuracy as complexity increases. At highest complexity, DeepSeek-V4-Flash misplaces 35% of recalled values while Qwen2.5-7B misplaces 74%. Ablations suggest this stems from reliance on semantic shortcuts rather than topological understanding. SA-RLVR successfully lifts JSON VPA from 26% to 63% and generalizes to held-out schemas, with consistent improvements in table domain.
AI.conclusion: Structure-aware rewards (SA-RLVR) can directly enhance multi-domain structural positioning in LLM outputs. The key insight is that LLMs rely on semantic shortcuts rather than understanding output structure topology, and this can be addressed through targeted reinforcement learning with structural fidelity metrics.

title: Saliency-Depth Conditioning for Zero-Shot Segmentation of Communication-Tower Components in Cluttered UAV Imagery
summary: Fine-grained segmentation of communication-tower components in UAV imagery is essential for automated inspection, yet task-specific models are hard to develop due to limited instance-level annotations. Zero-shot segmentation models offer a promising alternative, but in cluttered scenes, visually similar background structures interfere with component localization, causing missed instances and false positives. We propose a model-agnostic saliency-depth foreground-conditioning strategy combining appearance-based saliency with monocular relative depth to construct a coarse tower prior and suppress irrelevant content. We integrate this module with Grounded-SAM and SAM 3, yielding SD-Grounded-SAM and SD-SAM 3. SD-Grounded-SAM further applies geometric and depth-aware box refinement before mask generation, while SD-SAM 3 relies on SAM 3's internal setup. On TOW-300, a dataset of 340 communication-tower UAV images, our strategy improves both baselines: SD-SAM 3 achieves the strongest instance-segmentation performance, while SD-Grounded-SAM produces fewer false positives. Ablations confirm complementary gains from saliency, depth, and box refinement, improving robustness in cluttered scenes.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses fine-grained segmentation of communication-tower components in UAV imagery using zero-shot segmentation models. The authors propose a saliency-depth foreground-conditioning strategy that combines appearance-based saliency with monocular relative depth to create a coarse tower prior and suppress irrelevant background. This module is integrated with Grounded-SAM and SAM 3, resulting in SD-Grounded-SAM and SD-SAM 3. On the TOW-300 dataset (340 images), SD-SAM 3 achieves the best instance-segmentation performance while SD-Grounded-SAM produces fewer false positives.
AI.motivation: The key motivation is to overcome two challenges: (1) limited instance-level annotations making it difficult to develop task-specific models, and (2) visually similar background structures causing missed instances and false positives in cluttered scenes when using zero-shot segmentation models.
AI.method: The proposed method is a model-agnostic saliency-depth foreground-conditioning strategy that combines appearance-based saliency with monocular relative depth to construct a coarse tower prior and suppress irrelevant content. This module is integrated with two baselines: (1) Grounded-SAM, which additionally applies geometric and depth-aware box refinement before mask generation, and (2) SAM 3, which uses its internal setup.
AI.result: On TOW-300 dataset (340 communication-tower UAV images), the strategy improves both baselines. SD-SAM 3 achieves the strongest instance-segmentation performance, while SD-Grounded-SAM produces fewer false positives. Ablation studies confirm complementary gains from saliency, depth, and box refinement, improving robustness in cluttered scenes.
AI.conclusion: The saliency-depth foreground-conditioning strategy is effective for improving zero-shot segmentation models in cluttered UAV imagery of communication towers. The combination of appearance-based saliency and monocular depth provides complementary benefits, with different trade-offs between recall (SD-SAM 3) and precision (SD-Grounded-SAM).

title: Rethinking the Transferable Adversarial Attacks and Robust Defense in Federated Learning
summary: The development of federated learning (FL) techniques has helped improve the privacy preservation of users' data and extended the applications of machine learning models. However, the involvement of a large number of users in FL also creates open opportunities for different adversaries, such as poisoning attacks, Byzantine attacks, and adversarial example attacks. Yet, recent research has disclosed that existing poisoning attacks and Byzantine attacks can not achieve satisfactory penetration in realistic FL scenarios caused by strong assumptions, \textit{e.g.,} client selection rate, and the ratio of malicious attackers. In this paper, the transferability of adversarial examples among different client models is analyzed to understand the relation between adversarial examples and clients' data distribution. Moreover, to mitigate the attacks of transferable adversarial examples, we design a defense mechanism stemming from the transferability of model robustness by adversarial training. As a result, through theoretical analysis of transferability, we gain insights into adversarial examples and the vulnerability of federated learning systems. Our proposed adversarial attack and defense methods are evaluated via real-life datasets in various settings to show their performance over the existing state-of-the-art methods.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes the transferability of adversarial examples in federated learning and proposes a defense mechanism using adversarial training. It addresses limitations of existing poisoning and Byzantine attacks in realistic FL scenarios by examining how adversarial examples transfer across client models with different data distributions.
AI.motivation: Existing poisoning and Byzantine attacks in federated learning fail to achieve satisfactory penetration in realistic scenarios due to strong assumptions about client selection rates and malicious attacker ratios. The authors aim to understand the relationship between adversarial examples and clients' data distribution through transferability analysis, and develop effective defenses against transferable adversarial attacks.
AI.method: 1) Analyze the transferability of adversarial examples among different client models to understand their relationship with data distribution; 2) Design a defense mechanism based on adversarial training that leverages the transferability of model robustness; 3) Validate proposed methods through real-life datasets under various settings.
AI.result: The paper provides theoretical insights into adversarial examples and the vulnerability of federated learning systems. The proposed adversarial attack and defense methods demonstrate superior performance over existing state-of-the-art methods when evaluated on real-life datasets.
AI.conclusion: Through theoretical analysis of transferability, the authors gain insights into adversarial example behavior and FL system vulnerabilities. The proposed attack and defense approaches outperform current state-of-the-art methods, offering more practical and effective solutions for security in federated learning environments.

title: Can your AI agent be cheaper? Investigating the effects of task specifications on token spend in agentic coding tasks
summary: Agentic coding workflows are now widely deployed in real-world systems. With long-horizon reasoning and tool use, token usage has become an important consideration for both cost and efficiency. Two engineers using AI will solve the same problem differently. How the specification of a task shapes an agent's token spend, and whether that spend can be predicted in advance, are open questions. Here, we study the effects of different task specifications on agentic token spend with the Kimi K3 model at three thinking efforts. Across $2,700$ runs, we show that reducing a full task specification to a bare user story raises token spend by $29.7\%$, while run-to-run variance remains unaffected by any prompt changes. We show that prompt-sensitivity is task-dependent, running from $13\%$ to $115\%$. We fit a simple predictor that can price a full distribution of task specifications and thinking effort configurations from a single cheap probe on an unseen task within $36\%$, improving over prior work in predicting token spend. Our work provides initial results quantifying the effects of task specification on agentic token spend and introduces a method that can be used to systematically evaluate the cost of AI coding workflows.

AI.tldr: This paper studies how different task specifications affect token consumption in AI coding agents, using the Kimi K3 model across 2,700 runs. They find that bare user stories increase token spend by ~30% compared to full specifications, and develop a predictor that can estimate token costs within 36% accuracy from a single probe.
AI.motivation: To understand how task specification details affect AI agent token spend, and whether token consumption can be predicted in advance. This is important for cost and efficiency in real-world AI coding deployments.
AI.method: Studied Kimi K3 model at three thinking efforts across 2,700 runs, comparing full task specifications vs bare user stories. Fitted a simple predictor using a single cheap probe on unseen tasks.
AI.result: Reducing to bare user story raises token spend by 29.7%. Run-to-run variance remains unaffected by prompt changes. Prompt-sensitivity ranges from 13% to 115% depending on task. The predictor achieves within 36% accuracy, improving over prior work.
AI.conclusion: Task specification significantly impacts token spend (up to 30% increase with minimal specs), and token consumption can be reasonably predicted from a single probe. This provides a method to systematically evaluate AI coding workflow costs.

title: VGA-BenchV2: An Expanded Unified Benchmark and Multi-Model Framework for Evaluating Video Aesthetics and Generation Quality
summary: We introduce VGA-BenchV2, an extended human-aligned benchmark and optimization framework for jointly evaluating and improving video generation quality and aesthetic value. Built upon VGA-Bench, VGA-BenchV2 preserves the original fine-grained taxonomy with two primary dimensions-Aesthetic and Generation-and 52 sub-dimensions. Guided by this taxonomy, we curate 1,016 diverse prompts and collect over 60,000 videos generated by 12 mainstream video generation models. More importantly, VGA-BenchV2 substantially expands human-labeled supervision by adding 36,000 task-level annotations, including 16,200 for aesthetic quality, 13,200 for aesthetic tagging, and 6,600 for generation quality, corresponding to 13.46x, 11.15x, and 1.55x scale-ups over VGA-Bench, respectively. Leveraging this enlarged annotation corpus, we develop a hybrid evaluator architecture consisting of VAQA-Net for continuous aesthetic scoring and two Qwen-based Large Vision-Language Model evaluators, VTag-Net and VGQA-Net, for aesthetic tagging and generation quality assessment. Extensive experiments demonstrate strong alignment with human judgments across diverse generation models. Beyond evaluation, VGA-BenchV2 further introduces an evaluation-to-optimization pipeline, where the learned aesthetic evaluator serves as a reward model for reinforcement learning-based generator fine-tuning. This closes the loop from benchmark construction and human supervision to automated evaluation and model optimization, enabling video generators to improve not only in realism but also in aesthetic quality and human preference alignment. Resources are available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/BestiVictoryLab/VGA-Bench.

AI.tldr: VGA-BenchV2 is an extended human-aligned benchmark and optimization framework for evaluating and improving video generation quality and aesthetic value. It contains 1,016 prompts, 60,000+ videos from 12 models, and 36,000+ human annotations. The framework includes hybrid evaluators (VAQA-Net, VTag-Net, VGQA-Net) and introduces an evaluation-to-optimization pipeline using reinforcement learning.
AI.motivation: Existing video generation benchmarks lack sufficient human-aligned evaluation metrics, especially for aesthetic quality. The need for comprehensive evaluation across both technical generation quality and aesthetic value, combined with the desire to optimize models based on these metrics, motivated the development of VGA-BenchV2.
AI.method: The framework preserves VGA-Bench's fine-grained taxonomy with two primary dimensions (Aesthetic and Generation) and 52 sub-dimensions. It curates 1,016 diverse prompts and collects over 60,000 videos from 12 mainstream video generation models. A hybrid evaluator architecture is developed: VAQA-Net for continuous aesthetic scoring, VTag-Net for aesthetic tagging, and VGQA-Net for generation quality assessment, all using Qwen-based Large Vision-Language Models. An evaluation-to-optimization pipeline is introduced using the learned aesthetic evaluator as a reward model for reinforcement learning-based generator fine-tuning.
AI.result: VGA-BenchV2 substantially expands human-labeled supervision with 36,000 task-level annotations (16,200 for aesthetic quality, 13,200 for aesthetic tagging, 6,600 for generation quality), representing 13.46x, 11.15x, and 1.55x scale-ups over VGA-Bench respectively. Extensive experiments demonstrate strong alignment with human judgments across diverse generation models.
AI.conclusion: VGA-BenchV2 successfully closes the loop from benchmark construction and human supervision to automated evaluation and model optimization. It enables video generators to improve not only in realism but also in aesthetic quality and human preference alignment through the evaluation-to-optimization pipeline.

title: Drift Variation Autoencoder: Unifying Generation and Representation Learning through Conditional Posterior Flow Matching
summary: Stochastic masking, cropping, or modality removal makes deterministic reconstruction an incomplete target: one observation can admit many clean completions. This work takes the corresponding posterior $P(X\mid C)$ as the common statistical object for conditional generation and generatively sufficient representation learning. Drift Variation autoencoder trains a masked encoder $Z=E(C)$ and a conditional flow decoder with one clean-prediction Flow Matching loss. The analysis first decomposes the ideal conditional KL into generator approximation and the representation deficiency $I(X;C\mid Z)$. It then derives orthogonal risk decompositions for conditional Flow Matching. For an affine Gaussian path, the clean-prediction representation gap is zero if and only if $P(X\mid Z)=P(X\mid C)$. Thus the encoder-dependent excess clean-prediction risk induced by Flow Matching and the profiled ideal conditional KL have the same posterior-sufficient zero set, without being numerically equal objectives. An exact conditional field with a zero-noise endpoint then generates $P(X\mid Z)$ and hence $P(X\mid C)$ at a joint ideal optimum. The result extends to continuous multimodal product spaces when the complete modality tuple remains the Flow target for every observation mask. On CrossGeom-4, an 18-run controlled benchmark, observable factors have linear-probe $R^2$ of $0.9990$-$0.9992$, shuffling the joint model's encoder condition increases conditional error by $13.5\times$-$15.7\times$, and joint target attention reduces disagreement on an unobserved factor shared by two outputs by $90.1$-$92.8\%$ relative to independent target decoders. Visible modalities are also generated and reconstructed, directly validating the full-tuple objective. Unconditional mode balance remains imperfect, delimiting the empirical claim to a controlled multimodal proof of concept.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses the problem of incomplete deterministic reconstruction in stochastic masking/cropping/modality removal scenarios. It proposes Drift Variation Autoencoder (DVAE), which uses a masked encoder and conditional flow decoder with Flow Matching loss to learn the posterior P(X|C) for conditional generation and representation learning. The theoretical analysis shows that for affine Gaussian paths, the representation gap is zero iff P(X|Z) = P(X|C). Empirical results on CrossGeom-4 show excellent linear-probe R² (0.9990-0.9992) and significant improvements from joint target attention.
AI.motivation: The core problem is that stochastic masking, cropping, or modality removal creates ambiguity - one observation can admit many clean completions. Traditional deterministic reconstruction is insufficient. The work aims to model the posterior P(X|C) as the fundamental statistical object for both conditional generation and representation learning.
AI.method:
The proposed method Drift Variation Autoencoder (DVAE) consists of:
1. Masked encoder Z = E(C) that processes incomplete observations
2. Conditional flow decoder using Flow Matching loss for clean prediction
3. Theoretical analysis decomposing ideal conditional KL and deriving orthogonal risk decompositions
4. Joint target attention mechanism for multimodal settings
5. Exact conditional field with zero-noise endpoint for generating P(X|Z)
AI.result:
On CrossGeom-4 (18-run controlled benchmark):
- Linear-probe R² for observable factors: 0.9990-0.9992
- Shuffling encoder condition increases conditional error by 13.5×-15.7×
- Joint target attention reduces disagreement on unobserved factor by 90.1-92.8% relative to independent decoders
- Visible modalities are generated and reconstructed, validating full-tuple objective
AI.conclusion: The theoretical analysis establishes that encoder-dependent excess clean-prediction risk and profiled ideal conditional KL share the same posterior-sufficient zero set. The empirical results demonstrate a controlled multimodal proof of concept where representation learning successfully captures the posterior structure. Limitation: Unconditional mode balance remains imperfect, bounding the empirical claim to a controlled proof of concept.

title: Paint What You See: Benchmarking Dexterous Visual Tool Use in Multimodal Agents
summary: Evaluation is shifting from static QA toward agentic settings where models act through external tools. We identify a critical yet underexplored capability within this space - dexterous visual tool use: fine-grained, closed-loop parameterized visual action in which models infer tool parameters from visual evidence, and those parameters directly govern the final result. Existing benchmarks cover web navigation, GUI operation, and software engineering, but rarely target this coupling between visual evidence and execution precision. We propose EASEL, a benchmark evaluating a controlled instance of dexterous visual tool use that adopts reference-guided visual reconstruction as its primary proxy task: the agent incrementally paints a canvas to match a reference image. EASEL additionally includes semantic tasks spanning region annotation, handwriting, and path planning. We further provide EASEL-Data, a 440k-sample two-stage curriculum dataset for trajectory supervision, and EASEL-9B to investigate its effect on this capability. Evaluation of 25 models reveals that current multimodal agents systematically struggle on EASEL. Reconstruction similarity bottlenecks at low levels (0.40-0.54), while trajectory diagnostics expose severe closed-loop instability - models typically saturate early or degrade post-peak. Semantic tasks reveal sharp capability boundaries in precision annotation and path planning. EASEL-9B, trained on EASEL-Data, surpasses the base model by a relative 6.3%, ranking third among all evaluated models.

AI.tldr: EASEL is a benchmark for evaluating dexterous visual tool use in multimodal agents, where models infer tool parameters from visual evidence to perform precise visual actions like incremental canvas painting to match reference images. Evaluation of 25 models reveals significant struggles with this capability, while EASEL-9B trained on the 440k-sample EASEL-Data achieves 6.3% relative improvement over the base model.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks cover web navigation, GUI operation, and software engineering, but rarely target the coupling between visual evidence and execution precision in dexterous visual tool use. This capability involves fine-grained, closed-loop parameterized visual action where models infer tool parameters from visual evidence that directly govern the final result.
AI.method: The authors propose EASEL benchmark with reference-guided visual reconstruction as the primary proxy task, where agents incrementally paint a canvas to match a reference image. The benchmark includes semantic tasks spanning region annotation, handwriting, and path planning. They also provide EASEL-Data, a 440k-sample two-stage curriculum dataset for trajectory supervision, and EASEL-9B model trained on this data.
AI.result: Evaluation of 25 models reveals that current multimodal agents systematically struggle on EASEL. Reconstruction similarity bottlenecks at low levels (0.40-0.54), while trajectory diagnostics expose severe closed-loop instability - models typically saturate early or degrade post-peak. Semantic tasks reveal sharp capability boundaries in precision annotation and path planning. EASEL-9B, trained on EASEL-Data, surpasses the base model by a relative 6.3%, ranking third among all evaluated models.
AI.conclusion: The research identifies a critical yet underexplored capability in agentic AI settings - dexterous visual tool use. Current multimodal agents cannot perform well on this benchmark, highlighting significant limitations in their ability to couple visual evidence with execution precision. The EASEL-9B model demonstrates that dedicated training on trajectory supervision data can improve this capability, though substantial room for improvement remains.

title: Automatic weld seam segmentation for industrial quality control: a comparison of RGB and polarimetric imaging with CNN and transformer architectures
summary: Visual inspection of welded assemblies remains one of the least automated stages in many industrial production processes, still depending largely on the experience of human operators and thus subject to inter-operator variability; the manufacturing of special-purpose machinery cabins, the setting of this study, is one representative case. This work evaluates the feasibility of automatic weld seam segmentation from RGB and polarimetric imagery, comparing controlled laboratory acquisitions with images captured under real, uncontrolled conditions. Convolutional neural network (CNN) architectures and transformer-based architectures are benchmarked under a unified, threshold-independent protocol, training each CNN with three random seeds to separate genuine effects from seed noise. In controlled RGB conditions, CNN models reach a mean mask mAP50 of up to 0.87, but drop to 0.22-0.48 under uncontrolled acquisition, showing that the acquisition setup is a first-order component of the inspection system. Polarimetric imaging with alignment-preserving geometric augmentation localizes previously unseen welds with a mean mask mAP50 up to 0.93: on par with, rather than ahead of, the best controlled-RGB result, but reaching that accuracy on uncontrolled RGB without requiring acquisition control. The clearest architectural finding concerns viewpoint robustness. In-distribution, transformers and CNNs are broadly comparable; but under a test-time viewpoint shift, the transformer models, and RF-DETR in particular, retain high accuracy while every CNN collapses. The gap holds across three seeds and a resolution-matched control, pointing to architecture rather than training resolution. Within the CNN family, capacity brings no reliable in-distribution gain once seed variance is accounted for: small CNNs suffice for fixed viewpoints, transformers for variable ones.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates automatic weld seam segmentation from RGB and polarimetric imagery in industrial manufacturing settings. It benchmarks CNNs vs transformers under controlled vs uncontrolled acquisition conditions, finding that transformers (especially RF-DETR) show superior viewpoint robustness while CNNs collapse under viewpoint shifts. Polarimetric imaging achieves mAP50 of 0.93 in uncontrolled conditions without requiring acquisition control.
AI.motivation: Visual inspection of welded assemblies remains largely manual, dependent on human operators with inter-operator variability. The manufacturing of special-purpose machinery cabins represents a representative case where automation is needed but lacking.
AI.method: The study compares convolutional neural network (CNN) architectures with transformer-based architectures under a unified, threshold-independent protocol. Training uses three random seeds per model to separate genuine effects from seed noise. Experiments compare controlled laboratory acquisitions with images captured under real, uncontrolled conditions. Polarimetric imaging with alignment-preserving geometric augmentation is also evaluated.
AI.result: In controlled RGB conditions, CNN models achieve mean mask mAP50 up to 0.87, but performance drops to 0.22-0.48 under uncontrolled acquisition. Polarimetric imaging with alignment-preserving geometric augmentation achieves mean mask mAP50 up to 0.93, reaching accuracy comparable to the best controlled-RGB result but without requiring acquisition control. The key architectural finding shows that while transformers and CNNs perform similarly in-distribution, under test-time viewpoint shift, transformers (particularly RF-DETR) retain high accuracy while all CNN models collapse. This gap persists across three seeds and a resolution-matched control.
AI.conclusion: The acquisition setup is a first-order component of weld inspection systems. Transformers offer superior viewpoint robustness compared to CNNs, making them preferable for variable viewpoints. Within the CNN family, capacity provides no reliable in-distribution gain once seed variance is accounted for—small CNNs suffice for fixed viewpoints. The study demonstrates that polarimetric imaging can achieve high accuracy in uncontrolled industrial environments without requiring strict acquisition control.

title: SNAP-KG: Streaming Node Assignment via Projection for Knowledge Graph Entity Integration
comment: Accepted at the 25th International Semantic Web Conference (ISWC 2026)
summary: Knowledge graph (KG) construction pipelines must continuously integrate newly arriving entities into a growing graph. Unlike inserting triples between existing nodes, a newly arriving entity has no graph connectivity: it emerges from the acquisition phase as a raw feature vector and must be assigned to a semantic community before entity resolution and link prediction can operate over a tractable candidate set. Existing multi-view graph clustering methods exploit multiple relation types as structural views, but are transductive: they assume a fixed graph and cannot assign unseen entities without retraining. We propose SNAP-KG (Streaming Node Assignment via Projection for Knowledge Graph Entity Integration), a framework supporting graph-structural multi-view relational clustering and inductive inference for streaming entities. SNAP-KG trains a projector to map a new entity directly to the learned embedding space using only raw features, enabling immediate cluster assignment without graph access or model retraining. Experiments on five benchmark multi-view graph datasets and a production-scale KG of 2.4 million nodes demonstrate multiple orders-of-magnitude inference speedups over retraining-based approaches and competitive clustering quality. As a candidate scoping mechanism for downstream tasks, SNAP-KG achieves 62-75% candidate search reduction on the five benchmark datasets and 97% on OGB-WikiKG2 for entity resolution and link prediction.

AI.tldr: SNAP-KG is a framework for integrating streaming entities into knowledge graphs by learning a projector that maps raw feature vectors directly to learned embedding spaces, enabling immediate cluster assignment without graph access or retraining.
AI.motivation: Existing multi-view graph clustering methods are transductive and cannot assign unseen entities without retraining. Newly arriving entities emerge as raw feature vectors with no graph connectivity, making it challenging to assign them to semantic communities before entity resolution and link prediction can operate.
AI.method: SNAP-KG trains a projector to map new entities directly to the learned embedding space using only raw features. This enables immediate cluster assignment without graph access or model retraining, supporting both graph-structural multi-view relational clustering and inductive inference for streaming entities.
AI.result: Experiments on five benchmark multi-view graph datasets and a production-scale KG of 2.4 million nodes demonstrate multiple orders-of-magnitude inference speedups over retraining-based approaches with competitive clustering quality. As a candidate scoping mechanism, SNAP-KG achieves 62-75% candidate search reduction on five benchmarks and 97% on OGB-WikiKG2 for entity resolution and link prediction.
AI.conclusion: SNAP-KG provides an effective solution for streaming entity integration in knowledge graphs, offering significant inference speedups while maintaining competitive clustering quality and substantially reducing candidate search space for downstream tasks.

title: Distance Is Not Enough: Forget-Retain Alignment Gap Predicts LLM Relearning Robustness
summary: Machine unlearning aims to make a model forget specific data, yet unlearned LLMs often fail to stay unlearned: brief fine-tuning can revive removed knowledge. Existing robustness predictors rely on global weight-space displacement, but distance alone can be misleading when random or destructive updates collapse performance. We argue that relearning robustness depends on update structure: robust unlearning should affect forget-critical weights while sparing retain-critical ones. We introduce the Forget-Retain Alignment Gap (FRAG), a training-free predictor that scores an update's forget-retain alignment without running a relearning attack, and separates selective from dense updates more reliably than global distance. Building on the forget-critical, retain-sparing principle, Forget-Retain Pruning (FRP) improves relearning robustness. Our results suggest that weight selectivity better explains robustness than distance alone. Code is available at https://github.com/Yi1-Chen/FRAG.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses the vulnerability of machine unlearning in LLMs, where brief fine-tuning can revive removed knowledge. The authors propose FRAG, a training-free predictor that measures forget-retain alignment without relearning attacks, and FRP, a pruning method that improves robustness by affecting forget-critical weights while sparing retain-critical ones. The key insight is that weight selectivity (update structure) is more predictive of relearning robustness than global distance measures.
AI.motivation: Machine unlearning aims to make models forget specific data, but unlearned LLMs are vulnerable: brief fine-tuning can revive removed knowledge. Existing robustness predictors rely on global weight-space displacement, but distance alone can be misleading when random or destructive updates collapse performance. This vulnerability limits the practical deployment of machine unlearning.
AI.method: 1) FRAG (Forget-Retain Alignment Gap): A training-free predictor that scores an update's forget-retain alignment without running a relearning attack. It separates selective from dense updates more reliably than global distance. 2) FRP (Forget-Retain Pruning): A method that improves relearning robustness by affecting forget-critical weights while sparing retain-critical ones, based on the forget-critical, retain-sparing principle.
AI.result: The proposed FRAG predictor more reliably separates selective from dense updates compared to global distance measures. FRP improves relearning robustness. Weight selectivity better explains robustness than distance alone.
AI.conclusion: Relearning robustness in machine unlearning depends on update structure rather than global weight displacement. The Forget-Retain Alignment Gap (FRAG) is an effective training-free predictor of robustness without requiring relearning attacks. Forget-Retain Pruning (FRP) successfully improves relearning robustness by targeting forget-critical weights while sparing retain-critical ones. Weight selectivity is a better predictor of robustness than distance-based metrics.

title: PAGS: Autofocusing Photoacoustic Tomography via Speed-of-Sound-Adaptive Gaussian Splatting
summary: Photoacoustic computed tomography (PACT) combines optical absorption contrast with acoustic detection for high-resolution deep-tissue imaging. A persistent challenge is that unknown speed-of-sound (SoS) heterogeneity changes acoustic time-of-flight, causing defocusing artifacts when reconstruction assumes a uniform SoS. Existing SoS-adaptive methods either rely on calibrated acoustic priors or optimize dense physical medium models, which becomes expensive and difficult to scale in 3D. We propose PAGS, a differentiable framework for blind autofocusing PACT via speed-of-sound-adaptive Gaussian splatting. PAGS represents the initial pressure field with sparse Gaussian photoacoustic (PA) sources and replaces explicit medium recovery with a compact anisotropic path-averaged SoS (ASoS) field parameterized by spherical harmonic probes. This latent propagation field directly controls source-to-transducer arrival-time alignment, while an analytic Gaussian acoustic projection maps the source representation to transducer signals efficiently. The resulting closed-loop signal-domain optimization jointly updates the Gaussian PA source parameters and the ASoS field from measured data, without calibrated SoS priors. Experiments on simulated and physical phantom data demonstrate improved reconstruction sharpness under heterogeneous acoustic media, robustness to sparse-view sampling, and computational benefits from the analytic Gaussian projection.

AI.tldr: PAGS is a differentiable framework for blind autofocusing photoacoustic computed tomography (PACT) that handles speed-of-sound heterogeneity without requiring calibrated priors. It uses Gaussian splatting to represent photoacoustic sources and a compact anisotropic path-averaged SoS field parameterized by spherical harmonic probes for efficient signal-domain optimization.
AI.motivation: Unknown speed-of-sound (SoS) heterogeneity in tissue changes acoustic time-of-flight, causing defocusing artifacts when reconstruction assumes uniform SoS. Existing SoS-adaptive methods either rely on calibrated acoustic priors or optimize dense physical models, which are expensive and difficult to scale in 3D.
AI.method: PAGS represents the initial pressure field with sparse Gaussian photoacoustic (PA) sources and replaces explicit medium recovery with a compact anisotropic path-averaged SoS (ASoS) field parameterized by spherical harmonic probes. This latent propagation field directly controls source-to-transducer arrival-time alignment. An analytic Gaussian acoustic projection efficiently maps the source representation to transducer signals, enabling closed-loop signal-domain optimization that jointly updates Gaussian PA source parameters and the ASoS field from measured data without calibrated SoS priors.
AI.result: Experiments on simulated and physical phantom data demonstrate: (1) improved reconstruction sharpness under heterogeneous acoustic media, (2) robustness to sparse-view sampling, and (3) computational benefits from the analytic Gaussian projection.
AI.conclusion: PAGS provides an effective solution for handling SoS heterogeneity in PACT by combining differentiable Gaussian splatting with a compact ASoS representation, achieving improved image quality without requiring calibrated acoustic priors while remaining computationally scalable for 3D applications.

title: Bayesian Flow Networks for Offline Trajectory Planning
summary: Offline reinforcement learning (RL) leverages static datasets to learn decision policies without real-time environment interaction. While recent sequence-modeling approaches rely on continuous diffusion models for trajectory synthesis, applying these methods to discrete planning tasks requires a categorical formulation rather than the standard Gaussian construction. We present BFN-RL, a unified generative modeling framework for offline RL based on Bayesian Flow Networks (BFNs). By iteratively evolving distribution parameters rather than noisy data instances, BFN-RL natively models both discrete and continuous trajectory spaces within a single probabilistic formulation. The categorical planner generates future state sequences, and a learned inverse-dynamics model converts consecutive generated states into actions. Evaluations in discrete planning and continuous control show that BFN-RL can generate effective trajectories across both categorical and continuous state spaces. Our results establish BFNs as a versatile generative foundation for offline trajectory planning across data modalities.

AI.tldr: BFN-RL is a unified generative modeling framework for offline reinforcement learning that uses Bayesian Flow Networks to handle both discrete and continuous trajectory spaces within a single probabilistic formulation, addressing the limitation of diffusion models that typically require Gaussian (continuous) formulations.
AI.motivation: Current sequence-modeling approaches for offline RL rely on continuous diffusion models, but discrete planning tasks require categorical formulations rather than standard Gaussian constructions. There is a need for a unified framework that can handle both data modalities.
AI.method: BFN-RL iteratively evolves distribution parameters rather than noisy data instances. It uses: 1) A categorical planner that generates future state sequences, and 2) A learned inverse-dynamics model that converts consecutive generated states into actions.
AI.result: BFN-RL can generate effective trajectories across both categorical (discrete planning) and continuous (continuous control) state spaces, demonstrating versatility across data modalities.
AI.conclusion: Bayesian Flow Networks (BFNs) serve as a versatile generative foundation for offline trajectory planning across different data modalities, successfully unifying discrete and continuous trajectory modeling within one framework.

title: Training Alignment Auditors via Reinforcement Learning
comment: 82 pages, 15 figures. Code, prompts, and evaluation data are available at https://github.com/paulrosu11/training-auditing-agents-public
summary: Alignment auditing of frontier models increasingly relies on LLM auditors to surface undesirable behaviors at scale, but current automated auditors can struggle with coherent investigation and audit realism. In this work, we improve LLM auditors with reinforcement learning. In our best training environment, the policy investigates target models that potentially possess hidden behaviors planted via their system prompt. An LLM judge, which knows whether the target has a hidden behavior, holistically compares the policy's investigation to a reference investigation to determine the reward. With systematic ablations, we find that pairwise rewards yield more robust training compared to pointwise rewards, and that adding targets without planted behaviors helps maintain a low false positive rate. Training improves investigation quality against targets with planted behaviors, the rate of concerning behaviors surfaced in unmodified production models, and audit realism, while false-positive rates stay below 1%. Furthermore, auditing capabilities generalize across scaffolds: performance on AuditBench's adversarially fine-tuned targets substantially improves [Sheshadri et al., 2026].

AI.tldr: This paper presents RL-augmented LLM auditors that improve alignment auditing of frontier models by learning to investigate hidden undesirable behaviors planted in target models through system prompts. The method uses pairwise comparisons by an LLM judge to provide rewards, achieving better investigation quality while maintaining false positive rates below 1% and generalizing across different scaffolds.
AI.motivation: Current automated LLM auditors struggle with coherent investigation and audit realism when surfacing undesirable behaviors at scale. The authors aim to improve auditors' investigation capabilities through reinforcement learning, making auditing more effective and realistic.
AI.method: The approach uses a training environment where: (1) A policy LLM investigates target models potentially containing hidden behaviors via system prompts; (2) An LLM judge with knowledge of hidden behaviors compares the policy's investigation to a reference investigation using pairwise rewards; (3) Systematic ablations compare pairwise vs pointwise rewards and test adding targets without planted behaviors. Training involves improving investigation quality against planted behavior targets while maintaining low false positive rates.
AI.result: Pairwise rewards yield more robust training compared to pointwise rewards. Adding targets without planted behaviors helps maintain low false positive rates. Training improves: (1) investigation quality against targets with planted behaviors, (2) the rate of concerning behaviors surfaced in unmodified production models, and (3) audit realism. False-positive rates stay below 1%. Auditing capabilities generalize across scaffolds with substantially improved performance on AuditBench's adversarially fine-tuned targets.
AI.conclusion: Reinforcement learning is an effective approach for improving LLM auditors. The key insights are that pairwise rewards provide more robust training signals than pointwise rewards, and including clean targets helps control false positives. The method successfully improves investigation quality, increases detection of concerning behaviors in production models, enhances audit realism, and generalizes across different scaffold implementations while maintaining very low false positive rates.

title: 4DStreamCtrl: Interactive Video Generation with Online 4D Control
summary: Generative video models now synthesize footage nearly indistinguishable from reality. Their promise as interactive tools hinges on fine-grained control of how objects and the camera move over time, yet each existing approach captures only part of this: camera-parameter methods steer the viewpoint but cannot move objects, 2D-trajectory methods act in the image plane and ignore depth and occlusion, and recent 3D methods add geometry but run only offline at a fixed length. In particular, none combines 3D-consistent control of both camera and objects with real-time, streaming generation. Here we show that camera motion, object trajectories, and depth can be unified into a single 3D point-track representation, from which one model performs joint camera and object control, depth editing, and motion transfer in a single forward pass. To learn this interface at scale, we mine in-the-wild video for 3D motion supervision, yielding OpenVidHD-Motion3D, and encode it with a lightweight Geometric Motion Head that plugs into a pretrained video diffusion model. Because this encoder is temporally separable, we distill the model into a causal streaming student that generates arbitrarily long video in four denoising steps at memory independent of length. This unified design surpasses prior camera-only, 2D, and offline-3D methods in motion-control precision while covering modalities they address only in isolation. 4DStreamCtrl runs at 20 FPS on a single high-end GPU for 480p video and stays temporally coherent over hundreds of frames, enabling, to our knowledge, interactive 4D-controllable streaming generation for the first time. More broadly, grounding generation in explicit 3D geometry with efficient causal inference points toward interactive world models with closed-loop spatiotemporal control, from controllable simulators to real-time visual imagination for embodied agents.

AI.tldr: 4DStreamCtrl achieves real-time 4D-controllable video generation by unifying camera motion, object trajectories, and depth into a single 3D point-track representation, enabling joint camera and object control, depth editing, and motion transfer in a single forward pass.
AI.motivation: Existing video generation methods have limitations: camera-parameter methods control viewpoint but cannot move objects, 2D-trajectory methods ignore depth and occlusion, and 3D methods are offline with fixed length. No prior work combines 3D-consistent control of both camera and objects with real-time streaming generation.
AI.method: The approach uses a unified 3D point-track representation encoding camera motion, object trajectories, and depth. A lightweight Geometric Motion Head encodes this representation into a pretrained video diffusion model. The model is trained on OpenVidHD-Motion3D, a dataset mined from in-the-wild videos for 3D motion supervision. For efficient inference, the model is distilled into a causal streaming student that generates arbitrarily long videos in just four denoising steps with memory independent of sequence length.
AI.result: 4DStreamCtrl surpasses prior camera-only, 2D, and offline-3D methods in motion-control precision while covering all their modalities. It runs at 20 FPS on a single high-end GPU for 480p video and maintains temporal coherence over hundreds of frames, enabling the first interactive 4D-controllable streaming generation.
AI.conclusion: Grounding video generation in explicit 3D geometry with efficient causal inference enables interactive world models with closed-loop spatiotemporal control. This approach points toward applications in controllable simulators and real-time visual imagination for embodied agents.

title: Simultaneous inference of environmental and interaction forces in collective dynamics
summary: Collective dynamics arise in a wide range of physical, biological, and engineering applications. Examples include cell migration, swarm robotics, social dynamics, and animal behavior. A defining characteristic of these systems is the emergence of large-scale coordination from local interactions among agents; a fundamental question is thus to understand the local interactions that give rise to the observed emergent dynamics. We are interested in methods for learning interactions generally, which can describe a wide class of physical systems exhibiting collective dynamics defined by an interaction kernel, without a priori assumptions on the analytical form of this kernel (i.e. it is nonparametric). The advantage of this kernel-based approach is that it incorporates the underlying physics of the model (i.e. collective dynamics), which more general equation-learning approaches may ignore, potentially limiting their effectiveness for model accuracy and predictions. In this work, we extend existing variational learning approaches to collective systems with both interaction kernels and environmental/intra-agent forces. The proposed framework simultaneously infers the interaction kernel non-parametrically while learning the environmental force using either semi-parametric or fully nonparametric representations. The methodology is validated on several benchmark models exhibiting synchronization, alignment, attraction-repulsion, and external environmental forces. We also introduce a model-selection procedure based on our nonparametric learning framework to identify models that optimally explain a given set of trajectory observations. By exploiting the feature-identification capability of the learned models, the proposed procedure can distinguish among different collective dynamics frameworks and recover mechanistic interaction mechanisms directly from trajectory data.
