title: Activation-Space Order-Swap Geometry: A Site-Asymmetry Audit
comment: 18 pages, 2 figures. Under review at the NeurReps Proceedings Track
summary: Order-dependent activation statistics are often interpreted as evidence of interaction, but that interpretation can be confounded by where interventions enter the network. We introduce a no-fit site-asymmetry audit. For a twice-differentiable readout, the open-path order-swap decomposes into a canonical additive response measured by single interventions and an antisymmetrized second difference free of first-order and pure self-curvature terms to second order. Across six open-weight language-model families, the single-intervention baseline explains 84.3-97.7 percent of the bracket norm (mean 93.7 percent), while the no-interaction self-curvature term is 1.8-5.2 times larger than the corrected residual in the two families with the plus/minus injection split. The corrected residual clears a generic-interaction null in three of six families under a confound-free prompt split and two of six after configuration robustness. A known-positive surrogate recovers planted mixed interaction, while a matched site-separation test changes the baseline share and a random architecture reproduces the first-order regime. The same estimator transfers to released non-language references: trained residual fractions fall below a fixed Gaussian-direction null in 11/12 contrasts (5/6 ViT-B/16, 6/6 ResNet-50), a portability check rather than pooled evidence. The contribution is a reusable measurement criterion: run the single-intervention baseline before reading an order-swap vector as interaction or geometric structure; if it explains the vector, form the second difference instead. All claims are scoped to activation-space interventions at distinct sites; we do not claim that representation geometry is globally Abelian.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a "no-fit site-asymmetry audit" method to distinguish whether order-dependent activation statistics in neural networks represent genuine interactions or are artifacts of intervention placement. Using single-intervention baselines as a confound control, the study finds that 84.3-97.7% of order-swap effects in language models are explained by first-order additive responses, challenging the interpretation of order effects as interaction evidence.
AI.motivation: Order-dependent activation statistics are often interpreted as evidence of interaction between network components, but this interpretation can be confounded by where interventions enter the network. The authors seek to develop a method that can distinguish genuine interactions from artifacts of intervention placement.
AI.method: The authors introduce an open-path order-swap decomposition that separates the effect into: (1) a canonical additive response measured by single interventions, and (2) an antisymmetrized second difference free of first-order and pure self-curvature terms to second order. They test across six open-weight language-model families, use ViT-B/16 and ResNet-50 as non-language references, and apply various control tests including site-separation tests and random architecture baselines.
AI.result: The single-intervention baseline explains 84.3-97.7% of the bracket norm (mean 93.7%). The self-curvature term is 1.8-5.2 times larger than the corrected residual in two families with plus/minus injection split. The corrected residual clears a generic-interaction null in 3/6 families under confound-free prompt split and 2/6 after configuration robustness. For non-language references, trained residual fractions fall below a fixed Gaussian-direction null in 11/12 contrasts.
AI.conclusion: Most order-swap effects in language models are attributable to first-order additive responses rather than genuine interactions. The contribution is a reusable measurement criterion: run the single-intervention baseline before interpreting an order-swap vector as interaction or geometric structure. The method is scoped to activation-space interventions at distinct sites; the authors do not claim representation geometry is globally Abelian.

title: ProgRouter: Online Progress-Guided Orchestration for Multi-Agent LLM Workflows under Quality-Cost Tradeoffs
comment: Accepted in Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026. Index Terms: Collaborative agentic workflows, LLM agent orchestration, Quality-cost trade-off, Task progress prediction, Online decision-making
summary: Multi-agent large language model (LLM) workflows have emerged as a powerful paradigm for solving complex, open-ended tasks through collaborative reasoning among specialized LLM agents, but they incur substantial operating costs due to repeated LLM invocations and long-horizon context accumulation. Existing cascade routing methods make one-shot, query-level decisions and cannot adapt to the dynamic, state-dependent nature of multi-step workflows, in which the right LLM at each step depends on evolving task progress, remaining task difficulty, and cost-efficiency requirements. We present ProgRouter, an online progress-guided routing framework that adaptively selects LLM agents across workflow steps to preserve task-solving quality while adhering to time and cost budgets. ProgRouter introduces a multi-view task progress scorer that combines coarse workflow outcome regimes with fine-grained signals on subtask completion, progress trends, and workflow state quality. Then, a dual-path task progress predictor and an adaptive meta-gating mechanism estimate the progress gain for each candidate routed LLM. ProgRouter makes online step-wise routing decisions that balance progress gain, task time budgets, and long-term operating cost efficiency. Experiments on HumanEval Plus, MBPP, MATH-500, and ASQA, spanning agentic code generation, mathematical reasoning, and retrieval-augmented long-form question answering, demonstrate that ProgRouter reduces the operating cost relative to key baselines while maintaining strong task-solving performance.

title: Plans You Can Check: Verifier-Grounded Learning of an Open-Weight Planner for Executable Video-Editing
comment: Accepted to the Main Conference of EMNLP '26
summary: Practical video editing is not only pixel generation: an editor must turn a brief, a clip pool, music metadata, and hard constraints into an executable timeline. We study this decision layer as \emph{executable video-editing planning} and introduce RefineCut, which, unlike workflow systems that wrap a prompted frontier model, trains a compact open-weight planner for it. The planner edits a typed timeline through structured patches covering clip selection, trimming, ordering, transitions, and duration and music alignment; a deterministic verifier applies each patch and checks it against an explicit constraint ledger. Because editing has no single ground-truth repair, we do not imitate teachers directly: RefineCut replays every multi-teacher branch through the verifier and keeps verifier-best repairs as supervision. A second stage, RefineCut-Evo, lets the student score its own repairs with the verifier and a task rubric and trains on high-margin preference pairs, so the final $8$B planner runs in a closed verifier loop with no teacher calls at inference. On RefineCut-Bench ($3{,}578$ tasks, $7{,}971$ captioned clips, $499$ music tracks, explicit ledgers), verifier-replayed distillation lifts the planner from $0.620$ to $0.858$ on the protocol-specific Video-Editing Score and RefineCut-Evo reaches $0.924$; the gain transfers to Llama-3.1-8B and GLM-4-9B, and in the same closed loop the $8$B planner matches or exceeds its frontier teachers. Code and RefineCut-Bench are publicly released; see the Data Availability statement.

AI.tldr: RefineCut is a compact open-weight planner for executable video-editing planning that transforms briefs, clip pools, music metadata, and hard constraints into executable timelines. It uses structured patches for editing operations and a deterministic verifier for constraint checking. The system employs verifier-replayed multi-teacher distillation and a preference learning stage (RefineCut-Evo) to train without direct teacher imitation. On RefineCut-Bench, it achieves 0.924 Video-Editing Score and matches/exceeds frontier teachers in closed-loop inference.
AI.motivation: Practical video editing requires complex decision-making beyond pixel generation - editors must transform briefs, clip pools, music metadata, and hard constraints into executable timelines. Existing workflow systems simply wrap prompted frontier models rather than training dedicated planners for this decision layer.
AI.method: RefineCut trains a compact planner using structured patches covering clip selection, trimming, ordering, transitions, duration, and music alignment. A deterministic verifier applies each patch and checks against an explicit constraint ledger. The training approach uses multi-teacher replay where all branches are evaluated through the verifier, keeping verifier-best repairs as supervision. RefineCut-Evo adds preference learning where the student scores its own repairs using the verifier and task rubric, training on high-margin preference pairs to enable closed-loop inference without teacher calls.
AI.result: On RefineCut-Bench (3,578 tasks, 7,971 captioned clips, 499 music tracks), verifier-replayed distillation improved the planner from 0.620 to 0.858 on the Video-Editing Score. RefineCut-Evo achieved 0.924. The gains transfer to Llama-3.1-8B and GLM-4-9B. In closed-loop inference, the 8B planner matches or exceeds its frontier teachers.
AI.conclusion: Training a dedicated compact planner with verifier-based supervision and preference learning enables effective video-editing planning that matches or exceeds frontier models while running in a closed loop without teacher calls at inference time. The approach demonstrates the value of treating video editing as a planning problem rather than just pixel generation.

title: Two Dimensions Govern Agnostic Multiclass Transductive Learning
summary: In transductive classification, an adversary fixes a labeled population, one label is hidden uniformly, and the learner sees all remaining labels. For binary classes, agnostic transductive and PAC learning have the same minimax rate. Whether this extends to multiclass learning was open, especially for unbounded label spaces where uniform convergence can fail. We resolve the question up to logarithmic factors. For every multiclass class $\mathcal H$ with DS dimension $d_{DS}$ and Natarajan dimension $d_{\mathrm N}$, the optimal agnostic transductive excess error satisfies $\widetildeΘ\left(\frac{d_{DS}}{n}+\sqrt{\frac{d_{\mathrm N}}{n}}\right).$ The result holds for arbitrary label spaces. The two terms are both necessary. A DS pseudo-cube gives the realizable $d_{DS}/n$ obstruction, while a Natarajan cube with repeated points and fair labels gives the agnostic $\sqrt{d_{\mathrm N}/n}$ obstruction. The upper bound uses a random-reservation principle. The learner deliberately ignores a constant fraction of the visible labels, which makes the true test point uniform in a large unseen block. We combine realizable compression, a label-space reduction, and inside-menu agnostic compression across this finite-population split. A new without-replacement multiplicative-weights lemma preserves the fast $d_{DS}/n$ term. Consequently, agnostic multiclass PAC and transductive learning obey the same two-dimension law up to logarithmic factors.

AI.tldr: This paper resolves whether the equivalence between agnostic transductive and PAC learning minimax rates (known for binary classes) extends to multiclass learning. The answer is yes, with optimal rates Θ̃(d_DS/n + √(d_N/n)) for any label space, where d_DS is DS dimension and d_N is Natarajan dimension.
AI.motivation: The key question was whether binary class equivalence extends to multiclass learning, especially for unbounded label spaces where uniform convergence can fail. This was previously open.
AI.method: The approach uses: (1) Random-reservation principle - deliberately ignoring a constant fraction of visible labels to make test points uniform in unseen blocks; (2) Realizable compression; (3) Label-space reduction; (4) Inside-menu agnostic compression across finite-population split; (5) A new without-replacement multiplicative-weights lemma.
AI.result: The optimal agnostic transductive excess error satisfies Θ̃(d_DS/n + √(d_N/n)) for any multiclass class H. Both terms are necessary: DS pseudo-cube gives realizable d_DS/n obstruction; Natarajan cube with repeated points and fair labels gives agnostic √(d_N/n) obstruction.
AI.conclusion: Agnostic multiclass PAC and transductive learning obey the same two-dimension law up to logarithmic factors, establishing fundamental equivalence between these learning paradigms.

title: AsymSpec: Context-Asymmetric Speculative Decoding for Agentic LLMs
summary: Agentic LLM pipelines face escalating inference costs as context accumulates across retrieval, tool use, and multi-turn interactions. To control latency, deployments routinely compress inputs, but this degrades task accuracy. Speculative decoding (SD) accelerates generation losslessly, yet it assumes the drafter and verifier share an identical context, preventing SD from resolving the accuracy-overhead trade-off. We propose AsymSpec, an asymmetric speculative decoding framework that breaks this symmetry: a lightweight drafter reads the full input while the large verifier operates on the compressed view. The drafter steers the verifier via a contrastive $δ$-fusion of logits, modulated by a divergence-aware acceptance gate that preserves verification stability and high draft acceptance rates. Evaluated across four agentic capabilities and two end-to-end agent benchmarks, AsymSpec reaches $\approx 90\%$ of full-context accuracy on average, delivering $1.3$--$1.7\times$ throughput speedups at $0.2$--$0.3\times$ the compute cost on isolated text capabilities. These results show that asymmetric context access yields substantial gains precisely when compression discards critical reasoning signals.

AI.tldr: AsymSpec is an asymmetric speculative decoding framework that solves the accuracy-overhead trade-off in agentic LLM pipelines by having a lightweight drafter access full context while a large verifier operates on compressed input, achieving ~90% full-context accuracy with 1.3-1.7x speedups.
AI.motivation: Agentic LLM pipelines face escalating inference costs as context accumulates across retrieval, tool use, and multi-turn interactions. Existing solutions like input compression degrade accuracy, while speculative decoding assumes symmetric context access between drafter and verifier, preventing resolution of the accuracy-overhead trade-off.
AI.method: AsymSpec breaks context symmetry by having a lightweight drafter read the full input while the large verifier operates on a compressed view. The drafter steers the verifier via a contrastive δ-fusion of logits, modulated by a divergence-aware acceptance gate that preserves verification stability and high draft acceptance rates.
AI.result: Evaluated across four agentic capabilities and two end-to-end agent benchmarks, AsymSpec achieves approximately 90% of full-context accuracy on average, delivering 1.3--1.7x throughput speedups at 0.2--0.3x the compute cost on isolated text capabilities.
AI.conclusion: Asymmetric context access yields substantial gains precisely when compression discards critical reasoning signals, successfully resolving the accuracy-overhead trade-off in agentic LLM inference.

title: SeVeR: Selective Visual Exposure and Retrieval for 3D Medical Image Question Answering
summary: Volumetric medical VQA requires reasoning over long and redundant 3D visual token sequences, especially in multi-sequence MRI where complementary modalities provide diverse diagnostic cues but expose the decoder to many repeated anatomical regions. To investigate reasoning under multi-sequence visual redundancy, we first introduce BreMRIs-VQA, a clinically curated breast MRI benchmark with 1.19M QA pairs from 71.0K sequences and 12.9K patients, covering both free-text and multiple-choice questions. We further propose SeVeR, a selective visual exposure framework that compresses dense volumes into modality-wise prototypes and retrieves complementary multi-level evidence with change-aware gated attention during decoding, trained with a marginal-utility self-consistency objective that suppresses unhelpful retrieval. Experiments on BreMRIs-VQA and public benchmarks show that SeVeR improves both discriminative and generative performance while exposing substantially fewer visual tokens.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces SeVeR, a selective visual exposure framework for volumetric medical VQA that addresses the challenge of reasoning over long, redundant 3D visual token sequences in multi-sequence MRI. The method compresses dense volumes into modality-wise prototypes and retrieves complementary multi-level evidence using change-aware gated attention.
AI.motivation: Volumetric medical VQA requires reasoning over long and redundant 3D visual token sequences, especially in multi-sequence MRI where complementary modalities provide diverse diagnostic cues but expose the decoder to many repeated anatomical regions. Existing methods struggle with visual redundancy and inefficient token usage.
AI.method: The paper proposes SeVeR with three key components: 1) Modality-wise prototype compression that compresses dense volumes into prototypes; 2) Change-aware gated attention for retrieving complementary multi-level evidence during decoding; 3) Marginal-utility self-consistency training objective that suppresses unhelpful retrieval.
AI.result: SeVeR improves both discriminative and generative performance while exposing substantially fewer visual tokens. The benchmark BreMRIs-VQA contains 1.19M QA pairs from 71.0K sequences and 12.9K patients, covering both free-text and multiple-choice questions.
AI.conclusion: SeVeR effectively addresses visual redundancy in multi-sequence MRI VQA by compressing volumes into prototypes and selectively retrieving evidence, achieving improved performance with reduced visual token exposure.

title: Neither Precision Nor Architecture Alone: Controlled Tests of Failure Remedies for Physics-Informed Neural Networks
comment: 11 pages, 5 figures, 6 tables; appendix with full proofs included
summary: Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) frequently fail on stiff or advection-dominated PDEs, and two recent accounts offer competing remedies: switching from FP32 to FP64 to repair an L-BFGS stopping artifact, or replacing the MLP with a state-space-model (SSM) backbone plus sub-sequence alignment to counter architectural simplicity bias. We test both under matched, seed-paired controls in a pre-registered 144-run study spanning convection, reaction, and wave, plus an independent 85-run convection/wave study; success is relative $\ell_2$ error below $0.05$. The two remedies act on disjoint regime-and-seed slices: neither substitutes for the other. On hard convection ($β{=}50$), alignment recovers 2/5 seeds in FP32 and 3/5 in FP64, where the unaligned SSM succeeds on 0/5 seeds at either precision and the vanilla MLP moves only from 0/5 to 1/5 across the precision switch---the recoveries trace to the alignment objective, not the backbone. On reaction the backbone alone already succeeds on 3/5--4/5 seeds, so each remedy covers a regime the other does not. Responses are also seed-specific: the same precision switch flips individual seeds in opposite directions and, on wave, lowers median error with no statistically significant success gain. Tightening the inner L-BFGS tolerance in an independent repeated-step runner likewise lowers median error at a large runtime cost, with success counts unchanged. Precision, stopping, backbone, and alignment must therefore be evaluated jointly and reported per seed.

AI.tldr: This paper compares two remedies for PINN failures on stiff/advection-dominated PDEs: precision switching (FP32→FP64) and SSM backbone with alignment. A 144-run pre-registered study finds the remedies work on disjoint regime-and-seed slices—neither substitutes for the other. Success is highly seed-specific, requiring joint evaluation and per-seed reporting of precision, stopping, backbone, and alignment factors.
AI.motivation: Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) frequently fail on stiff or advection-dominated PDEs. Two competing remedies exist: (1) switching from FP32 to FP64 to fix L-BFGS stopping artifacts, and (2) replacing MLP with SSM backbone plus sub-sequence alignment to address architectural simplicity bias. However, it was unclear whether these remedies are complementary or redundant.
AI.method: Pre-registered 144-run study with matched seed-paired controls across convection, reaction, and wave PDEs, plus an independent 85-run convection/wave study. Success defined as relative ℓ2 error below 0.05. Tested both remedies under controlled conditions, also examined tightening L-BFGS tolerance in a separate experiment.
AI.result: The two remedies act on disjoint regime-and-seed slices—neither substitutes for the other. On hard convection (β=50), alignment recovers 2/5 seeds in FP32 and 3/5 in FP64, while unaligned SSM succeeds on 0/5 seeds at either precision, and vanilla MLP only improves from 0/5 to 1/5 with precision switch. On reaction, backbone alone succeeds on 3/5–4/5 seeds. Responses are seed-specific: same precision switch affects individual seeds differently. On wave, precision lowers median error but not success rate. Tightening L-BFGS tolerance lowers median error at high runtime cost with unchanged success.
AI.conclusion: Precision, stopping criteria, backbone architecture, and alignment must be evaluated jointly and reported per seed. The remedies are complementary—each covers regimes the other does not. Future PINN research and practice should report these factors together with seed-level results rather than aggregated statistics.

title: Imitation Learning for Connection-Tableau Construction
summary: An automated theorem prover builds a proof step by step, choosing at each point what to add and what to remove. We cast this construction as a policy acting in a transition system induced by a formal calculus, which fixes which steps are sound: for clausal connection tableaux, leanCoP-style search and plCoP/rlCoP-style planning then become stateful policies over one interface, and policy-learning methods apply directly. We equip such policies with a graph neural network that scores proof edits from structure that transfers across problems, train it by imitation learning from found proofs, and measure how performance holds as we remove search scaffolding, from full symbolic backtracking to a policy the network drives alone. Within a fixed step budget on M2k, MPTP2078-bushy, and TPTP v9.2.1, learned policies solve up to 46% more problems than leanCoP, and reach proofs in an order of magnitude fewer steps.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a learned policy approach for automated theorem proving that uses graph neural networks trained by imitation learning to guide proof search, achieving up to 46% improvement over the leanCoP prover while requiring an order of magnitude fewer proof steps.
AI.motivation: Automated theorem proving typically relies on symbolic search with extensive backtracking. The goal is to replace or augment this search with learned policies that can guide proof construction more efficiently, transferring structural knowledge across problems.
AI.method: The approach models theorem proving as a policy over a transition system induced by clausal connection tableaux. A graph neural network scores proof edits based on structural features that transfer across problems. Training is performed via imitation learning from existing proofs. The method is tested by progressively removing search scaffolding from full symbolic backtracking to a pure neural network-driven policy.
AI.result: Learned policies solve up to 46% more problems than leanCoP within a fixed step budget on M2k, MPTP2078-bushy, and TPTP v9.2.1 datasets, and reach proofs in approximately 10x fewer steps.
AI.conclusion: The combination of clausal connection calculi with learned neural policies provides a viable approach to improving automated theorem proving efficiency, with the GNN effectively capturing transferable structure across mathematical problems.

title: MAMA-FLUX.2: Image-to-Image Synthesis of Post-Contrast Breast DCE-MRI for the MAMA-SYNTH Challenge
summary: Dynamic contrast-enhanced breast MRI is central to cancer diagnosis and monitoring, but requires gadolinium-based contrast agents. In this work, we address pre-to-post contrast breast MRI synthesis for the MAMA-SYNTH challenge. We propose MAMA-FLUX.2, a conditional latent flow-matching approach based on FLUX.2-Klein-4B. The pre-contrast image is encoded as spatial conditioning, while the model predicts the flow field associated with the post-contrast target latent. To adapt the pretrained model efficiently, we use LoRA fine-tuning and introduce a regional training objective combining global flow matching, tumor-region supervision, and stable foreground regularization. We further investigate LoRA rank, intensity windowing, and regional loss weights on axial slices, prioritizing clinically relevant tumor-focused metrics. Our ablation study shows that moderate tumor and stable-foreground weighting improves the trade-off between image fidelity and tumor-region accuracy. The final model achieves the best overall balance with LoRA rank/$α=64/64$, $\mathrm{MHA}_{\max}=25$, $λ_{\mathrm{tumor}}=0.25$, and $λ_{\mathrm{stable}}=0.1$. These results demonstrate that compact pretrained rectified-flow transformers can be adapted for contrast-enhanced MRI synthesis using parameter-efficient fine-tuning and task-aware regional losses.

AI.tldr: This paper presents MAMA-FLUX.2, a conditional latent flow-matching approach for synthesizing post-contrast breast MRI images from pre-contrast images, addressing the need to avoid gadolinium-based contrast agents in clinical diagnosis.
AI.motivation: Dynamic contrast-enhanced breast MRI is essential for cancer diagnosis and monitoring, but requires gadolinium-based contrast agents which pose risks. This work aims to synthesize post-contrast images from pre-contrast images to eliminate the need for contrast agents.
AI.method: The proposed MAMA-FLUX.2 is based on FLUX.2-Klein-4B, using pre-contrast images as spatial conditioning to predict flow fields for post-contrast target latents. The model is efficiently adapted using LoRA fine-tuning with a regional training objective combining global flow matching, tumor-region supervision, and stable foreground regularization. Ablation studies tested LoRA rank, intensity windowing, and regional loss weights on axial slices.
AI.result: The final model achieves optimal balance with LoRA rank/α=64/64, MHA_max=25, λ_tumor=0.25, and λ_stable=0.1. Moderate tumor and stable-foreground weighting improves the trade-off between image fidelity and tumor-region accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Compact pretrained rectified-flow transformers can be successfully adapted for contrast-enhanced MRI synthesis using parameter-efficient fine-tuning (LoRA) and task-aware regional losses, demonstrating the viability of this approach for clinical applications.

title: Beyond Pairwise Feedback: Listwise Vision-Language Supervision for Preference-Based Reward Learning
comment: 13 pages, 10 figures. Srivalli Katkuri and Maxwell Kawada contributed equally to this work
summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) have emerged as a powerful source of supervision for reinforcement learning, enabling agents to leverage rich semantic knowledge during training. Inspired by the success of preference-based reward learning (PbRL) in reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF), vision-language model generated image-based preferences provide an effective source for learning reward functions. This can be done by visually comparing two outcomes through the Bradley-Terry (BT) model. However, this pairwise formulation utilizes only two observations at a time, despite VLMs being capable of ranking multiple candidates. The Plackett-Luce (PL) formulation can shape a reward model with listwise rankings as opposed to pairwise preferences, allowing for a more suited use of a VLM based ranking. In this work, to our knowledge, we introduce the first framework that combines VLM-generated preferences with the Plackett-Luce model for reward learning. We evaluate our approach on Meta-World manipulation tasks and show that Plackett-Luce (PL) reward models can train robotic policies from VLM-generated rankings as effectively as pairwise Bradley-Terry, $K$-wise Bradley-Terry, and RL-VLM-F baselines. Across all environments, at least one PL ranking size ($K \in \{3,4,5\}$) consistently performs with or outperforms other methods in mean success rate. Unlike pairwise methods, which are restricted to $K=2$, PL supports different ranking sizes and can therefore be adapted to the environment and desired feedback format. Our best PL configuration achieves an 86% mean final success rate and matches the Oracle baseline on Drawer Open. Overall, these results demonstrate that listwise VLM preference supervision is a competitive and flexible approach to reward learning for reinforcement learning.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces the first framework combining VLM-generated preferences with the Plackett-Luce model for reward learning in reinforcement learning. Unlike traditional pairwise Bradley-Terry methods (K=2), this listwise approach supports ranking multiple candidates (K∈{3,4,5}), providing more flexible feedback for training robotic policies.
AI.motivation: Vision-language models can provide rich semantic supervision for RL, but current preference-based reward learning methods only use pairwise comparisons (Bradley-Terry model) despite VLMs being capable of ranking multiple candidates. The Plackett-Luce model offers a more suitable framework for utilizing VLM-based rankings as it handles listwise rankings rather than just pairwise preferences.
AI.method: The authors combine VLM-generated preferences with the Plackett-Luce (PL) model for reward learning. They evaluate on Meta-World manipulation tasks, testing PL with different ranking sizes (K=3,4,5) and comparing against pairwise Bradley-Terry (K=2), K-wise Bradley-Terry, and RL-VLM-F baselines.
AI.result: Plackett-Luce reward models can train robotic policies from VLM-generated rankings as effectively as pairwise and K-wise Bradley-Terry methods. Across all environments, at least one PL ranking size (K∈{3,4,5}) consistently performs with or outperforms other methods in mean success rate. The best PL configuration achieves 86% mean final success rate and matches the Oracle baseline on Drawer Open.
AI.conclusion: Listwise VLM preference supervision is a competitive and flexible approach to reward learning for reinforcement learning. Unlike pairwise methods restricted to K=2, PL supports different ranking sizes that can be adapted to the environment and desired feedback format.

title: Trace Integrity for LLM Data Agents: A Vision for Auditable Structured Reasoning in Real-World Systems
summary: Answer accuracy is an insufficient reliability signal for LLM data agents. In structured-data tasks, a benchmark-correct answer can be produced by an invalid trace. This paper introduces Trace Integrity, a deployment reliability criterion for evaluating whether the computation recorded behind an answer is explicit, executable, schema-valid, operator-faithful, replayable, answer-consistent, and auditable. We identify the Structure Gap as the deployment failure mode that makes Trace Integrity necessary: natural-language reasoning and free-form rationales do not reliably specify the operator-level programs required by real-world systems. We operationalize Trace Integrity with execution contracts, structured artifacts that bind user intent to schema elements, operator plans, assumptions, executable queries, verification status, and final-answer linkage. We also introduce CAIT (Correct Answer / Invalid Trace) Rate, which measures how often answer-only evaluation counts computationally unsupported outputs as successes. In an empirical demonstration on BIRD Mini-Dev, Direct SQL, Operation Summary + SQL, and Contract-First SQL achieve answer accuracies of 20%, 22%, and 24%, while their Trace Integrity Pass Rates are 39%, 43%, and 40% and their CAIT Rates remain high at 55%, 59.1%, and 45.8%, showing that answer accuracy, trace validity, and silent-failure risk are distinct evaluation signals. Real-world LLM data agents should, therefore, be evaluated not only by whether their outputs match a reference answer, but by whether those outputs are backed by auditable computation.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Trace Integrity as a new reliability criterion for LLM data agents, addressing the problem that benchmark-correct answers can be produced by invalid computational traces. The authors identify the "Structure Gap" as a deployment failure mode where natural-language reasoning fails to specify operator-level programs. They propose execution contracts as structured artifacts and introduce the CAIT Rate metric to measure silent failures. Empirical results on BIRD Mini-Dev show significant discrepancies between answer accuracy (20-24%) and Trace Integrity Pass Rates (39-43%), with high CAIT Rates (45.8-59.1%), demonstrating these are distinct evaluation signals.
AI.motivation: The core problem is that current LLM evaluation relies on answer accuracy alone, which is insufficient because correct answers can be generated through invalid computational traces. This creates a "Structure Gap" where natural-language reasoning and free-form rationales do not reliably specify the operator-level programs required by real-world systems. This leads to silent failures that current benchmarks miss.
AI.method: The paper introduces: (1) Trace Integrity as a deployment reliability criterion with seven properties: explicit, executable, schema-valid, operator-faithful, replayable, answer-consistent, and auditable; (2) Execution contracts as structured artifacts that bind user intent to schema elements, operator plans, assumptions, executable queries, verification status, and final-answer linkage; (3) CAIT (Correct Answer / Invalid Trace) Rate to measure how often answer-only evaluation counts computationally unsupported outputs as successes. The method was empirically demonstrated on BIRD Mini-Dev benchmark.
AI.result: On BIRD Mini-Dev, three methods (Direct SQL, Operation Summary + SQL, Contract-First SQL) achieved answer accuracies of 20%, 22%, and 24% respectively. Their Trace Integrity Pass Rates were 39%, 43%, and 40% respectively. Most notably, their CAIT Rates remained high at 55%, 59.1%, and 45.8% respectively, meaning that over half of the "correct" answers in some methods were actually produced by invalid traces.
AI.conclusion: Answer accuracy, trace validity, and silent-failure risk are distinct and should all be evaluated separately. Real-world LLM data agents should be evaluated not only by whether outputs match reference answers, but by whether those outputs are backed by auditable computation. Trace Integrity provides a necessary complement to answer accuracy for deployment reliability.

title: Diffusion Transformers for Roof Graph Synthesis and Reconstruction
comment: Pre-review manuscript. Accepted at the ICPR 2026 Workshop on Pattern Recognition in Remote Sensing (PRRS)
summary: We present RoofDiT, a generative framework for 2D roof graph synthesis and reconstruction. Roofs are compactly described as planar graphs of junctions and structural edges, but existing methods often rely on fixed geometric rules or direct reconstruction objectives. RoofDiT instead models roof structures directly as vertex-edge graphs and learns a conditional generative prior over their geometry and connectivity. Our framework follows a two-stage design: a diffusion transformer generates roof vertices, and an edge prediction module infers the corresponding graph topology. To improve geometric fidelity, RoofDiT combines relative geometry-aware attention with footprint and aerial-image conditioning, while using an alignment regularizer to encourage common horizontal, vertical, and diagonal roof patterns. The same model supports unconditional generation, footprint-conditioned synthesis, and image-guided reconstruction by changing the conditioning signal. Experiments show improved graph generation quality over a diffusion baseline, favorable performance against a straight-skeleton prior in the footprint-conditioned setting, and the highest edge F1 among compared methods for image-guided reconstruction.

AI.tldr: RoofDiT is a generative framework for 2D roof graph synthesis and reconstruction that models roof structures as vertex-edge graphs and learns a conditional generative prior. It uses a two-stage approach: a diffusion transformer generates roof vertices, and an edge prediction module infers graph topology. The framework supports unconditional generation, footprint-conditioned synthesis, and image-guided reconstruction.
AI.motivation: Existing roof modeling methods often rely on fixed geometric rules or direct reconstruction objectives. This paper aims to model roof structures directly as vertex-edge graphs and learn a conditional generative prior over their geometry and connectivity, enabling more flexible and accurate roof synthesis and reconstruction.
AI.method: RoofDiT follows a two-stage design: (1) a diffusion transformer generates roof vertices, and (2) an edge prediction module infers the corresponding graph topology. Key technical contributions include relative geometry-aware attention, footprint and aerial-image conditioning, and an alignment regularizer to encourage common horizontal, vertical, and diagonal roof patterns.
AI.result: Experiments demonstrate: (1) improved graph generation quality over a diffusion baseline, (2) favorable performance against a straight-skeleton prior in the footprint-conditioned setting, and (3) the highest edge F1 among compared methods for image-guided reconstruction.
AI.conclusion: RoofDiT successfully models roof structures as vertex-edge graphs and learns a conditional generative prior. The two-stage design with diffusion transformer and edge prediction, combined with geometry-aware attention and conditioning signals, enables versatile roof synthesis and reconstruction with state-of-the-art performance across multiple settings.

title: Escaping Low-Dimensional Overlap: Multi-Task Model Merging via High-Dimensional Sparse Disentanglement
summary: Model merging provides an efficient way to construct multi-task generalist models without additional training, but its performance often degrades under severe task interference. Task interference in model merging primarily stems from \textit{superposition}, where task-specific features become entangled within the parameter space. This entanglement renders conventional decomposition methods insufficient for effectively isolating useful task directions from interfering components. In this paper, we propose a sparse-representation-based merging framework that uses Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) to project task vectors into a high-dimensional sparse feature space, enabling feature-level disentanglement before fusion. To reduce computational overhead, we further introduce a lightweight Group-Ranked Zeroth-Order Optimizer (GR-ZOO) to identify task-critical layers for selective merging. Experiments on both Qwen2.5-1.5B and Qwen2.5-7B demonstrate that our method consistently outperforms representative baselines, including Task Arithmetic, TIES-Merge, DARE, Fisher-Merge,and several recent training-free merging methods, across mathematical reasoning, code generation, instruction following, and general knowledge tasks. In a highly conflicting four-task setting on Qwen2.5-1.5B, our method further achieves a 2.78\% improvement over the strongest baseline.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a sparse-representation-based model merging framework that uses Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) to disentangle task-specific features in a high-dimensional space before fusion, combined with a lightweight Group-Ranked Zeroth-Order Optimizer (GR-ZOO) for selective layer merging to handle task interference in multi-task generalist models.
AI.motivation: Model merging faces performance degradation under severe task interference, primarily caused by superposition where task-specific features become entangled in parameter space. Existing decomposition methods fail to effectively isolate useful task directions from interfering components.
AI.method: The proposed framework uses Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) to project task vectors into a high-dimensional sparse feature space, enabling feature-level disentanglement before fusion. A lightweight Group-Ranked Zeroth-Order Optimizer (GR-ZOO) is introduced to identify task-critical layers for selective merging, reducing computational overhead.
AI.result: Experiments on Qwen2.5-1.5B and Qwen2.5-7B show consistent improvements over baselines (Task Arithmetic, TIES-Merge, DARE, Fisher-Merge, and other training-free methods) across mathematical reasoning, code generation, instruction following, and general knowledge tasks. In a highly conflicting four-task setting on Qwen2.5-1.5B, the method achieves 2.78% improvement over the strongest baseline.
AI.conclusion: The sparse-representation-based merging framework with GR-ZOO effectively addresses task interference in model merging through feature-level disentanglement and selective layer merging, outperforming existing training-free merging methods.

title: SwarmWorld: Stigmergic technological evolution in societies of language-model agents
summary: Collective intelligence can emerge when individuals coordinate through a shared environment, allowing local actions to accumulate into durable social organization. Language-model agents offer a new substrate for this process, yet most multi-agent systems rely on direct conversation, predefined roles, or centralized workflows. It remains unclear whether decentralized agents can build functional technologies and outperform independent search. Here, initially homogeneous LLM agents in SwarmWorld self-organize without assigned roles or recipes into evolving technological societies. Agents explore a spatial environment, process resources, test materials, construct persistent artifacts, and write executable controllers evaluated by a deterministic simulator under unseen disturbances after the agents are removed. SwarmWorld splits cognition from consequence: agents propose architectures and controllers within fixed action and material schemas, while the simulated world determines function. Shared societies develop broader, more resilient technological portfolios than a strong best-of-N isolated-search baseline, although isolated search remains competitive for the strongest artifact. Agents differentiate into exploration, construction, maintenance, and coordination behaviors, transitioning as the world matures. Technologies accumulate through collaborative construction, executable inheritance, and persistent agent-artifact networks, with most reuse beginning through physical observation rather than communication. Explicit cultural mechanisms amplify collaboration and organization, but functional benefits depend on outcome and timescale. Physical stigmergy alone supports capable societies, while interaction drives persistent technological ecologies rather than universally superior individual inventions.

title: Towards Purified Multi-Label Test-Time Adaptation of Vision-Language Models
summary: Test-time adaptation (TTA) has been widely explored in single-label recognition, effectively mitigating distribution shifts, especially when combined with vision-language models. However, real-world images often contain multiple objects, while the more practical multi-label test-time adaptation (MLTTA) has received little attention so far. Recent cache-based TTA methods have shown promising efficiency and effectiveness, yet directly extending them to multi-label scenarios suffers from a one-to-many mapping problem: a shared global representation entangling co-occurring objects is stored as class-wise cache prototypes, inducing dominant-label bias and compromised cache calibration. While introducing region-level cues helps isolate class-specific evidence, such regional evidence can also be unreliable under distribution shifts, making its identification and utilization non-trivial. To address these issues, we introduce PuRF, a novel PuRiFication-driven cache-based method for multi-label test-time adaptation of vision-language models. Specifically, PuRF first performs region purification to identify reliable regions, providing comprehensive regional cues for multi-label recognition and enabling fine-grained alignment. Based on these purified regions, PuRF conducts cache purification to enhance cache representation and adaptability, where episodic purification builds a discriminative region-based cache, and temporal refreshing further promotes long-term cache adaptability. Experiments demonstrate that PuRF consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving a notable 4.05% mAP improvement on ViT-B/32 across five datasets.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces PuRF, a novel cache-based method for multi-label test-time adaptation (MLTTA) of vision-language models. It addresses the one-to-many mapping problem in existing cache-based TTA methods by proposing region purification and cache purification mechanisms to handle the dominant-label bias and compromised cache calibration issues in multi-label scenarios.
AI.motivation: While test-time adaptation (TTA) has been well-explored for single-label recognition, multi-label test-time adaptation (MLTTA) remains under-explored despite real-world images often containing multiple objects. Existing cache-based TTA methods suffer from a one-to-many mapping problem when extended to multi-label scenarios, where a shared global representation entangling co-occurring objects is stored as class-wise cache prototypes, leading to dominant-label bias and compromised cache calibration. Additionally, regional evidence can be unreliable under distribution shifts.
AI.method: The proposed PuRF method introduces two key mechanisms: (1) Region purification to identify reliable regions, providing comprehensive regional cues for multi-label recognition and enabling fine-grained alignment; (2) Cache purification to enhance cache representation and adaptability, including episodic purification to build a discriminative region-based cache and temporal refreshing to promote long-term cache adaptability.
AI.result: PuRF consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving a notable 4.05% mAP improvement on ViT-B/32 across five datasets.
AI.conclusion: PuRF effectively addresses the challenges in multi-label test-time adaptation by purifying both region-level features and cache representations, providing a promising solution for adapting vision-language models to distribution shifts in multi-label recognition scenarios.

title: PaSta: Noisy Node Classification with Partial Label Learning
summary: Noisy node classification problem is a fundamental yet challenging task for real-world graph-related web services, where node labels are often corrupted or unreliable due to weak supervision or automatic annotation. However, existing methods typically train models based on one-hot labels, which not only makes models susceptible to overfitting on noisy labels, but also leads to error accumulation after pseudo-label-guided enhancement. In this paper, we propose a novel Partial label-based Self-training framework (PaSta for short) that leverages partial label learning technique to overcome the limitations of existing methods. Specifically, PaSta first trains multiple annotators to comprehensively capture the class distribution of nodes and aggregates their predictions to construct high-quality partial labels. Subsequently, we design a partial label-based classification model with two well-crafted loss functions to guide the model learning at both label and representation spaces. To further enhance the robustness against noisy labels, we introduce a self-training strategy where the labels refined by partial label learning are then used to further optimize the annotators in a closed-loop iterative manner. Extensive experiments on five datasets demonstrate that, compared with existing state-of-the-art methods, PaSta achieves an average improvement of 1.1% in classification performance under various noise settings.

AI.tldr: PaSta is a novel partial label-based self-training framework for noisy node classification in graphs. It addresses the limitations of existing methods that use one-hot labels by leveraging partial label learning, multiple annotators, and a closed-loop self-training strategy to achieve 1.1% average improvement over state-of-the-art methods.
AI.motivation: Real-world graph services often have noisy or unreliable node labels due to weak supervision or automatic annotation. Existing methods train models using one-hot labels, which causes overfitting on noisy labels and error accumulation after pseudo-label enhancement. There was a need for a more robust approach to handle label noise in node classification.
AI.method: PaSta uses three key components: (1) Multiple annotators to capture class distribution, with predictions aggregated to construct high-quality partial labels; (2) A partial label-based classification model with two designed loss functions for label and representation spaces; (3) A self-training strategy where partial label learning-refined labels are used to iteratively optimize annotators in a closed-loop manner.
AI.result: PaSta achieves an average improvement of 1.1% in classification performance compared to existing state-of-the-art methods across five datasets under various noise settings.
AI.conclusion: The proposed partial label learning approach effectively addresses the noisy node classification problem by mitigating overfitting on noisy labels and preventing error accumulation through iterative self-training, demonstrating superior performance over existing methods.

title: Planetary Prediction Engine: Autonomous Geospatial Prediction via Intelligent Data Selection and Foundation Model Embeddings
summary: Addressing critical global challenges, from food security and disaster risk to disease outbreaks and socio-economic vulnerability, demands high-fidelity geospatial modeling. However, building predictive planetary models remains bottlenecked by a fragmented data ecosystem, requiring manual data retrieval, multimodal data curation and fusion along with iterative model selection. We present the Planetary Prediction Engine (PPE), an autonomous AI system that executes this end-to-end workflow directly from natural-language queries. PPE synthesizes multimodal datasets on the fly, retrieving spatiotemporally relevant covariates across open-web and Earth observation platforms (Data Commons, Google Earth Engine) and fusing them with geospatial foundation model embeddings (PDFM, AlphaEarth). Simultaneously, it searches over task-tailored model architecture families with automated overfitting guards. Across diverse tasks, geographies, and scientific domains, PPE consistently outperforms state-of-the-art or manually tuned expert baselines. For US spatial regression, PPE improves mean $R^2$ across 21 CDC health indicators (76.8% vs. 60.0%), FEMA national risk indices (64.9% vs. 60.0%), and the Social Vulnerability Index (66.2% vs. 58.6%). For spatial downscaling in data-scarce settings, PPE integrates localized proxies to double baseline accuracy in Nigerian food security indicators ($R^2$ of 66.1% vs. 31.5%). For epidemiological nowcasting of the 2026 DRC Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak, PPE achieves a Recall@10 of 83.3% (identifying 15 of 18 newly invaded health zones across five weekly forecasts), a +10.3 percentage-point improvement over the public state-of-the-art modeling (~73%). By combining autonomous multimodal planetary data discovery with targeted model optimization, PPE lowers the technical barrier to planetary-scale analytics, enabling rapid, customized, expert-level deployment.

AI.tldr: The Planetary Prediction Engine (PPE) is an autonomous AI system that enables end-to-end geospatial predictive modeling from natural-language queries, synthesizing multimodal datasets and optimizing model architectures automatically.
AI.motivation: Building predictive planetary models for global challenges (food security, disaster risk, disease outbreaks, socio-economic vulnerability) is bottlenecked by a fragmented data ecosystem requiring manual data retrieval, multimodal data curation and fusion, and iterative model selection.
AI.method: PPE executes the full workflow from natural-language queries by: (1) synthesizing multimodal datasets on the fly, retrieving spatiotemporally relevant covariates across open-web and Earth observation platforms (Data Commons, Google Earth Engine); (2) fusing data with geospatial foundation model embeddings (PDFM, AlphaEarth); (3) searching over task-tailored model architecture families with automated overfitting guards.
AI.result: PPE consistently outperforms state-of-the-art and manually tuned expert baselines across diverse tasks: (1) US spatial regression: 76.8% vs 60.0% mean R² for 21 CDC health indicators, 64.9% vs 60.0% for FEMA risk indices, 66.2% vs 58.6% for Social Vulnerability Index; (2) Spatial downscaling in data-scarce settings: R² of 66.1% vs 31.5% (doubled baseline accuracy) for Nigerian food security indicators; (3) Epidemiological nowcasting: Recall@10 of 83.3% (15/18 health zones) for 2026 DRC Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak, +10.3 percentage points over public state-of-the-art (~73%).
AI.conclusion: PPE combines autonomous multimodal planetary data discovery with targeted model optimization, lowering the technical barrier to planetary-scale analytics and enabling rapid, customized, expert-level deployment.

title: Deep Learning Segmentation of Diffusion-Weighted MRI Acute Ischaemic Stroke: A Pragmatic Evaluation Across Three Datasets
summary:
Objective: Diffusion-weighted MRI (DWI-MRI) is the gold standard for visualizing and quantifying acute ischaemic stroke (AIS). Although deep learning methods can accurately segment AIS lesions, the optimal image inputs and model architecture remain uncertain. We evaluated whether accurate AIS lesion segmentation can be achieved using a pragmatic deep learning approach with minimal preprocessing and clinically feasible inference times.
  Materials and Methods: Self-configured nnU-Net models were trained on 1,744 DWI cases from local, national, and open-access datasets and tested on 436 cases. Four experimental conditions were evaluated using five-fold cross-validation: with or without brain extraction and using either DWI alone or DWI plus apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) images as inputs. Two architectures were compared: the baseline nnU-Net (base) and a residual encoder nnU-Net (ResEnc). Performance was benchmarked against the DeepISLES ensemble model from the 2022 ISLES challenge.
  Results: In the test set (n=436), the base model achieved a median (IQR) Dice similarity coefficient (DSC) of 0.84 (0.19). For the base model, only two of six pairwise comparisons between input configurations showed significant differences. ResEnc produced small but significant improvements in DSC compared with the base model for DWI, DWI+brain extraction, and DWI+ADC inputs (all p<0.02), but not for DWI+ADC+brain extraction (p>0.50). The base model significantly outperformed DeepISLES, particularly in patients with smaller infarct volumes (signed-rank test, p<0.01).
  Conclusions: A baseline nnU-Net trained on DWI alone, without preprocessing, enabled fast and accurate AIS lesion segmentation. This streamlined approach may facilitate clinical research and support acute stroke imaging workflows

AI.tldr: A study demonstrating that a baseline nnU-Net model trained on DWI-MRI alone can achieve accurate acute ischemic stroke (AIS) lesion segmentation (median DSC of 0.84) with fast inference times, outperforming the DeepISLES ensemble model particularly for smaller infarct volumes.
AI.motivation: To address the clinical need for fast and accurate AIS lesion segmentation by evaluating whether a pragmatic deep learning approach with minimal preprocessing can achieve clinically feasible inference times while maintaining accuracy, since current deep learning methods have uncertainty about optimal image inputs and model architectures.
AI.method: Trained self-configured nnU-Net models on 1,744 DWI cases from combined datasets, tested on 436 cases using five-fold cross-validation. Evaluated four experimental conditions: with/without brain extraction and DWI alone vs DWI+ADC. Compared baseline nnU-Net (base) vs residual encoder nnU-Net (ResEnc). Benchmarked against DeepISLES ensemble from 2022 ISLES challenge.
AI.result: Base model achieved median DSC of 0.84 (IQR 0.19). Only 2 of 6 pairwise input comparisons showed significant differences. ResEnc provided small but significant DSC improvements over base for DWI, DWI+brain extraction, and DWI+ADC inputs (p<0.02), but not for DWI+ADC+brain extraction (p>0.50). Base model significantly outperformed DeepISLES, especially for smaller infarct volumes (p<0.01).
AI.conclusion: A baseline nnU-Net trained on DWI alone without preprocessing enables fast and accurate AIS lesion segmentation, offering a streamlined approach that may facilitate clinical research and support acute stroke imaging workflows.

title: Refusal geometry reflects refusal training: diverse refusal prefixes can raise stable rank and weaken refusal vector ablation attacks
summary: Refusal training protects AI models from jailbreaks by training models to decline unsafe queries, reducing the risk of misuse. Recent work finds that refusal behavior in aligned language models can be mediated by a single activation direction or a low-dimensional refusal subspace shared across harmful prompts: ablating those directions suppresses refusals while largely preserves other model capabilities. Yet it remains unclear why safety-critical features in a wide range of models emerge and concentrated, low-dimensional structure. In a case study of OLMo-2-0425-1B-Instruct we find that the refusal geometry reflects refusal training: activation updates resulting from refusal-completion first-token losses explain the resulting refusal direction and refusal subspace. We study refusal directions through the training dynamics across refusal datasets and reveal that their brittleness is associated with repetitive refusal starts, which in turn is linked to concentration of gradients and refusal features in a low-dimensional subspace. Across frozen-model analyses and controlled synthetic fine-tuning, we find evidence of a hardening lever: diverse refusal starts can raise stable ranks of gradients and activation changes, making refusals harder to remove with a vector ablation attack.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates why refusal behavior in aligned language models emerges in low-dimensional subspaces and why it's vulnerable to vector ablation attacks. Through case studies on OLMo-2-0425-1B-Instruct, the authors find that refusal geometry directly reflects refusal training dynamics, and that repetitive refusal patterns lead to concentrated gradients making refusals brittle. They propose a hardening lever using diverse refusal starts to increase gradient rank and improve robustness against ablation attacks.
AI.motivation: To understand why safety-critical features in aligned language models emerge in concentrated, low-dimensional structures and why refusal behavior can be easily suppressed through ablation attacks, despite models being trained to refuse harmful prompts.
AI.method: Case study on OLMo-2-0425-1B-Instruct combining frozen-model analyses with controlled synthetic fine-tuning. The authors examined refusal training dynamics across refusal datasets, analyzed activation updates from refusal-completion first-token losses, and studied the relationship between gradient concentration and refusal brittleness.
AI.result: Refusal geometry directly reflects refusal training: activation updates from refusal-completion losses explain both the refusal direction and subspace. Brittleness is associated with repetitive refusal starts, which leads to gradient and refusal feature concentration in low-dimensional subspaces. Using diverse refusal starts can raise the rank of gradients and activation changes, making refusals harder to remove via vector ablation.
AI.conclusion: The concentration of refusal features in low-dimensional subspaces is not accidental but reflects the training dynamics of refusal training. By encouraging diverse refusal starts during training, models can develop more robust refusal behaviors that are less vulnerable to ablation attacks, offering a practical hardening lever for improving AI safety.

title: What Does an Evaluation License? A Commit-Bound Census of Claim-Relative Inference in Inspect Evals
comment: 31 pages; major revision; adds a commit-bound 124-unit Inspect Evals census, typed evidence-stopping taxonomy, executable claim-replay contract, full scientific appendix, and public reproducibility package
summary: Evaluation artifacts specify a forward computation: a task, scorer, and reported metric. They do not necessarily license the claim attached to that metric because the historical evidence and alternative semantics needed to replay it may be unbound. We formalize this missing claim-replay layer through a frozen substrate D, a grounded family F, a claim query q, and the resulting identified set. We then census all 124 mechanically eligible Inspect Evals units at a pinned commit. Every unit receives a terminal disposition; 110 stop before deterministic inference because required historical evidence or semantic grounding is unavailable. Where execution closes, exact values, winners, complete orders, and pairwise relations separate by claim resolution and by primary versus review family. The audit therefore returns typed stops, instability witnesses, and stable substructure rather than forcing one evaluator meaning or one robust/not-robust label.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses a fundamental problem in AI evaluation: evaluation artifacts (tasks, scorers, metrics) may not actually support the claims made about them because the evidence needed to reproduce results is unavailable. The authors formalize this through a framework involving frozen substrates, grounded families, and claim queries, then audit 124 Inspect Evals units finding that 110 cannot be deterministically replayed due to missing historical evidence or semantic grounding.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to expose a critical gap in AI evaluation practice: evaluation artifacts specify forward computations but lack the necessary historical evidence and semantic grounding to actually verify the claims attached to metrics. This creates a reproducibility crisis where evaluation results cannot be independently verified.
AI.method: The authors formalize the problem through four components: (1) a frozen substrate D representing the evaluation setup, (2) a grounded family F providing semantic interpretation, (3) a claim query q about the evaluation, and (4) the resulting identified set of valid interpretations. They then empirically census all 124 mechanically eligible Inspect Evals units at a pinned commit, assigning each a terminal disposition based on whether execution can complete.
AI.result: Out of 124 evaluation units, 110 stop before deterministic inference due to unavailable historical evidence or semantic grounding. Where execution does close, exact values, winners, complete orders, and pairwise relations can be determined, separating by claim resolution and by primary versus review family. The audit returns typed stops, instability witnesses, and stable substructure rather than binary labels.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that evaluation claims cannot be taken at face value without examining the replay layer—the historical evidence and semantic grounding needed to reproduce results. Rather than forcing one evaluator meaning or a simple robust/not-robust label, the approach provides nuanced typed classifications of why evaluations fail to replay and identifies what substructure remains stable.

title: CloSeR: Unified Relational Distillation from Closed-Set Teachers for Category Discovery
comment: Accepted as a conference paper at ECCV 2026
summary: Generalized Category Discovery (GCD) is an intriguing open-world problem that has garnered increasing attention: given partially labelled data, the goal is to correctly recognize known classes while discovering coherent novel categories from unlabelled samples. Recent GCD methods typically adapt foundation models by jointly optimizing supervised classification and unsupervised discovery objectives on mixed labelled and unlabelled data. While effective, this coupled training can entangle closed-set recognition and open-set discovery, leading to objective conflict and biased predictions, and may disturb the semantic geometry of pretrained representations under limited labels and noisy pseudo-labels. We propose CloSeR, a simple plug-and-play framework that injects Closed-Set Relational knowledge into GCD training. CloSeR first builds a domain-adapted closed-set teacher by tuning lightweight block-wise adapters on labelled known-class data while keeping the foundation model backbone frozen, thereby preserving pretrained priors at low training cost. It then transfers the teacher's knowledge to downstream GCD via Unified Relational Distillation (URD), which distills complementary global sample-to-prototype relations to anchor known-class semantics and local sample-to-sample relations to preserve neighborhood structure, using separate feature pathways to reduce optimization interference. CloSeR is head-agnostic and readily integrates with both parametric and non-parametric GCD methods. Extensive experiments with DINO and DINOv2 backbones on six benchmarks (CIFAR-10/100, ImageNet-100, CUB, Stanford-Cars, and FGVC-Aircraft) show consistent gains over GCD baselines, achieving state-of-the-art performance. Project page: https://visual-ai.github.io/closer/

AI.tldr: CloSeR is a plug-and-play framework that improves Generalized Category Discovery (GCD) by injecting closed-set relational knowledge. It uses a domain-adapted teacher built with lightweight adapters, and transfers knowledge via Unified Relational Distillation (URD) that preserves both global prototype relations and local neighborhood structure. The method is head-agnostic and works with both parametric and non-parametric GCD approaches.
AI.motivation: Current GCD methods jointly optimize supervised classification and unsupervised discovery objectives, which entangles closed-set recognition and open-set discovery, causing objective conflict, biased predictions, and disturbance to semantic geometry of pretrained representations under limited labels and noisy pseudo-labels.
AI.method: CloSeR builds a domain-adapted closed-set teacher by tuning lightweight block-wise adapters on labelled known-class data while keeping the foundation model backbone frozen. It then transfers knowledge to downstream GCD via Unified Relational Distillation (URD), which distills global sample-to-prototype relations and local sample-to-sample relations using separate feature pathways to reduce optimization interference.
AI.result: Extensive experiments with DINO and DINOv2 backbones on six benchmarks (CIFAR-10/100, ImageNet-100, CUB, Stanford-Cars, and FGVC-Aircraft) show consistent gains over GCD baselines, achieving state-of-the-art performance.
AI.conclusion: CloSeR provides a simple yet effective plug-and-play solution that preserves pretrained priors at low training cost while reducing optimization interference between closed-set recognition and open-set discovery. It is head-agnostic and readily integrates with both parametric and non-parametric GCD methods.

title: Joint Initialization of Flux Networks and Effective Multiplication Factor for Physics-Informed Neural Networks Solving Neutron Diffusion Problems
summary: Efficient determination of the effective multiplication factor (keff) is an important computational task in reactor core neutronics analysis. Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) incorporate neutron diffusion equations and boundary conditions into network training to efficiently determine the neutron flux distribution and keff. To further improve the efficiency of keff calculations using PINNs, a Joint Initialization Physics-Informed Neural Network (JI-PINN) is proposed in this work. In this method, a low-resolution approximate solution to the K-eigenvalue problem is used to construct a joint initial state for the flux network parameters and keff, and both are then jointly optimized under physical constraints. The proposed method was validated on a two-dimensional two-group two-material case, the IAEA 2D benchmark, a two-dimensional two-group four-material case, and a three-dimensional single-group case. For these test cases, the total computational time was reduced by 25.4%, 38.2%, 49.4%, and 28.9%, respectively, while comparable solution accuracy was maintained. The occurrence of anomalous results associated with marked deviations of keff from the reference value was also reduced. The proposed method provides a more efficient and robust initialization strategy for solving neutron diffusion K-eigenvalue problem with PINNs.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a Joint Initialization Physics-Informed Neural Network (JI-PINN) to improve computational efficiency in determining the effective multiplication factor (keff) for reactor core neutronics. The method uses a low-resolution approximate solution to initialize both flux network parameters and keff, which are then jointly optimized under physical constraints.
AI.motivation: Efficient determination of keff is a critical computational task in reactor core neutronics analysis. While Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) can incorporate neutron diffusion equations and boundary conditions into network training, there is a need to further improve the efficiency of keff calculations.
AI.method: The proposed JI-PINN method uses a low-resolution approximate solution to the K-eigenvalue problem to construct a joint initial state for the flux network parameters and keff. Both parameters are then jointly optimized under physical constraints (neutron diffusion equations and boundary conditions).
AI.result: The method was validated on four test cases: (1) 2D two-group two-material case - 25.4% time reduction; (2) IAEA 2D benchmark - 38.2% time reduction; (3) 2D two-group four-material case - 49.4% time reduction; (4) 3D single-group case - 28.9% time reduction. Comparable solution accuracy was maintained, and the occurrence of anomalous results with marked keff deviations was reduced.
AI.conclusion: The JI-PINN provides a more efficient and robust initialization strategy for solving neutron diffusion K-eigenvalue problems with PINNs, achieving significant computational time reductions (25-50%) while maintaining accuracy and reducing anomalous results.

title: Unsupervised Anatomical Feature Learning via Diffusion Models: Enhanced Medical Image Segmentation with Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models
comment: 15 pages, 5 figures. Submitted for peer review
summary: Acquiring pixel-level annotations for medical image segmentation is a severe bottleneck. Traditional U-Net architectures, while effective, learn local texture patterns and lack awareness of global anatomical structures, leading to boundary delineation failures in low-data regimes. This research paper proposes utilizing unsupervised Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models (DDPMs) to extract anatomical features. We train a DDPM on 21 unlabeled abdominal CT scans to learn structural representations, transferring the encoder weights to a downstream segmentation task evaluated on the BTCV multi-organ dataset. Diffusion pretraining significantly improved liver segmentation: Dice increased from $0.75\pm0.36$ to $0.93\pm0.16$ ($p < 5.33\times10^{-26}$, 0.529 Cohen's d), Average Surface Distance (ASD) decreased by 66%, and 95th-percentile Hausdorff Distance (HD95) reduced by 45%. For kidney segmentation, Dice improved from $0.90\pm0.19$ to $0.95\pm0.10$ ($p < 4.01\times10^{-11}$). Multi-organ pooled performance showed a 68% variance reduction and a 74% improvement in boundary precision (Dice $0.95\pm0.07$). Crucially, frozen encoder models retained > 80% of fine-tuned performance without exposure to segmentation labels, proving the existence of learned anatomical priors. In low-data scenarios, diffusion-pretrained models maintained robust performance with only 50% (Dice: 0.92 liver, 0.94 kidney), 25%, and even 10% (Dice: 0.89 liver, 0.71 kidney) of labeled data. Using unlabeled images for diffusion-based pretraining successfully embeds robust anatomical features prior to human supervision, transforming U-Nets into anatomy-aware systems.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses the scarcity of pixel-level annotations in medical image segmentation by using unsupervised Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models (DDPMs) to pretrain U-Net encoders on unlabeled abdominal CT scans. The approach achieves significant improvements in liver, kidney, and multi-organ segmentation on the BTCV dataset, while also demonstrating robust performance in low-data regimes.
AI.motivation: Pixel-level annotations for medical image segmentation are expensive and time-consuming to obtain. Traditional U-Net architectures learn local texture patterns but lack awareness of global anatomical structures, leading to boundary delineation failures especially in low-data regimes.
AI.method: Train a DDPM on 21 unlabeled abdominal CT scans to learn structural representations, then transfer the encoder weights to a downstream segmentation network (U-Net) evaluated on the BTCV multi-organ dataset.
AI.result: Liver segmentation: Dice increased from 0.75±0.36 to 0.93±0.16 (p<5.33×10⁻²⁶), ASD decreased by 66%, HD95 reduced by 45%. Kidney: Dice improved from 0.90±0.19 to 0.95±0.10 (p<4.01×10⁻¹¹). Multi-organ: Dice 0.95±0.07 with 68% variance reduction and 74% boundary precision improvement. Frozen encoder retained >80% of fine-tuned performance. Low-data scenarios (50%/25%/10% labeled data) maintained robust performance (e.g., 10%: Dice 0.89 liver, 0.71 kidney).
AI.conclusion: Using unlabeled images for diffusion-based pretraining successfully embeds robust anatomical features prior to human supervision, transforming U-Nets into anatomy-aware systems. The learned anatomical priors are preserved even in frozen encoder models.

title: Resolving Multi-Modal Regression by Difference-Quotient-Based Clustering:Fast Coarse Conditional-Label Assignment
summary: Multimodal regression suffers from the mean-collapse pathology: under squared loss, an unconstrained regressor converges to the conditional mean, which for K > 1 lies away from all modes. We attribute this failure to pairwise contradictions--samples with nearly identical inputs but distant outputs--and propose Difference-Quotient Clustering (DQC), which partitions data to minimize intra-cluster output-vs-input discrepancy. Each sample is assigned to the cluster that minimizes its maximum contradiction ratio; a logits generator and a conditional network are then trained on the resulting labels. Since the generating modality is unknown at test time, we evaluate via minimum squared error (minMSE) against all K true outputs. On synthetic benchmarks (K=5, 10), DQC achieves test minMSE 0.19 (K=5, nx=500), versus 0.09 for an oracle, 1.08 for random labels, and 1.33 for mean collapse. We observe two empirical regularities: larger intra-cluster contradictions require deeper networks, and oracle labels generalize from fewer samples than cluster-derived equivalents. The clustering is a hard, parallelizable O(n^2/2) front-end for coarse conditional assignment, reducing the burden of downstream generative refinement. A second-stage re-clustering on residual errors is outlined as future work.

AI.tldr: The paper addresses mean-collapse pathology in multimodal regression, where standard regressors converge to the conditional mean away from all modes. The authors propose Difference-Quotient Clustering (DQC) to partition data by minimizing intra-cluster output-vs-input discrepancy, training a logits generator and conditional network on cluster assignments.
AI.motivation: Multimodal regression suffers from mean-collapse pathology: under squared loss, unconstrained regressors converge to the conditional mean, which for K > 1 modes lies away from all modes. This failure is attributed to pairwise contradictions - samples with nearly identical inputs but distant outputs.
AI.method: Difference-Quotient Clustering (DQC) partitions data to minimize intra-cluster output-vs-input discrepancy. Each sample is assigned to the cluster that minimizes its maximum contradiction ratio. A logits generator and a conditional network are then trained on the resulting labels. Evaluation uses minimum squared error (minMSE) against all K true outputs since the generating modality is unknown at test time.
AI.result: On synthetic benchmarks (K=5, 10, nx=500), DQC achieves test minMSE of 0.19, compared to 0.09 for oracle, 1.08 for random labels, and 1.33 for mean collapse. Two empirical regularities observed: (1) larger intra-cluster contradictions require deeper networks, (2) oracle labels generalize from fewer samples than cluster-derived equivalents.
AI.conclusion: DQC provides a hard, parallelizable O(n^2/2) front-end for coarse conditional assignment, reducing the burden of downstream generative refinement. The clustering approach effectively addresses mean-collapse by explicitly handling multimodal output distributions. Future work includes second-stage re-clustering on residual errors.

title: Skeleton-based Zero-Shot Spatio-Temporal Action Localization via Weakly-Supervised Pretraining
summary: We propose a novel pretraining strategy for skeleton-based zero-shot spatio-temporal action localization to estimate unseen actions for person instances while overcoming high annotation costs for training via new target actions and pretraining using large-scale action scenery datasets. Specifically, our approach, termed Skeleton-Language feature Pooling Switching, introduces a weakly-supervised vision-language pretraining mechanism. This mechanism transitions pooling kernels from pretraining, which aggregates skeleton features at the video level and aligns them with each video's known action text embeddings, to the inference phase that computes instance-level features without training via target actions. Furthermore, we propose Scene-Mixed Discriminative Contrastive Learning to distinguish actions at the instance level within the combined scene through the MIL framework. Our experiments on four public spatio-temporal action localization and classification datasets demonstrate that the proposed method effectively addresses annotation limitations.
