title: A Storage-Retrieval Gap in Parametric Knowledge Graph Memory
comment: 12 pages, 2 figures, 7 tables, accepted at SKGi 2026
summary: Graph retrieval-augmented generation places retrieved subgraphs into the model's context window at query time, paying a recurring token cost and exposing source data on every call. We study an alternative: compiling a knowledge graph offline into a bank of LoRA adapters, one per entity, that serve as a parametric knowledge layer queried by injecting weights rather than text, at zero query-time context cost. On the MetaQA dataset, we find that subgraph-trained adapters encode context-free factual knowledge that generalizes to unseen questions: on single-valued relations the adapter gains $+0.243$ exact-match score over a base model that is nearly blind closed-book ($0.007$), and only the correct adapter recovers this knowledge (an oracle gap of $+0.283$ over the base model). However, the stored knowledge is not recoverable by similarity: given a query with no subgraph, embedding-based and weight-space geometry retrieval both perform at chance, because a semantically neighbouring entity's adapter does not contain the answer - knowledge is stored locally and does not transfer. Weight geometry correlates with subgraph semantics ($ρ= +0.329$) but not with functional retrievability. We quantify the byte and context-token costs against graph retrieval-augmented generation and discuss deployment implications. Our results establish that parametric knowledge graph memory is feasible for storing knowledge, and identify selecting and composing the right adapters by a mechanism other than semantic similarity as the central open problem - motivating a learned, query-conditioned composition mechanism.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes an alternative to graph retrieval-augmented generation (GRAG): compiling a knowledge graph offline into LoRA adapters per entity, enabling zero query-time context cost by injecting weights instead of text. On MetaQA, adapter-trained models show significant gains in factual knowledge retention (+0.243 EM over base model), but retrieval via semantic similarity or weight-space geometry fails at chance levels, indicating knowledge is stored locally without transfer. The study establishes parametric knowledge graph memory as feasible but identifies learned query-conditioned composition as the key open problem.
AI.motivation: Graph retrieval-augmented generation (GRAG) incurs recurring token costs and exposes source data on every query. This paper seeks an alternative approach that compiles knowledge offline into parametric form (LoRA adapters) to eliminate query-time context costs and data exposure, while maintaining knowledge retrieval capabilities.
AI.method: The approach involves training LoRA adapters on knowledge graph subgraphs, with one adapter per entity. These adapters serve as a parametric knowledge layer queried by injecting weights rather than text. Experiments on MetaQA dataset evaluate: (1) exact-match scores for factual knowledge generalization, (2) retrieval via embedding similarity and weight-space geometry, and (3) correlation between weight geometry and subgraph semantics.
AI.result: On single-valued relations, the adapter achieves +0.243 exact-match score improvement over a nearly blind closed-book base model (0.007), with an oracle gap of +0.283 over the base model. However, both embedding-based and weight-space geometry retrieval perform at chance when no subgraph is provided, as neighboring entity adapters do not contain answers. Weight geometry correlates with subgraph semantics (ρ = +0.329) but not with functional retrievability.
AI.conclusion: Parametric knowledge graph memory via LoRA adapters is feasible for storing factual knowledge. However, current retrieval mechanisms fail because knowledge is stored locally without transfer. The central open problem is selecting and composing the right adapters through mechanisms other than semantic similarity, motivating a learned, query-conditioned composition mechanism.

title: Difficulty-Aware Sample Allocation for Adaptive Data Augmentation in Semantic Segmentation
summary: Data augmentation is a standard component of modern semantic segmentation pipelines, but most augmentation techniques allocate transformations uniformly across training samples or adapt to a single difficulty signal such as loss. This ignores the fact that segmentation difficulty is multi-factorial, since ambiguous predictions, persistent optimization errors, rare classes, and complex object boundaries can each make a sample informative in different ways. This paper introduces Difficulty-Aware Sample Allocation (DASA), an architecture-agnostic framework that assigns stronger augmentation to samples estimated to be more difficult. DASA combines prediction ambiguity, training loss, class rarity, and boundary complexity into a normalized difficulty score, then maps that score to sample-specific augmentation strength during iterative training. Experiments on Oxford-IIIT Pet and binary Pascal VOC segmentation with U-Net, DeepLabV3, and SegFormer-B0 show that DASA improves over standard training and is competitive with or stronger than single-signal adaptive baselines. On Oxford-IIIT Pet, DASA improves DeepLabV3 from 0.633 to 0.740 mIoU. On binary Pascal VOC, DASA obtains the best foreground IoU for all three evaluated architectures. These results attest to the value of multi-factor difficulty estimation as a practical mechanism for directing augmentation where it is most useful.

title: FedQoS: Federated QoS-Risk Learning for Heterogeneous Indoor-Outdoor Access Selection
comment: Accepted at the IEEE PIMRC 2026 Workshop on Intelligent Aerial and Spaceborne Systems for 6G (6G-SAGA): AI Native SAGIN for Indoor, Personal, and Mobile Radio Communications, 7 pages, 3 figures
summary: Reliable access selection in dynamic and heterogeneous indoor-outdoor environments is challenging because instantaneous radio measurements alone cannot capture future QoS degradation caused by mobility, blockage, traffic load, and resource competition. This paper proposes FedQoS, a federated QoS-risk learning framework for predicting the future reliability of candidate access links and supporting access-node selection without centralizing user-level network data. In FedQoS, each access node locally learns from its observed network logs, including radio, traffic, load, and service-context features, while a global QoS-risk predictor is trained through federated aggregation. The learned model estimates the probability of QoS failure for each candidate link, and the controller uses these risk scores to select reliable access nodes under dynamic network conditions. To evaluate the framework, we construct physics-based synthetic indoor-outdoor wireless datasets using the Sionna framework, covering normal traffic, mobility, event-driven congestion, and non-IID client observations. Simulation results show that learning-based access selection substantially reduces the QoS-failure rate compared with signal-based and historical-QoS heuristic methods. FedQoS achieves near-centralized predictive performance and provides clear reliability gains under mild non-IID data while remaining competitive under the more challenging severe non-IID condition. These results demonstrate the potential of federated QoS-risk learning for reliable, data-local access selection in dynamic wireless environments.

AI.tldr: FedQoS is a federated QoS-risk learning framework that predicts future reliability of candidate access links in dynamic indoor-outdoor wireless environments without centralizing user-level network data. Access nodes locally learn from network logs (radio, traffic, load, service-context features), and a global predictor is trained through federated aggregation to estimate QoS failure probability for access selection.
AI.motivation: Reliable access selection in dynamic and heterogeneous indoor-outdoor environments is challenging because instantaneous radio measurements alone cannot capture future QoS degradation caused by mobility, blockage, traffic load, and resource competition.
AI.method: FedQoS uses federated learning where each access node locally learns from observed network logs (radio, traffic, load, and service-context features). A global QoS-risk predictor is trained through federated aggregation. The learned model estimates the probability of QoS failure for each candidate link, and the controller uses these risk scores for reliable access node selection under dynamic network conditions.
AI.result: Learning-based access selection substantially reduces QoS-failure rate compared with signal-based and historical-QoS heuristic methods. FedQoS achieves near-centralized predictive performance with clear reliability gains under mild non-IID data, remaining competitive under severe non-IID conditions.
AI.conclusion: Federated QoS-risk learning demonstrates potential for reliable, data-local access selection in dynamic wireless environments, balancing privacy with predictive performance.

title: LongVU-TTT: Causal Test-Time Training for Visual Resampling in Long Video Understanding
summary: Long-video MLLMs must model temporal change before a limited visual-token budget removes most frame evidence. We introduce LongVU-TTT, which inserts a convolutional Test-Time Training (TTT) resampler with causal fast-weight updates between the vision encoder and the LLM. Its grouped 2D fast weights adapt to each video and contextualize frame features before compression, while a hybrid uniform-and-change-aware selector retains explicit visual evidence for downstream reasoning. Under controlled conditions, TTT-Conv improves over TTT-MLP by up to +2.12 and bidirectional Mamba2 by up to +3.04 on MLVU, and it is stronger than attention- and fixed-state recurrent resamplers across three benchmarks. Analysis shows that the fast weights behave as a temporal aggregation state rather than a reliable long-horizon episodic memory: their benefit attenuates as evidence becomes more distant, motivating explicit frame retention. LongVU-TTT processes up to 512 frames before reducing them to 128 LLM frames and achieves competitive performance across five video understanding benchmarks.

AI.tldr: LongVU-TTT addresses the challenge of modeling temporal change in long-video multimodal language models when limited visual-token budgets remove most frame evidence. It introduces a convolutional Test-Time Training (TTT) resampler with causal fast-weight updates between the vision encoder and LLM, featuring grouped 2D fast weights that adapt to each video and contextualize frame features before compression, combined with a hybrid uniform-and-change-aware selector for explicit frame retention. The method processes up to 512 frames and reduces them to 128 LLM frames.
AI.motivation: Long-video MLLMs must model temporal change, but limited visual-token budgets remove most frame evidence. This creates a fundamental tension between maintaining temporal understanding and fitting within computational constraints.
AI.method: The approach introduces a convolutional Test-Time Training (TTT) resampler with causal fast-weight updates inserted between the vision encoder and LLM. Key innovations include: (1) Grouped 2D fast weights that adapt to each video and contextualize frame features before compression, and (2) A hybrid uniform-and-change-aware selector that retains explicit visual evidence for downstream reasoning.
AI.result: TTT-Conv improves over TTT-MLP by up to +2.12 and bidirectional Mamba2 by up to +3.04 on MLVU. It outperforms attention- and fixed-state recurrent resamplers across three benchmarks. The fast weights behave as a temporal aggregation state rather than reliable long-horizon episodic memory, with benefits attenuating as evidence becomes more distant.
AI.conclusion: LongVU-TTT achieves competitive performance across five video understanding benchmarks by combining adaptive TTT resampling with explicit frame retention. The analysis reveals that while fast-weight temporal aggregation helps, the benefit diminishes over longer time horizons, justifying the hybrid approach of explicit frame retention alongside learned temporal modeling.

title: Resilient Decentralized Wireless Federated Learning via Gradient Tracking with AdamW
comment: Accepted at the 2026 IEEE Global Communications Conference (GLOBECOM 2026), IoT and Sensor Networks Symposium, 7 pages, 5 figures
summary: Wireless Internet-of-Things (IoT) edge networks require decentralized learning (DecL) methods that can operate reliably under both heterogeneous local data and communication-constrained wireless links. However, existing decentralized optimization schemes often incur substantial communication overhead and degraded performance when transmissions are constrained by strict airtime budgets, fading channels, and packet losses. This paper proposes QEF-GT-AdamW, a communication-efficient and outage-resilient algorithm for DecL over wireless communication (WCom) networks. The proposed method combines gradient tracking to mitigate the effect of non-IID data, AdamW-based adaptive optimization to improve training stability, and dual-stream biased quantization with error feedback to reduce communication payloads for both model and tracking exchanges. To address unreliable broadcast communication, the proposed framework further employs a local fallback strategy when scheduled packets are not successfully received. We explicitly model the effect of bandwidth, transmit power, airtime constraints, and fading channels on DecL performance, and establish convergence guarantees for the proposed algorithm under compressed and unreliable wireless communication. Experimental results on heterogeneous MNIST and CIFAR-10 settings show that QEF-GT-AdamW consistently improves robustness and convergence performance over representative DecL baselines while achieving favorable accuracy-communication trade-offs under limited wireless resources.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes QEF-GT-AdamW, a communication-efficient and outage-resilient decentralized learning algorithm for wireless IoT edge networks. It combines gradient tracking, AdamW optimization, dual-stream biased quantization with error feedback, and a local fallback strategy to address heterogeneous data and communication constraints in wireless environments.
AI.motivation: Wireless IoT edge networks require decentralized learning methods that can handle heterogeneous local data and communication-constrained wireless links. Existing decentralized optimization schemes suffer from substantial communication overhead and degraded performance under strict airtime budgets, fading channels, and packet losses.
AI.method: The proposed QEF-GT-AdamW algorithm integrates four key components: (1) gradient tracking to mitigate non-IID data effects, (2) AdamW-based adaptive optimization for training stability, (3) dual-stream biased quantization with error feedback to reduce communication payloads, and (4) a local fallback strategy for handling failed packet transmissions. The framework explicitly models bandwidth, transmit power, airtime constraints, and fading channels.
AI.result: Experimental results on heterogeneous MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets show that QEF-GT-AdamW consistently improves robustness and convergence performance over representative DecL baselines while achieving favorable accuracy-communication trade-offs under limited wireless resources.
AI.conclusion: QEF-GT-AdamW effectively addresses the challenges of decentralized learning in wireless IoT edge networks by combining gradient tracking, adaptive optimization, communication compression, and outage resilience. The algorithm demonstrates superior performance in handling non-IID data and communication constraints, making it suitable for practical wireless IoT deployments.

title: MIMONet: Multi-scale Input and Multi-scale Output Network for Salient Object Detection
summary: The existing methods for saliency detection task focus on the application of multi-level features, aiming to take advantage of the respective strengths of high- and low-level features. However, because the inputs of these models are single-size images, their multi-level features have difficulty in learning the knowledge of size variations of salient objects. Object-scale variation learning has great potential for detecting multi-scale objects, which has not been fully explored by existing methods. To improve the recognition ability of a model for objects with different sizes, we are inspired by the image pyramid to propose a Multi-scale Input and Multi-scale Output Network (MIMONet). In MIMONet, we extract multi-level features for three images with different resolutions to form three encoder branches, and information will be exchanged between the branches. The advantage of this approach is that the features of one branch can learn the knowledge of target size variation from the features of the other two branches. In addition, we design a Multi-scale Perception (MSP) module, in which the input feature layer is divided into several sub-layers with different resolutions. Capturing the multi-level structure information of the objects in these sub-layers can make the objects more fully perceived. For network training, we propose a Joint Saliency Loss (JSL), which can constrain multiple saliency maps output by the network to identify the same foreground objects, and induce their boundaries to be preserved clearly. Experimental results show that MIMONet has stronger detection capabilities and harvests better evaluation scores on multiple datasets compared to existing models. The code of our model will be released.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes MIMONet, a Multi-scale Input and Multi-scale Output Network for saliency detection, which addresses the limitation of existing methods that fail to learn size variations of salient objects from single-size image inputs.
AI.motivation: Existing saliency detection methods use multi-level features from single-size images, but struggle to learn knowledge of size variations of salient objects. This limits their ability to detect multi-scale objects effectively.
AI.method: MIMONet uses three encoder branches with different input resolutions to extract multi-level features, enabling cross-branch learning of size variations. A Multi-scale Perception (MSP) module divides input features into sub-layers of different resolutions to capture multi-level structure information. For training, a Joint Saliency Loss (JSL) is proposed to constrain multiple output saliency maps to identify the same foreground objects while preserving clear boundaries.
AI.result: Experimental results demonstrate that MIMONet achieves stronger detection capabilities and better evaluation scores on multiple datasets compared to existing models.
AI.conclusion: The proposed MIMONet effectively addresses the object-scale variation problem in saliency detection through multi-scale input/output design and cross-branch feature learning, outperforming existing state-of-the-art methods.

title: Reflection Steering: Disentangling Reflection from Reasoning in Activation Space for Token-Efficient Inference
summary: Large reasoning models often produce reasoning traces with verification, revision, and backtracking. When reflection merely re-checks established results, it wastes reasoning tokens and increases latency. Most existing reflection steering methods add a label-derived mean-difference direction across preset layers, but its entanglement with reasoning and length signals destabilizes the accuracy-efficiency trade-off. In this paper, we propose Reflection Steering, a training-free framework for controlling reflection-associated computation within LLMs by disentangling reflection-related activations from general reasoning. Specifically, we contrast reflective and non-reflective hidden states at each LLM layer, denoise the resulting reflection directions with PCA, and orthogonalize them against general-reasoning directions. To limit downstream amplification from early-layer interventions, we calibrate each layer across multiple intervention strengths on a small set, retain only stable layers, and apply bounded projection removal to their residual-stream activations. We conduct extensive experiments across two public benchmarks and three open-weight LLMs against state-of-the-art activation-steering baselines. Results show that Reflection Steering reduces reasoning tokens by 16.9% on average across six matched settings. Besides, our method further introduces a bounded reflection intervention-strength parameter $α$, enabling deployment-time adjustment to balance token savings, accuracy, and generation stability.

AI.tldr: Reflection Steering is a training-free framework that reduces unnecessary reflection computation in large reasoning models by identifying and removing reflection-related activations from the residual stream. It contrasts reflective vs non-reflective hidden states, denoises with PCA, orthogonalizes against general reasoning, and applies bounded projection removal with a tunable parameter α for accuracy-efficiency trade-off. Achieves 16.9% token reduction on average.
AI.motivation: Large reasoning models waste reasoning tokens on reflection that merely re-checks established results. Existing reflection steering methods add label-derived mean-difference directions across preset layers, but this entangles reflection signals with reasoning and length signals, destabilizing the accuracy-efficiency trade-off.
AI.method:
1) Contrast reflective and non-reflective hidden states at each LLM layer to extract reflection directions
2) Denoise reflection directions using PCA
3) Orthogonalize against general-reasoning directions to disentangle reflection from reasoning
4) Calibrate each layer across multiple intervention strengths on a small set
5) Retain only stable layers (layers with consistent performance across strengths)
6) Apply bounded projection removal to residual-stream activations
7) Introduce bounded reflection intervention-strength parameter α for deployment-time adjustment
AI.result: Reduces reasoning tokens by 16.9% on average across six matched settings (two public benchmarks, three open-weight LLMs). The method enables tunable trade-off between token savings, accuracy, and generation stability via parameter α.
AI.conclusion: Reflection Steering successfully reduces unnecessary reflection computation without training. By disentangling reflection-related activations from general reasoning and using bounded interventions, it achieves significant token savings while maintaining accuracy and stability. The tunable parameter α provides flexible control over the accuracy-efficiency trade-off for deployment.

title: InteractGesture: Progressive Chunk Guidance for Continuous Streaming Co-Speech Gesture Control
summary: Co-speech gesture generation has made significant progress toward realistic full-body motion from speaker audio, yet existing models lack fine-grained spatial controllability of individual joints. To address this, we introduce \emph{InteractGesture}, a model-agnostic, inference-time method for spatially controllable gesture generation. \emph{InteractGesture} guides target latent estimates of a diffusion sampler through a differentiable RVQ-VAE decoder, backpropagating spatial control gradients to adjust motion latents during sampling. A primary challenge in streaming co-speech generation is chunk-wise dependency: standard sequential inference freezes prior chunks, preventing spatial constraints in future chunks from adjusting preceding trajectories and causing boundary inconsistencies. To overcome this limitation, we propose \emph{Progressive Chunk Guidance}, a chunk-window strategy that maintains an active set of editable chunk latents with staggered delays, enabling spatial constraints to propagate gradients backward across chunk boundaries during streaming generation. Experiments on the BEAT2 dataset show that \emph{InteractGesture} improves multi-joint spatial control while preserving overall gesture quality. Furthermore, our approach supports diverse applications, including sparse joint positioning, dense joint trajectory control, and directional pointing. Our project page is available at https://exitudio.github.io/interactgesture-page .

title: Interpreting Protein Language Model Embeddings via Orthogonal Projection for Protein Fitness Prediction
summary: Recently, there has been a growing adoption of protein language models (PLMs) in biomedical science. Their embeddings provide a rich numerical representation of protein sequences which achieve state-of-the-art performance on several downstream tasks including protein fitness prediction. However, PLM embeddings are not directly interpretable and, thereby, it remains unclear what features they encode. To gain insight into which biochemical properties of the protein are driving the prediction, we leverage an orthogonal projection technique that removes linear effects of known tabular features from embeddings and extend it to high-order and interaction effects. In this way, we remove the effects of interpretable biochemical features from PLM embeddings. In an ablation study, we show that this leads to a decrease in performance for a downstream classifier trained only on the embeddings to predict protein fitness. In an additional evaluation, we find that these biochemical features explain a substantial part of the variance in the predictions of this classifier. Hence, we can show that PLM embeddings encode patterns correlated with biochemical properties and quantify their contribution to predicting protein fitness. This computationally efficient approach is not limited to the features or embeddings considered here and is readily transferable to problem settings beyond protein fitness prediction.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates what biochemical properties are encoded in protein language model (PLM) embeddings by using orthogonal projection to remove the effects of known tabular features from these embeddings, demonstrating that PLMs capture biochemically relevant information useful for protein fitness prediction.
AI.motivation: Protein language models have achieved state-of-the-art performance on downstream tasks like protein fitness prediction, but their embeddings are not directly interpretable. It remains unclear what biochemical properties the embeddings actually encode, limiting understanding of why these models work.
AI.method: The authors apply an orthogonal projection technique to remove linear effects of known tabular features from PLM embeddings, extending this approach to high-order and interaction effects. They then conduct an ablation study where a downstream classifier is trained only on the residual embeddings (with biochemical features removed) to predict protein fitness.
AI.result: Removing biochemical features from PLM embeddings leads to decreased downstream classifier performance. Additionally, these biochemical features explain a substantial portion of variance in the predictions, demonstrating that PLM embeddings encode patterns correlated with interpretable biochemical properties.
AI.conclusion: PLM embeddings capture biochemically meaningful information beyond what is explicitly provided in tabular form. This computationally efficient approach is generalizable beyond protein fitness prediction and can be applied to other problem settings where interpretability of learned representations is needed.

title: Moving Beyond More Views: Redundancy-Aware Ego-Exo Fusion for Proficiency Estimation
summary: EgoExo proficiency estimation aims to assess action quality by integrating fine-grained motion cues from egocentric (1st-person) views with spatial context from multiple exocentric (3rd-person) views. Simply adding more exocentric views degrades EgoExo performance, as redundant or noisy perspectives dilute useful motion cues. Our analysis identifies two key causes: (1) Multiview redundancy - From the data perspective, certain views provide limited or noisy information, diluting discriminative cues; (2) Overfitting - From the feature perspective, conventional fusion increases representational complexity, causing the model to memorise view-specific patterns rather than learn generalisable representations. To address these issues, we propose two complementary modules: AdaMVS, which adaptively identifies and fuses the most informative view tokens under weak supervision from the data perspective, and VIB-GB, which combines Gradient Blending and Variational Information Bottleneck regularisation from the feature perspective to compress redundant signals and suppress overfitting during training. Experiments on EgoExo-4D and EgoExo-Fitness demonstrate that our method learns both which view to look at and how to fuse them, achieving new state-of-the-art results. Our source code is available at https://github.com/dx199771/AdaMVS

AI.tldr: This paper addresses ego-exo proficiency estimation by proposing two modules (AdaMVS and VIB-GB) to handle multiview redundancy and overfitting issues when fusing egocentric and multiple exocentric views. The method achieves state-of-the-art results on EgoExo-4D and EgoExo-Fitness datasets.
AI.motivation: Simply adding more exocentric views degrades EgoExo performance because redundant or noisy perspectives dilute useful motion cues. Two key causes were identified: (1) multiview redundancy from the data perspective - certain views provide limited or noisy information, and (2) overfitting from the feature perspective - conventional fusion increases representational complexity, causing the model to memorize view-specific patterns rather than learn generalizable representations.
AI.method: The authors propose two complementary modules: (1) AdaMVS, which adaptively identifies and fuses the most informative view tokens under weak supervision from the data perspective, and (2) VIB-GB, which combines Gradient Blending and Variational Information Bottleneck regularization from the feature perspective to compress redundant signals and suppress overfitting during training.
AI.result: Experiments on EgoExo-4D and EgoExo-Fitness demonstrate that the method learns both which view to look at and how to fuse them, achieving new state-of-the-art results.
AI.conclusion: The proposed approach effectively addresses the challenges of multiview redundancy and overfitting in ego-exo proficiency estimation by combining adaptive view selection (AdaMVS) with regularization techniques (VIB-GB), enabling the model to learn generalizable representations from multiple camera views.

title: Beyond Optimal Rates in Stochastic Optimization: Trajectory-Adaptive Stopping Rules
summary: Stochastic gradient descent (SGD) is typically analyzed at a deterministic horizon chosen before the algorithm is run, even though practical stopping decisions are made adaptively by inspecting the evolving trajectory. This mismatch creates a fundamental certification problem: fixed-time guarantees do not generally remain valid at data-dependent stopping times, while deterministic horizons derived from worst-case bounds can be highly conservative. We address this problem for strongly convex stochastic optimization by constructing fully observable, trajectory-adaptive upper confidence sequences for the squared distance of the last iterate to the optimizer and the suboptimality of a weighted average. These bounds hold simultaneously over time, attain the optimal $1/t$ decay rate up to iterated-logarithmic factors in the worst case, and adapt to the realized stochastic gradients, allowing SGD to stop as soon as a prescribed accuracy is certified without sacrificing statistical validity. Our approach treats the evolving SGD trajectory as a sequential experiment whose observations provide evidence about the unknown optimization error. To formalize this perspective, we develop new recursive confidence-sequence techniques and a general time-uniform empirical Bernstein inequality for adapted processes with time-varying conditional means and predictable ranges that may grow without bound. We further extend these confidence-sequence constructions to minibatch SGD, with the empirical Bernstein bounds exploiting the realized second-moment structure within each minibatch. Numerical experiments show that the resulting stopping rules can require several orders of magnitude fewer iterations than natural deterministic horizons.

AI.tldr: The paper addresses a fundamental certification problem in stochastic gradient descent (SGD) analysis: the mismatch between fixed-time theoretical guarantees and adaptive stopping decisions in practice. The authors construct trajectory-adaptive confidence sequences for strongly convex optimization that allow SGD to stop when a prescribed accuracy is certified while maintaining statistical validity.
AI.motivation: The core problem is that traditional SGD analysis assumes a deterministic horizon chosen before running the algorithm, but practical stopping decisions are made adaptively by inspecting the evolving trajectory. This creates a certification issue: fixed-time guarantees don't generally hold at data-dependent stopping times, and worst-case derived horizons can be highly conservative. The motivation is to develop methods that allow SGD to adaptively stop based on the actual observed trajectory without sacrificing statistical validity.
AI.method: The approach treats the evolving SGD trajectory as a sequential experiment whose observations provide evidence about the unknown optimization error. The methodology includes: (1) developing new recursive confidence-sequence techniques, (2) constructing a general time-uniform empirical Bernstein inequality for adapted processes with time-varying conditional means and predictable ranges that may grow without bound, and (3) extending these confidence-sequence constructions to minibatch SGD, exploiting the realized second-moment structure within each minibatch.
AI.result: The resulting bounds hold simultaneously over time, attain the optimal 1/t decay rate up to iterated-logarithmic factors in the worst case, and adapt to the realized stochastic gradients. The numerical experiments demonstrate that the resulting stopping rules can require several orders of magnitude fewer iterations than natural deterministic horizons.
AI.conclusion: The paper provides a principled framework for adaptive stopping in SGD that maintains statistical validity. By treating SGD as a sequential experiment and developing new empirical Bernstein inequalities for adapted processes, the authors enable data-dependent stopping times with theoretical guarantees. This bridges the gap between theoretical analysis and practical implementation of SGD, potentially leading to significant computational savings in practice.

title: TDFNet: Tri-projection Deformable Fusion Network for Panoramic Salient Object Detection
summary: Recent years have witnessed the growing potential of panoramic salient object detection in robotic vision, virtual reality, and related applications. However, projecting spherical scenes onto 2D planes inevitably introduces geometric distortions, which fundamentally limit the effectiveness of existing projection-based methods. Specifically, Equirectangular Projection (ERP) suffers from severe polar stretching distortions, while cube map projection introduces discontinuities across cube-face boundaries, resulting in degraded feature discriminability and compromised geometric consistency. To address these limitations, we propose TDFNet, the first Tri-projection Deformable Fusion Network for panoramic salient object detection, exploiting complementary projection representations to alleviate geometric distortions and improve detection performance.Specifically, we design a cross-projection deformable attention (CDA) module that leverages spatial correspondences between different projections to construct geometry-aware sampling locations, guiding deformable attention for cross-projection contextual aggregation and enhancing robustness against projection-induced deformations. Furthermore, we introduce a latitude-guided fusion module, which utilizes spherical latitude priors to construct geometric confidence weights for adaptively balancing ERP and CMP features. Meanwhile, LGF incorporates distortion-reduced semantic references from Tangent Projection to achieve cross-projection feature refinement and spatial alignment.By constructing a three-branch encoding architecture based on ERP, CMP, and Tangent Projection, TDFNet simultaneously preserves global spatial continuity, local geometric details, and fine-grained boundary information.

AI.tldr: TDFNet is the first Tri-projection Deformable Fusion Network for panoramic salient object detection, addressing geometric distortions in equirectangular and cube map projections through a three-branch architecture combining ERP, CMP, and Tangent Projection with cross-projection deformable attention and latitude-guided fusion modules.
AI.motivation: Existing projection-based methods for panoramic salient object detection suffer from geometric distortions: ERP has polar stretching distortions, while CMP has discontinuities across cube-face boundaries, compromising feature discriminability and geometric consistency.
AI.method: TDFNet uses a three-branch encoding architecture with ERP, CMP, and Tangent Projection. It includes: (1) Cross-projection deformable attention (CDA) module that leverages spatial correspondences between projections to construct geometry-aware sampling locations for cross-projection contextual aggregation; (2) Latitude-guided fusion module that uses spherical latitude priors to create geometric confidence weights for balancing ERP and CMP features, incorporating distortion-reduced semantic references from Tangent Projection.
AI.result: The network simultaneously preserves global spatial continuity (via ERP), local geometric details (via CMP), and fine-grained boundary information (via Tangent Projection), while enhancing robustness against projection-induced deformations through deformable attention and adaptive fusion.
AI.conclusion: TDFNet effectively addresses the fundamental limitations of projection-based panoramic salient object detection by fusing complementary projection representations, offering a promising approach for applications in robotic vision and virtual reality.

title: Physics-Informed Foresight Pruning for Sparse PINN Solvers of Nonlinear PDEs
comment: 7 pages, 1 figure, 6 Tables. Submitted to the AI4S 2026 Workshop, Scientific Machine Learning track
summary: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) often rely on over-parameterized models to optimize coupled solution and differential-residual objectives, leaving unclear how much capacity is necessary and what pruning should preserve. We study foresight pruning at initialization for sparse PirateNet PDE solvers. Standard neural tangent kernel spectrum-aware pruning (NTK-SAP) aims to preserve output-side training dynamics but may overlook parameters whose main influence arises through derivatives in the governing equations. We introduce physics-informed spectrum-aware pruning (PI-SAP), which assigns saliency using sensitivity of the PDE residual. Experiments on the Gray-Scott equations, complex Ginzburg-Landau equation, Burgers' equation, and linear convection equation show that PI-SAP more consistently preserves Gray-Scott residual fidelity and is competitive under aggressive sparsity. However, no criterion is uniformly optimal across equations or sparsity levels. Small-batch PINN-NTK diagnostics further show that residual fidelity, solution accuracy, and kernel conditioning are distinct objectives, motivating pruning methods that explicitly balance solution-side and residual-side training dynamics during optimization.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Physics-Informed Spectrum-Aware Pruning (PI-SAP) for sparse PirateNet PDE solvers, which uses PDE residual sensitivity for saliency assignment instead of standard NTK-SAP. Experiments on Gray-Scott, complex Ginzburg-Landau, Burgers', and linear convection equations show PI-SAP better preserves residual fidelity under aggressive sparsity, though no single criterion is universally optimal.
AI.motivation: PINNs rely on over-parameterized models to optimize coupled solution and differential-residual objectives, making it unclear how much model capacity is necessary. Standard NTK-SAP preserves output-side training dynamics but may overlook parameters whose influence arises through derivatives in governing equations.
AI.method: The authors propose PI-SAP, which assigns saliency using sensitivity of the PDE residual rather than output-side dynamics. They also use small-batch PINN-NTK diagnostics to analyze whether residual fidelity, solution accuracy, and kernel conditioning are distinct optimization objectives.
AI.result: PI-SAP more consistently preserves Gray-Scott residual fidelity and is competitive under aggressive sparsity. However, no criterion is uniformly optimal across equations or sparsity levels. The diagnostics further reveal that residual fidelity, solution accuracy, and kernel conditioning are distinct objectives.
AI.conclusion: PI-SAP effectively preserves residual-side training dynamics. The findings motivate pruning methods that explicitly balance solution-side and residual-side training dynamics during optimization, as these represent competing objectives.

title: Label-Free Foundational Model Selection for Medical Image Classification under Distribution Shift via Pseudo Label Discrepancy
comment: Accepted at MIRASOL Workshop, MICCAI 2026. 10 pages, 3 figures
summary: Foundation models are increasingly deployed for medical image analysis. However, under the inter-institutional distribution shift typical of deployment, their performance varies widely and cannot be known without target-domain labels, which are rarely available. This leaves a practical question unresolved: given several candidate foundational models and labeled-data from a source domain, which one to deploy in an unlabeled target domain? We propose a label-free selection criterion built on SUDO, a framework for evaluating clinical AI systems without ground-truth annotations. SUDO partitions the unlabeled target data by predicted probability and, for each region, measures a pseudo-label discrepancy reflecting class contamination; aggregated across regions, this yields a score (AURCC) requiring neither target annotation nor fine-tuning. We show that AURCC can be used to rank a variety of vision-language models (BioMedCLIP, CXR-CLIP, CheXzero, MedCLIP, MedImageInsight, CLIP) on chest X-ray classification across three inter-hospital shift scenarios, under zero-shot and MLP-probe regimes. The AURCC ranking recovers the ground-truth ranking with Spearman rho up to 0.943 (p<0.05). Against the natural baseline of ranking by held-out source accuracy, AURCC is competitive when the labeled source is large and yields a more accurate ranking once it is small; the regime of interest in resource-constrained settings.
