title: Beyond Scaling: Self-Evolving LLM Agents for Hardware Kernel Optimization via an Experience-Driven Workflow and Experience Graph Memory
summary: Hardware kernel optimization requires repeated compilation, correctness testing, profiling, and revision. LLM agents can automate parts of this process, and stronger foundation models, longer context windows, and longer execution horizons have improved optimization within individual tasks. These advances alone do not enable an agent to learn from completed optimization runs. Existing kernel-optimization agents seldom preserve a decision, its observed execution feedback, and the later decisions that use that evidence. Retaining every prior trajectory is also impractical because an expanding history competes with the current task for context. We present KOPE, an experience-driven framework for hardware kernel optimization. KOPE records optimization trajectories with correctness and performance feedback in Experience Graph Memory, then uses Active Context Management and Injection to retrieve relevant experience under a fixed token budget. The graph retains decision order, observed outcomes, and alternative branches, allowing evidence collected on the target hardware to inform later optimization steps and tasks. Under the same GLM-5.2 setting, the geometric mean of KOPE's per-operator speedups is $1.54\times$ that of CANNBot, the strongest competing baseline. In a complete 53-operator ablation, Active Context Management and Injection raises pass rate from 60.0\% to 84.6\%, increases the evaluator-reported positive-field geometric mean from 0.0382 to 0.0661, and reduces optimization token consumption from 15.9B to 1.113B tokens relative to passive agent-led context construction. Enabling Experience Graph Memory raises full-suite pass rate from 55.2\% to 84.6\% and yields a $1.43\times$ geometric-mean speedup on valid timing comparisons. These results support continual optimization through external experience while the foundation model remains fixed.

AI.tldr: KOPE is an experience-driven framework for hardware kernel optimization that uses LLM agents with Experience Graph Memory to record and retrieve optimization trajectories with feedback, under fixed token budgets.
AI.motivation: Existing kernel-optimization agents cannot learn from completed optimization runs - they don't preserve decisions, feedback, and later decisions that use that evidence. Retaining every prior trajectory is impractical due to context window limits.
AI.method: KOPE uses Experience Graph Memory to record optimization trajectories with correctness and performance feedback. It employs Active Context Management and Injection to retrieve relevant experience under fixed token budgets. The graph retains decision order, observed outcomes, and alternative branches.
AI.result: Under same GLM-5.2 setting, KOPE achieves 1.54x geometric mean speedup vs CANNBot. In 53-operator ablation: Active Context Management raises pass rate from 60.0% to 84.6%, increases evaluator-reported positive-field geometric mean from 0.0382 to 0.0661, and reduces token consumption from 15.9B to 1.113B tokens. Experience Graph Memory raises full-suite pass rate from 55.2% to 84.6% and yields 1.43x geometric-mean speedup on valid timing comparisons.
AI.conclusion: KOPE enables continual optimization through external experience while the foundation model remains fixed, demonstrating significant improvements in pass rates, speedups, and token efficiency.

title: Steer the Sampling, Not the Kernel Grid: Geometry-Guided Sampling Operator for Volumetric Segmentation
summary: Accurate 3D segmentation is central to quantitative lesion assessment and anatomy mapping for clinical planning and follow-up. Thin, elongated, and fine anatomical/pathological structures (e.g., vessels) are a particularly challenging case: a one-voxel boundary error can disconnect a branch and change clinically relevant topology. In encoder-decoder networks (e.g., U-Net), repeated downsampling and fixed-grid convolution blur or alias fine structures and weaken orientation cues, so early mistakes propagate across scales. We propose a geometry-guided local operator that steers where features are sampled, rather than deforming convolutional kernels, under a single formulation for both feature refinement (stride 1) and resolution reduction (stride > 1). At each voxel, it predicts a local orientation and bounded step sizes, samples symmetrically along these directions, and transforms paired samples into compact geometric and boundary cues with lightweight mixing; a cross-scale consensus aligns encoder and decoder features at skip connections to reduce geometric mismatch. Replacing all stride 1 and stride 2 operators in a 3D U-Net yields consistent improvements on BraTS, MSD Hepatic Vessel, and TDSC-ABUS, with notably better boundary metrics (e.g., BraTS Dice 86.1 to 88.9, HD95 7.1 to 6.2; TDSC-ABUS HD95 39.1 to 27.8) while reducing parameters from 2.3M to 0.8M. We further demonstrate that the operator can be integrated into other backbones (e.g., nnU-Net, Swin-UNETR, and MedNeXt) without changing their macro-architectures while providing consistent performance gains.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a geometry-guided local operator for 3D medical image segmentation that improves boundary accuracy for thin, elongated structures (e.g., vessels) while reducing model parameters. The operator steers feature sampling by predicting local orientations and step sizes at each voxel, with cross-scale consensus at skip connections to align encoder-decoder features.
AI.motivation: Accurate 3D segmentation of thin, elongated anatomical structures (like vessels) is clinically important but challenging. Existing encoder-decoder networks (U-Net) suffer from repeated downsampling and fixed-grid convolution that blur fine structures and cause early errors to propagate across scales. A one-voxel boundary error can disconnect a vessel branch and change clinically relevant topology.
AI.method: The proposed geometry-guided local operator steers feature sampling at each voxel by predicting local orientation and bounded step sizes. It samples symmetrically along predicted directions and transforms paired samples into geometric and boundary cues via lightweight mixing. The operator works for both feature refinement (stride 1) and resolution reduction (stride > 1). A cross-scale consensus mechanism aligns encoder and decoder features at skip connections to reduce geometric mismatch. This replaces all stride 1 and stride 2 operators in a 3D U-Net.
AI.result: Consistent improvements on BraTS (brain tumor segmentation), MSD Hepatic Vessel (liver vessel segmentation), and TDSC-ABUS (automated breast ultrasound) datasets. Notable boundary metric improvements: BraTS Dice increased from 86.1% to 88.9%, HD95 reduced from 7.1 to 6.2; TDSC-ABUS HD95 reduced from 39.1 to 27.8. Model parameters reduced from 2.3M to 0.8M. The operator integrates into other backbones (nnU-Net, Swin-UNETR, MedNeXt) without changing macro-architecture while providing consistent gains.
AI.conclusion: The geometry-guided local operator effectively addresses boundary segmentation challenges for thin structures in 3D medical imaging. By steering feature sampling based on predicted local orientations and using cross-scale consensus, it achieves superior boundary accuracy with significantly fewer parameters. The method is versatile and can enhance various backbone architectures without architectural modifications.

title: Individual Fairness in Hierarchical Clustering
summary: Hierarchical clustering produces ultrametric representations that impose strong global geometric constraints and may distort local similarities in ways that disproportionately affect individual data points. We study hierarchical clustering under an individual fairness requirement that bounds relative distortion within local $k$-nearest neighborhoods. We formulate this requirement as a feasibility problem over dominated ultrametrics and characterize the minimal multiplicative slack required for feasibility. We identify a sharp local threshold, prove stability under bounded perturbations, establish monotonicity in $k$, and show an intrinsic $Θ(\log n)$ separation between local and global realizability. Experiments on synthetic and real world datasets support our theoretical results.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses the tension between hierarchical clustering (which produces ultrametric representations with strong global constraints) and individual fairness (which requires bounded relative distortion within local k-nearest neighborhoods). The work characterizes the minimal multiplicative slack needed for feasibility, establishes theoretical thresholds and stability guarantees, and demonstrates a fundamental Θ(log n) separation between local and global realizability.
AI.motivation: Hierarchical clustering produces ultrametric representations that impose strong global geometric constraints, which can disproportionately distort local similarities for individual data points. This raises fairness concerns—instances where points in the same local neighborhood should have similar cluster assignments may be treated inconsistently due to global optimization pressures.
AI.method: The paper formulates individual fairness as a feasibility problem over dominated ultrametrics. It characterizes the minimal multiplicative slack required for feasibility, analyzes stability under bounded perturbations, and studies how feasibility changes with neighborhood size k.
AI.result: The authors identify a sharp local threshold for feasibility, prove stability under bounded perturbations, establish monotonicity in k, and demonstrate an intrinsic Θ(log n) separation between local and global realizability—meaning there exists a fundamental logarithmic gap between what can be achieved locally versus globally.
AI.conclusion: The theoretical findings are validated through experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets, confirming the practical relevance of the identified threshold and separation bound. This work provides a principled framework for understanding and addressing fairness in hierarchical clustering.

title: FlowMoDL: Model-Based Deep Learning with Conjugate-Gradient Data Consistency for Highly Accelerated 4D Flow MRI Reconstruction
summary: We present FlowMoDL, an unrolled neural network for highly accelerated 4D flow MRI reconstruction that directly optimizes for both anatomical magnitude and phase-derived velocity accuracy. Building on the MoDL framework, FlowMoDL alternates a learned (3+1)D spatiotemporal denoiser with conjugate-gradient data-consistency updates based on the SENSE forward model. A novel dual-pathway conditioning scheme adapts the denoiser features and data-consistency weighting, enabling a single model to handle varying acceleration factors ($10\times$ to $50\times$). To ensure physiological accuracy, the network is trained using a deep-supervision composite loss that explicitly penalizes velocity magnitude and angular errors, stabilized by a curriculum schedule. We evaluate FlowMoDL on the multi-center CMRx4DFlow dataset against classical and deep-learning baselines (CG-SENSE, MoDL, FlowVN, and FlowMRI-Net). A key advantage of FlowMoDL is its superior gradient step efficiency. When evaluated under an equivalent, limited budget of gradient steps, competing flow-specific networks degrade significantly. In contrast, FlowMoDL robustly converges and strictly outperforms all competitors across all acceleration factors in magnitude SSIM, nRMSE, relative velocity error, and angular error, successfully recovering sharp structural details and temporally coherent velocity fields.

AI.tldr: FlowMoDL is an unrolled neural network for highly accelerated 4D flow MRI reconstruction that optimizes for both anatomical magnitude and phase-derived velocity accuracy, using a learned (3+1)D spatiotemporal denoiser with CG data-consistency updates and a dual-pathway conditioning scheme to handle 10× to 50× acceleration factors.
AI.motivation: 4D flow MRI provides valuable anatomical and velocity information but suffers from long acquisition times. Existing deep learning methods for accelerated MRI reconstruction often lack robustness across varying acceleration factors and may not adequately preserve velocity accuracy, which is critical for flow quantification in cardiovascular imaging.
AI.method: FlowMoDL builds on the MoDL framework, alternating a learned (3+1)D spatiotemporal denoiser with conjugate-gradient data-consistency updates based on SENSE forward model. A novel dual-pathway conditioning scheme adapts denoiser features and data-consistency weighting for varying acceleration factors (10× to 50×). Training uses deep-supervision composite loss with explicit penalties for velocity magnitude and angular errors, stabilized by a curriculum schedule.
AI.result: FlowMoDL outperforms all competitors (CG-SENSE, MoDL, FlowVN, FlowMRI-Net) across all acceleration factors in magnitude SSIM, nRMSE, relative velocity error, and angular error on the multi-center CMRx4DFlow dataset. It demonstrates superior gradient step efficiency and robust convergence under limited gradient step budgets, successfully recovering sharp structural details and temporally coherent velocity fields.
AI.conclusion: FlowMoDL represents a significant advance in 4D flow MRI reconstruction, achieving state-of-the-art performance across wide acceleration ranges while maintaining physiological accuracy in both magnitude and velocity measurements. Its efficiency under limited computational budgets makes it practical for clinical deployment.

title: M-Fibration Theory with Applications to Neural Network Compression
summary: The purpose of this paper is to provide a general, comprehensive, theoretical framework that allows one to deal with fibrations on graphs labelled on a commutative monoid. This is a genuine extension of the theory of graph fibrations (as introduced in "Fibrations of Graphs" [Discrete Math., vol. 243, pp. 21-66, 2002]), that makes it possible to deal with weighted graphs, and also graphs labelled with other algebraic structures. The derived theory also lends itself naturally to consider approximate fibrations. As an example, we show how this framework can be applied to the compression of arbitrary neural networks (including CNNs), providing a strong theoretical underpinning to the recent results in "The role of fibration symmetries in geometric deep learning" [Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. USA, vol. 123, no. 4, p. e2416552123, 2026]

AI.tldr: This paper extends the theory of graph fibrations to handle graphs labeled on commutative monoids, enabling analysis of weighted graphs and approximate fibrations, with applications to neural network compression.
AI.motivation: The existing theory of graph fibrations (from 2002) is limited to unlabeled graphs. The authors seek to generalize this framework to accommodate weighted graphs and graphs with other algebraic label structures, which is necessary for practical applications in deep learning.
AI.method: The authors extend the theory of graph fibrations by allowing labels from a commutative monoid, creating a unified theoretical framework that subsumes the original theory as a special case.
AI.result: The generalized framework enables theoretical analysis of weighted graphs and approximate fibrations, and provides a mathematical foundation for compressing arbitrary neural networks including CNNs.
AI.conclusion: This work bridges graph theory and geometric deep learning by providing rigorous mathematical foundations for understanding symmetries in neural networks, with potential implications for network compression and architecture design.

title: Socialized Detector Learning: Trajectory-Guided and Reciprocal Distillation for Heterogeneous Object Detectors
summary: Object detection knowledge is fragmented across independently trained, heterogeneous detectors with complementary category supports. In socialized learning, this knowledge resides in a society, and learning aims to evolve the society collectively through exchange. However, aggregation-based socialization does not explicitly plan transfer order, whereas progressive multi-teacher distillation considers order but remains a one-way student enhancement in a shared category space. Building on Socialized Learning, we formulate Socialized Detector Learning (SDL) for heterogeneous, category-specialized object detectors and propose Trajectory-Guided and Reciprocal Distillation (TGRD).TGRD estimates directed operational Inter-Detector Transfer Difficulty (IDTD) from held-out feature-alignment residuals, precomputes a fixed score table, and greedily constructs a carrier trajectory. Along the trajectory, knowledge is progressively consolidated into a union-category carrier and then returned to experts through reciprocal transfer. A conditional proxy-certificate analysis shows that, under stated assumptions, the progressive certificate is no larger than an aggregated-target counterpart. On MS COCO with four heterogeneous experts and two carrier initializations, final carriers outperform epoch-matched simultaneous aggregation controls by 2.6 AP in both settings. Reciprocal detectors attain 20.8--28.4 AP on previously unsupported categories while remaining within 1.3 AP of original expert-specific performance. These results support order-aware progressive consolidation followed by reciprocal transfer as a viable mechanism for detector-society evolution.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes Socialized Detector Learning (SDL) with Trajectory-Guided and Reciprocal Distillation (TGRD) to enable knowledge transfer among heterogeneous, category-specialized object detectors. TGRD uses a greedy trajectory-based approach to progressively consolidate knowledge into a union-category carrier and then reciprocally transfer it back to experts.
AI.motivation: Existing aggregation-based socialization methods do not plan transfer order, while progressive multi-teacher distillation methods only consider one-way student enhancement in a shared category space. This work addresses the challenge of evolving a society of heterogeneous, category-specialized object detectors through order-aware progressive consolidation followed by reciprocal transfer.
AI.method: TGRD estimates directed operational Inter-Detector Transfer Difficulty (IDTD) from held-out feature-alignment residuals, precomputes a fixed score table, and greedily constructs a carrier trajectory. Along this trajectory, knowledge is progressively consolidated into a union-category carrier and then returned to experts through reciprocal transfer. A conditional proxy-certificate analysis provides theoretical support.
AI.result: On MS COCO with four heterogeneous experts and two carrier initializations, final carriers outperform epoch-matched simultaneous aggregation controls by 2.6 AP. Reciprocal detectors achieve 20.8-28.4 AP on previously unsupported categories while remaining within 1.3 AP of original expert-specific performance.
AI.conclusion: Order-aware progressive consolidation followed by reciprocal transfer is a viable mechanism for detector-society evolution, enabling detectors to learn new categories while maintaining their original expertise.

title: Frequency-aware forecasting for short-term typhoon gust prediction
summary: Accurate gust forecasting under typhoon conditions remains challenging due to the highly non-stationary and multi-scale characteristics of extreme wind fluctuations. Existing deep learning models often struggle to simultaneously capture long-term trends and rapid local variations, resulting in degraded performance during extreme events. We propose WDANet, a frequency-aware forecasting framework that integrates stationary wavelet decomposition, a Feature-wise Linear Modulation (FiLM) strategy, and a dual-branch encoder-decoder architecture, enabling separate modeling of trend and fluctuation components. Taking the offshore regions of the Western Pacific in China as an example, we conduct fine-grid wind gust prediction research. The results demonstrate that WDANet shows advantages for short lead times under the experimental setting across a 24-h forecasting horizon and achieves higher prediction accuracy than ECMWF-HRES within the first 6 h. During extreme wind events, WDANet more accurately captures gust peaks and attains the best RMSE and MAE performance. These results highlight its potential for offshore wind power operation, disaster warning, and risk mitigation.

AI.tldr: WDANet is a frequency-aware deep learning framework for accurate wind gust forecasting under typhoon conditions. It integrates stationary wavelet decomposition, FiLM modulation, and dual-branch encoder-decoder architecture to separately model trend and fluctuation components. The model outperforms ECMWF-HRES in the first 6 hours and achieves best performance during extreme wind events.
AI.motivation: Accurate gust forecasting under typhoon conditions is challenging due to the highly non-stationary and multi-scale characteristics of extreme wind fluctuations. Existing deep learning models struggle to simultaneously capture long-term trends and rapid local variations, leading to degraded performance during extreme events.
AI.method: WDANet integrates three key components: (1) stationary wavelet decomposition for multi-scale analysis, (2) Feature-wise Linear Modulation (FiLM) strategy for adaptive feature adjustment, and (3) a dual-branch encoder-decoder architecture enabling separate modeling of trend and fluctuation components. The case study focuses on offshore regions of the Western Pacific in China with fine-grid wind gust prediction.
AI.result: WDANet shows advantages for short lead times across a 24-h forecasting horizon and achieves higher prediction accuracy than ECMWF-HRES within the first 6 hours. During extreme wind events, WDANet more accurately captures gust peaks and attains the best RMSE and MAE performance.
AI.conclusion: WDANet demonstrates significant potential for offshore wind power operation, disaster warning, and risk mitigation due to its superior performance in capturing extreme wind events and short-term predictions.

title: THA-Flow Generative Model: Prosthesis Geometry Prediction from Preoperative CT
summary: Preoperative planning for total hip arthroplasty (THA) is commonly framed as selecting a single prosthesis configuration and placement for a patient's osseous anatomy. In practice, however, the same anatomy may admit several clinically reasonable solutions, making planning inherently a one-to-many problem that is better represented by a conditional probability distribution. We present THA-Flow, a conditional flow-matching model that generates three-dimensional prosthesis geometry directly from preoperative CT. Separate AutoencoderKL models compress preoperative bone anatomy and prosthesis geometry, while a three-dimensional UNet learns a rectified flow from Gaussian noise to the prosthesis latent space under spatial bone conditioning and optional structured prosthesis parameters. The retrospective cohort comprised 1,355 hips from 1,149 patients undergoing primary THA. Following rigid registration of postoperative CT to preoperative CT, the actual postoperative prostheses were transformed independently according to the pelvic and femoral registrations and represented as a dual-channel truncated signed distance field. The prosthesis autoencoder achieved a peak signal-to-noise ratio of 47.11 dB and a structural similarity index of 0.9964 on the validation set. Complete acetabular and femoral geometries were generated across seven major stem models representing 93.4% of the cohort. Repeated bone-conditioned sampling preserved component position, alignment, and the principal bone-prosthesis interfaces while allowing limited local geometric variation. To our knowledge, THA-Flow represents the first application of generative AI to three-dimensional surgical planning for THA.

AI.tldr: THA-Flow is the first generative AI model for three-dimensional surgical planning in total hip arthroplasty (THA). It uses a conditional flow-matching approach to generate 3D prosthesis geometry directly from preoperative CT scans, treating the planning process as a one-to-many problem rather than selecting a single solution.
AI.motivation: Preoperative planning for THA is traditionally framed as selecting a single prosthesis configuration. However, the same anatomy may admit several clinically reasonable solutions, making this inherently a one-to-many problem better represented by a conditional probability distribution.
AI.method: THA-Flow uses separate AutoencoderKL models to compress preoperative bone anatomy and prosthesis geometry into latent representations. A 3D UNet learns a rectified flow from Gaussian noise to prosthesis latent space under spatial bone conditioning and optional structured prosthesis parameters. Prostheses are represented as dual-channel truncated signed distance fields following rigid registration.
AI.result: The prosthesis autoencoder achieved a peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) of 47.11 dB and a structural similarity index (SSIM) of 0.9964 on validation. Complete acetabular and femoral geometries were generated across seven major stem models representing 93.4% of the cohort. Repeated bone-conditioned sampling preserved component position, alignment, and principal bone-prosthesis interfaces while allowing limited local geometric variation.
AI.conclusion: THA-Flow represents the first application of generative AI to three-dimensional surgical planning for THA, successfully generating diverse but clinically plausible prosthesis configurations from preoperative CT data. The model preserves key surgical parameters while introducing controlled geometric variation, suggesting potential for personalized surgical planning.

title: DCEO: Direct Causal Effect Optimization for Long-Term User Value Modeling in E-commerce Search
summary: Industrial e-commerce search systems ultimately aim to optimize the user-level long-term objective, such as n-day cumulative purchases or gross merchandise value (GMV) per user. However, such objectives are defined at the user level, whereas search ranking is based on item-level scores within each request. Existing methods typically bridge this granularity gap through manually designed multi-objective fusion, where predictions of multiple item-level objectives, such as clicks, carts, purchases, and transaction value, are combined into a ranking score that serves as a proxy for the ultimate objective. Such hand-crafted fusion schemes rely on a small set of manually tuned weights, limiting fine-grained personalization and leading to suboptimal alignment with the ultimate objective. In this paper, we propose DCEO (Direct Causal Effect Optimization), a data-driven framework for learning item-level proxy scores that are better aligned with the ultimate objective. We first aggregate the item-level proxy scores into a user-level proxy metric and quantify its alignment with the ultimate objective using a relative causal effect. We then develop an actor-critic framework, where the critic estimates the ultimate objective for a given user-level proxy metric, and the actor dynamically generates context-dependent fusion weights over multiple objectives to construct the item-level proxy scores and is trained to directly optimize the relative causal effect. Extensive offline experiments and analyses demonstrate the effectiveness and interpretability of DCEO. In addition, DCEO has been deployed in a large-scale industrial e-commerce search system, outperforming the conventional GMV proxy by 0.36% in GMV in a 41-day online A/B test.

AI.tldr: DCEO is a data-driven framework for optimizing e-commerce search ranking by learning item-level proxy scores that better align with user-level long-term objectives (like GMV). It uses an actor-critic approach where the critic estimates the ultimate objective and the actor generates context-dependent fusion weights for multiple objectives. Deployed in a large-scale industrial system, it achieved 0.36% GMV improvement in a 41-day A/B test.
AI.motivation: Existing methods use manually designed multi-objective fusion with hand-crafted weights, creating a granularity gap between user-level ultimate objectives (e.g., n-day cumulative purchases, GMV) and item-level search ranking scores. This limits fine-grained personalization and results in suboptimal alignment with the ultimate objective.
AI.method:
1) Aggregate item-level proxy scores into a user-level proxy metric
2) Quantify alignment with ultimate objective using relative causal effect
3) Actor-critic framework:
   - Critic: estimates ultimate objective for given user-level proxy metric
   - Actor: dynamically generates context-dependent fusion weights over multiple objectives
4) Train actor to directly optimize the relative causal effect
AI.result: Offline experiments demonstrate effectiveness and interpretability. In a large-scale industrial e-commerce search system, DCEO outperformed the conventional GMV proxy by 0.36% in GMV during a 41-day online A/B test.
AI.conclusion: DCEO successfully bridges the granularity gap between item-level ranking and user-level long-term objectives through a data-driven, causal-effect-based approach. The actor-critic framework enables context-dependent fusion weights, improving personalization and objective alignment. The real-world deployment and positive A/B test results validate its practical applicability in industrial settings.

title: DEFUSE: Generalizable Backdoor Defense for Self-Supervised Encoders with Generative Priors
summary: Self-supervised learning (SSL) encoders are vulnerable to backdoor attacks, posing threats to both visual SSL encoders and vision-language encoders. Existing defenses are typically designed for only one of these paradigms and rely on restrictive assumptions such as access to uninfected in-distribution data or precomputed pseudo-labels, which are difficult to satisfy in practice. To address these limitations, we propose DEFUSE, a generalizable backdoor detection framework for SSL encoders. Inspired by Bayesian posterior inference, we reformulate backdoor detection as a representation-conditioned image likelihood estimation problem parameterized by a conditional diffusion generative model. Uninfected representations tend to yield semantically consistent reconstructions, whereas backdoored ones are more likely to be mapped to the attacker's target class or semantically meaningless images, deviating from the original semantics and thereby exposing the backdoor. However, we find that the exact likelihood is intractable, because highly abstracted representations discard the low-level information necessary for pixel-faithful reconstruction. We therefore relax the objective to semantic reconstruction and evaluate it in a well-separated representation space provided by a reference encoder. Rather than training from scratch, we fine-tune a pretrained diffusion model, leveraging its generative prior to map data onto the natural image manifold while preserving semantic content. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DEFUSE substantially outperforms existing detectors across diverse attack settings, generalizing to both visual SSL and vision-language encoders. Notably, our method greatly reduces the reliance on prior knowledge about the victim encoder or the attack strategy. The source code is available at https://github.com/jsrdcht/DEFUSE .

AI.tldr: DEFUSE is a generalizable backdoor detection framework for self-supervised learning (SSL) encoders that works for both visual SSL and vision-language encoders. It reformulates backdoor detection as a representation-conditioned image likelihood estimation problem using a conditional diffusion generative model, where uninfected representations yield semantically consistent reconstructions while backdoored ones deviate from original semantics.
AI.motivation: Existing backdoor defenses are typically designed for only one SSL paradigm (visual or vision-language) and rely on restrictive assumptions such as access to uninfected in-distribution data or precomputed pseudo-labels, which are difficult to satisfy in practice.
AI.method: Inspired by Bayesian posterior inference, DEFUSE uses a conditional diffusion generative model to estimate image likelihood given representations. The method evaluates semantic reconstruction in a well-separated representation space provided by a reference encoder. A pretrained diffusion model is fine-tuned to map data onto the natural image manifold while preserving semantic content.
AI.result: DEFUSE substantially outperforms existing detectors across diverse attack settings, generalizing to both visual SSL and vision-language encoders. The method greatly reduces reliance on prior knowledge about the victim encoder or attack strategy.
AI.conclusion: This work provides a practical solution for detecting backdoor attacks in SSL encoders without restrictive assumptions about data availability or attack knowledge. The approach successfully bridges the gap between visual SSL and vision-language encoder defenses.

title: A Token-Level Analysis of Sampled-Token Reverse-KL On-Policy Distillation
summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) supervises a student on its own trajectories with token-level signals from a frozen teacher, yet how a sampled loss allocates updates across tokens remains poorly understood. We analyze the gradient of the per-token K2 estimator of reverse KL with respect to the student logits. The $\ell_1$ norm of this gradient factorizes into the absolute teacher--student log-probability gap and a student-side softmax factor that grows as the sampled token becomes less likely under the student. In our math-distillation runs, these per-token norms are highly non-uniform: low-student-probability tokens account for a disproportionate share of their sum and are also enriched in large teacher--student gaps. As a lightweight intervention suggested by this analysis, we study Surprise-aware Reweighting (SuRe), a detached, bounded weighting rule that further amplifies this existing allocation. Across two Qwen3 student scales, SuRe improves several math metrics over vanilla OPD and shows no clear degradation on the selected out-of-domain benchmarks. Our primary contribution is therefore a gradient-level characterization of reverse-KL OPD trained with the K2 estimator, with SuRe as one empirical instantiation.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes how token-level losses allocate updates in on-policy distillation (OPD), where a student model learns from its own trajectories supervised by a frozen teacher. The key finding is that low-probability tokens under the student receive disproportionate gradient magnitude. Based on this analysis, the authors propose Surprise-aware Reweighting (SuRe), which amplifies this effect, showing improvements on math benchmarks without degrading out-of-domain performance.
AI.motivation: Despite the widespread use of on-policy distillation (OPD), the mechanism of how the sampled loss allocates updates across different tokens remains poorly understood. The authors aim to characterize the gradient-level behavior of reverse KL OPD trained with the K2 estimator to understand this allocation.
AI.method: The authors analyze the gradient of the per-token K2 estimator of reverse KL with respect to student logits. They derive that the ℓ1 norm of this gradient factorizes into two components: (1) the absolute teacher-student log-probability gap, and (2) a student-side softmax factor that grows as the sampled token becomes less likely under the student. Empirically, they examine math-distillation runs and identify that per-token norms are highly non-uniform. Based on this analysis, they propose Surprise-aware Reweighting (SuRe), a detached and bounded weighting rule that further amplifies the existing allocation toward low-probability tokens.
AI.result: In math-distillation experiments, low-student-probability tokens account for a disproportionate share of the gradient norm sum and are also enriched in large teacher-student gaps. Across two Qwen3 student scales, SuRe improves several math metrics over vanilla OPD and shows no clear degradation on selected out-of-domain benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: The paper provides a gradient-level characterization of reverse-KL OPD trained with the K2 estimator, revealing that the loss naturally concentrates on surprising (low-probability) tokens. SuRe serves as an empirical instantiation that exploits this finding, demonstrating that further amplifying this allocation can improve math performance without harming generalization to other domains.

title: Precipitation Downscaling Using Foundation Model-Conditioned Diffusion
summary: High-resolution precipitation fields are essential for hydrological impact assessment, yet global climate model outputs are too coarse and biased for direct use. AI-based statistical downscaling with diffusion models offers a promising approach, but the mechanism by which large-scale atmospheric predictors condition generation remains largely unexplored. We investigate three conditioning strategies for a denoising diffusion probabilistic model applied to daily precipitation downscaling: channel concatenation of upsampled coarse predictors, cross-attention conditioning with a learned convolutional encoder, and cross-attention conditioning with the frozen encoder of the pretrained Prithvi WxC weather foundation model. All strategies are evaluated against an unconditioned baseline under identical conditions using probabilistic, distributional, spectral, and extreme-event metrics for the Colorado River Basin. Concatenation conditioning achieves the lowest point-wise CRPS and MSE, but tends to produce over-smoothed fields that suppress high-intensity events. In contrast, cross-attention conditioning provides substantially better distributional realism and modest improvements in spectral fidelity. Improvements are greatest for extremes: the Prithvi-WxC conditioned model retains over half of >100mm/day events, although estimates are uncertain due to limited samples. When trained on the full dataset, the learned convolutional model performs similarly to the foundation model-conditioned approach while requiring lower computational resources. However, the Prithvi-WxC-conditioned model achieves comparable performance with only five years of training data. These results indicate that cross-attention conditioning offers advantages over simple concatenation for probabilistic precipitation downscaling, and that pre-trained foundation model representations may offer benefits in data-limited settings.

AI.tldr: This paper compares three conditioning strategies for diffusion model-based daily precipitation downscaling: channel concatenation, learned cross-attention encoder, and pretrained Prithvi WxC foundation model encoder. Cross-attention conditioning outperforms concatenation in distributional realism and extreme event preservation, while foundation model conditioning enables good performance with limited training data.
AI.motivation: Global climate models produce coarse, biased precipitation outputs unsuitable for hydrological impact assessment. While AI-based statistical downscaling with diffusion models shows promise, the mechanism by which large-scale atmospheric predictors condition generation remains unexplored.
AI.method: Three conditioning strategies were evaluated for a denoising diffusion probabilistic model applied to daily precipitation downscaling: (1) channel concatenation of upsampled coarse predictors, (2) cross-attention conditioning with a learned convolutional encoder, and (3) cross-attention conditioning with the frozen encoder of the pretrained Prithvi WxC weather foundation model. All were compared against an unconditioned baseline using probabilistic (CRPS, MSE), distributional, spectral, and extreme-event metrics for the Colorado River Basin.
AI.result: Concatenation conditioning achieved the lowest point-wise CRPS and MSE but produced over-smoothed fields suppressing high-intensity events. Cross-attention conditioning provided substantially better distributional realism and modest spectral improvements. The Prithvi-WxC conditioned model retained over half of >100mm/day events. With full training data, the learned convolutional model performed similarly to the foundation model approach; with only five years of data, Prithvi-WxC achieved comparable performance while requiring lower computational resources.
AI.conclusion: Cross-attention conditioning offers advantages over simple concatenation for probabilistic precipitation downscaling. Pretrained foundation model representations may offer benefits in data-limited settings, enabling good performance with limited training data.

title: LDAC-Net: A Learnable Multi-Lag Differencing Attention-Convolution Network for Drift-Robust Recognition with Low-Cost MOX Gas Sensors
summary: Portable electronic-nose systems based on low-cost metal-oxide (MOX) gas sensors offer a practical solution for gas and odour recognition, but their signals are affected by slow chemical transients, drifting sensor offsets, scale variation, and cross-channel correlations. Existing pipelines commonly use fixed first-order temporal differencing (FOTD), which requires a manually selected lag and may discard useful response information. We propose LDAC-Net, an end-to-end learnable multi-lag differencing attention-convolution network that operates directly on multi-channel MOX signals. Its learnable differential feature enhancement front-end combines window-conditioned statistical affine normalisation, which compensates for window-specific offset and scale variation, with learnable multi-lag differencing, which weights and combines temporal differences across multiple lags. A compact attention-convolution backbone subsequently models local transients and longer-range temporal dependencies. On the 50-class SmellNet-Base task, LDAC-Net achieves 68.2% top-1 accuracy, exceeding the best FOTD-preprocessed comparison model by approximately 14 percentage points and the raw-input Transformer by more than 30 points. Ablation studies confirm the contributions of both proposed components. The representation also transfers to SmellNet-Mixtures, improving accuracy from 45.4% to 50.5%, and generalises to the 62-channel eNose-Drift benchmark under strong long-term drift, achieving 70.6% top-1 accuracy and 69.6% macro-F1. These results outperform the best comparison model with dataset-retuned FOTD preprocessing by 8.0 and 3.0 points, respectively, demonstrating that learnable, sensor-aware preprocessing is more effective than fixed handcrafted differencing for low-cost MOX gas-sensor recognition.

AI.tldr: LDAC-Net is an end-to-end learnable neural network for low-cost MOX gas sensor-based electronic nose systems. It addresses limitations of fixed first-order temporal differencing (FOTD) by introducing learnable multi-lag differencing and window-conditioned statistical affine normalisation. The method achieves 68.2% top-1 accuracy on SmellNet-Base (50 classes), 50.5% on SmellNet-Mixtures, and 70.6% top-1 accuracy with 69.6% macro-F1 on eNose-Drift benchmark, outperforming FOTD-based comparison models by 8-14 percentage points.
AI.motivation: Portable electronic-nose systems using low-cost MOX gas sensors face challenges including slow chemical transients, drifting sensor offsets, scale variation, and cross-channel correlations. Existing pipelines use fixed first-order temporal differencing (FOTD) which requires manual lag selection and may discard useful response information. The authors seek to develop a learnable, sensor-aware preprocessing approach that can better handle these domain-specific challenges.
AI.method: The proposed LDAC-Net consists of two main components: (1) A learnable differential feature enhancement front-end combining window-conditioned statistical affine normalisation (compensating for window-specific offset and scale variation) with learnable multi-lag differencing (weights and combines temporal differences across multiple lags); (2) A compact attention-convolution backbone that models both local transients and longer-range temporal dependencies. The entire pipeline is end-to-end trainable.
AI.result: On the 50-class SmellNet-Base task, LDAC-Net achieves 68.2% top-1 accuracy, exceeding the best FOTD-preprocessed comparison model by ~14 percentage points and the raw-input Transformer by >30 points. On SmellNet-Mixtures, accuracy improves from 45.4% to 50.5%. On the 62-channel eNose-Drift benchmark with strong long-term drift, LDAC-Net achieves 70.6% top-1 accuracy and 69.6% macro-F1, outperforming the best comparison model by 8.0 and 3.0 points respectively.
AI.conclusion: Learnable, sensor-aware preprocessing is more effective than fixed handcrafted differencing for low-cost MOX gas-sensor recognition. The proposed approach successfully handles the unique challenges of MOX sensors including drift, scale variation, and cross-channel correlations, and generalizes across different datasets and recognition tasks.

title: Learning Late, Guiding Early: Timestep-Decoupled Semantic Guidance for Fair Face Generation
summary: Demographic imbalance in synthetic face generation can propagate to downstream face recognition systems, making fairness an important consideration when diffusion models are used for data generation. Existing fairness-aware generation approaches often require model retraining, architectural modifications, or repeated guidance throughout the reverse diffusion process. In this work, we introduce Semantic Boundary Predictor (SBP), an inference-time framework that performs demographic guidance through a one-shot intervention during reverse denoising. Our approach is motivated by the observation that latent representations at different diffusion timesteps play distinct semantic roles: late-stage latents provide stronger demographic separability, whereas early-stage latents offer greater flexibility for semantic intervention. SBP leverages this timestep decoupling by learning linear semantic boundaries from late-stage latent representations while applying them only once at the initial noisy latent, allowing the remainder of the reverse denoising process to proceed unchanged. The method requires neither retraining nor fine-tuning of the underlying Latent Diffusion Model and operates without external balanced datasets. Experiments on CelebA-HQ demonstrate substantial improvements in demographic fairness, reducing fairness disparity by 98% for gender, 95% for binary race, and 15% for four-class race, while maintaining perceptual image quality across demographic groups. Owing to its one-shot inference strategy and model-agnostic design, SBP introduces only a small computational overhead and can be readily integrated with existing pre-trained latent diffusion models.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Semantic Boundary Predictor (SBP), an inference-time framework that enables demographic fairness in synthetic face generation by performing one-shot guidance during reverse denoising in latent diffusion models, without requiring model retraining or fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: Demographic imbalance in synthetic face generation can propagate to downstream face recognition systems, creating fairness concerns. Existing fairness-aware approaches require model retraining, architectural modifications, or repeated guidance, making them computationally expensive and difficult to deploy.
AI.method: SBP leverages timestep decoupling in diffusion models: late-stage latents provide stronger demographic separability while early-stage latents offer greater flexibility for semantic intervention. The method learns linear semantic boundaries from late-stage latent representations and applies them once at the initial noisy latent, allowing the rest of the reverse denoising to proceed unchanged. It requires no retraining, fine-tuning, or external balanced datasets.
AI.result: Experiments on CelebA-HQ show substantial fairness improvements: 98% reduction in gender disparity, 95% reduction in binary race disparity, and 15% reduction in four-class race disparity, while maintaining perceptual image quality across demographic groups.
AI.conclusion: SBP provides an effective, computationally efficient, and model-agnostic solution for demographic fairness in synthetic face generation. Its one-shot inference strategy and lack of requirement for retraining make it readily integrable with existing pre-trained latent diffusion models.

title: Adversarial Training of Linear Models under Stealthy Attacks
comment: This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication. Copyright may be transferred without notice, after which this version may no longer be accessible
summary: Predictive models are widely used in many fields, but are vulnerable to false data injection attacks. To address this, detection schemes and adversarial training have been proposed, but such approaches lack guarantees against stealthy attacks. We therefore propose a detector-based switched model, in which optimal attack strategies are stealthy. For linear prediction models, we derive a convex formulation of the resulting adversarial risk. The model incorporates protected features and introduces a hyperparameter modelling attack probability, enabling an explicit performance trade-off between clean and attacked data regimes. Numerical simulations on real and synthetic data show improved performance on partially attacked data, even for misspecified attack probabilities.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses vulnerabilities of predictive models to false data injection attacks by proposing a detector-based switched model with optimal stealthy attack strategies. For linear prediction models, a convex formulation of adversarial risk is derived, incorporating protected features and a hyperparameter for attack probability to enable performance trade-offs between clean and attacked data regimes.
AI.motivation: Predictive models are widely used but vulnerable to false data injection attacks. Existing solutions like detection schemes and adversarial training lack guarantees against stealthy attacks, necessitating a new approach with theoretical guarantees.
AI.method: The authors propose a detector-based switched model that incorporates protected features and introduces a hyperparameter modeling attack probability. For linear prediction models, they derive a convex formulation of the resulting adversarial risk, enabling explicit performance trade-off between clean and attacked data regimes.
AI.result: Numerical simulations on real and synthetic data demonstrate improved performance on partially attacked data, with robustness even when attack probabilities are misspecified.
AI.conclusion: The proposed detector-based switched model provides a principled approach to handling stealthy attacks with theoretical guarantees. The convex formulation enables efficient optimization, and the method shows practical effectiveness even under model misspecification.

title: LUTSeg: A Longitudinal Multi-Expert Dataset for Ulcer Tissue Segmentation
summary: Quantifying wound tissue composition is essential for monitoring chronic ulcer progression and guiding treatment decisions. However, pixel-level annotations are costly, and multi-tissue wound datasets remain scarce, particularly for neglected diseases such as leprosy. We introduce LUTSeg, a longitudinal chronic ulcer dataset comprising 141 images from 39 patients with wound masks and five tissue categories annotated by five expert clinicians, including a multi-expert gold-standard subset for inter-rater agreement analysis. To establish an initial benchmark for LUTSeg, we further propose TiSage, a semi-supervised tissue segmentation framework that integrates multi-scale semantic priors from a frozen medical vision-language model within a teacher-student architecture. We evaluate TiSage on LUTSeg and DFUTissue, showing improvements over supervised and semi-supervised baselines in most low-label settings. Code & data: https://github.com/carlosh93/TiSage

AI.tldr: LUTSeg is a new longitudinal chronic ulcer dataset with 141 images from 39 patients, featuring wound masks and five tissue categories annotated by five clinicians. TiSage is a semi-supervised segmentation framework using a teacher-student architecture with frozen medical vision-language model priors, demonstrating improved performance over baselines in low-label settings.
AI.motivation: Quantifying wound tissue composition is essential for chronic ulcer monitoring and treatment guidance, but pixel-level annotations are costly and multi-tissue wound datasets are scarce, particularly for neglected diseases like leprosy.
AI.method: TiSage employs a teacher-student architecture that integrates multi-scale semantic priors from a frozen medical vision-language model, enabling semi-supervised tissue segmentation with limited annotations.
AI.result: TiSage outperforms supervised and semi-supervised baselines in most low-label settings when evaluated on LUTSeg and DFUTissue datasets.
AI.conclusion: The proposed LUTSeg dataset addresses the scarcity of multi-tissue wound datasets, and TiSage demonstrates the effectiveness of leveraging frozen medical vision-language models for semi-supervised wound tissue segmentation in low-label scenarios.

title: Modeling spatio-temporal locality in multi-step forecasting of geo-referenced time series
summary: Forecasting future measurements from geographically distributed sensors is essential across many domains. However, the spatial distribution of these sensors raises multiple challenges, primarily due to spatial autocorrelation phenomena, that introduce inter-dependencies among nearby locations, that cannot therefore be treated independently. While some existing approaches can capture such phenomena, they generally model the spatial dimension globally across all locations. On the other hand, the method we propose in this paper, called SPALT, focuses on capturing spatial relationships among time series with similar trends, even if they occur at different times, thus modeling the spatio-temporal locality. SPALT leverages linear model trees, which allow us to consider the spatial autocorrelation locally: during the tree-building process, the adopted heuristics group time series exhibiting similar trends into the same node, on which additional features considering the spatial dimension are selectively injected. Additionally, we propose a new pruning strategy, based on Reduced Error Pruning, that also considers the spatio-temporal locality during the tree simplification. Designed for a multi-step setting, SPALT provides forecasts for multiple future time steps across multiple sensors simultaneously. The characteristics exhibited by SPALT can provide significant benefits in different domains, where measurements come from distributed sensors. In this paper, we focus on data produced by sensors located in multiple renewable power plants measuring their energy production at regular, short intervals. Experiments on 3 real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of SPALT in forecasting the production of energy at different time horizons, and its superior performance in comparison with tree-based models and state-of-the-art neural networks that incorporate both temporal and spatial dimensions.

AI.tldr: SPALT is a novel forecasting method for geographically distributed sensors that captures spatio-temporal locality by grouping time series with similar trends into linear model tree nodes, selectively injecting spatial features, and using a spatio-temporal-aware pruning strategy. It provides multi-step forecasts across multiple sensors simultaneously for renewable energy production data.
AI.motivation: Forecasting distributed sensor data is challenging due to spatial autocorrelation (inter-dependencies among nearby locations). Existing approaches either ignore spatial relationships or model them globally across all locations, failing to capture local spatio-temporal patterns where similar trends may occur at different times and locations.
AI.method: SPALT uses linear model trees to capture spatial autocorrelation locally. During tree construction, heuristics group time series with similar trends into the same node, where spatial dimension features are selectively injected. A new Reduced Error Pruning strategy is proposed that considers spatio-temporal locality during tree simplification. The method operates in a multi-step setting to forecast multiple future time steps across multiple sensors.
AI.result: Experiments on 3 real-world renewable energy production datasets demonstrate SPALT's effectiveness in forecasting energy production at different time horizons. SPALT shows superior performance compared to tree-based models and state-of-the-art neural networks incorporating both temporal and spatial dimensions.
AI.conclusion: SPALT successfully addresses the challenge of forecasting from geographically distributed sensors by modeling spatio-temporal locality through linear model trees and spatial feature injection. The method outperforms existing approaches, offering significant benefits for applications involving distributed sensor measurements such as renewable energy production forecasting.

title: Embedding NDRE Trajectories into Contrastive Learning for Label-Free, Physiology-Aware Crop-Stress Staging and DSS Outputs
summary: Timely detection of crop stress is critical for sustaining yields under increasing drought frequency, yet conventional vegetation index thresholds or image-based clustering often fail to capture stress progression, limiting their value for farm decision-making. To address this gap, we present EigenCL, a physiology-guided contrastive learning framework that stages crop stress from Sentinel-2 NDRE trajectories, with the goal of providing interpretable and transferable stress diagnostics for decision support systems (DSS). EigenCL was trained on 10,000 maize NDRE patches from drought-affected Iowa fields in 2020 and tested on Nebraska fields in 2023 without retraining, with validation incorporating soil-moisture records, U.S. Drought Monitor maps, and county-level yield statistics. The model produced four physiologically coherent stress clusters (Healthy, Mild, Moderate, Severe), significantly outperforming baselines including K-Means, SimCLR, ProtoCLR, and an ablation model (Silhouette = 0.748, DBI = 0.35, CHI = 49,624). Clusters aligned with maize growth stages, with severe stress peaking around tasseling-silking (VT-R1), a stage known to drive yield loss; moreover, EigenCL clusters correlated with soil moisture at 0-14-day lags (rho up to 0.72) and matched yield anomalies in drought-affected counties. By embedding NDRE trajectory dynamics into contrastive learning, EigenCL enables early stress alerts and interpretable DSS outputs (e.g., heatmaps, scouting priorities, regional risk indices), extending beyond single-date NDRE thresholds and supporting scalable monitoring for climate-smart agronomy.

AI.tldr: EigenCL is a physiology-guided contrastive learning framework that stages crop stress from Sentinel-2 NDRE trajectories, providing interpretable and transferable stress diagnostics for decision support systems. It outperformed baseline methods and produced four physiologically coherent stress clusters aligned with maize growth stages.
AI.motivation: Timely detection of crop stress is critical for sustaining yields under increasing drought frequency. Conventional vegetation index thresholds or image-based clustering methods fail to capture stress progression, limiting their value for farm decision-making. There is a need for more sophisticated, interpretable, and transferable stress diagnostics.
AI.method: EigenCL uses physiology-guided contrastive learning trained on 10,000 maize NDRE patches from drought-affected Iowa fields in 2020 and tested on Nebraska fields in 2023 without retraining. The model embeds NDRE trajectory dynamics into contrastive learning. Validation incorporated soil-moisture records, U.S. Drought Monitor maps, and county-level yield statistics.
AI.result: EigenCL produced four physiologically coherent stress clusters (Healthy, Mild, Moderate, Severe), significantly outperforming baselines including K-Means, SimCLR, ProtoCLR, and an ablation model (Silhouette = 0.748, DBI = 0.35, CHI = 49,624). Clusters aligned with maize growth stages, with severe stress peaking around tasseling-silking (VT-R1). EigenCL clusters correlated with soil moisture at 0-14-day lags (rho up to 0.72) and matched yield anomalies in drought-affected counties.
AI.conclusion: By embedding NDRE trajectory dynamics into contrastive learning, EigenCL enables early stress alerts and interpretable DSS outputs (e.g., heatmaps, scouting priorities, regional risk indices). It extends beyond single-date NDRE thresholds and supports scalable monitoring for climate-smart agronomy. The cross-temporal and cross-regional generalization (Iowa to Nebraska, 2020 to 2023) demonstrates strong transferability.

title: Tropospheric temperature and humidity profile retrieval from Meteosat Flexible Combined Imager based on deep learning
comment: 27 pages, 11 figures. Supporting information has 12 pages and 17 figures. Submitted for publication in Journal of Geophysical Research: Atmospheres
summary: The Meteosat Third Generation (MTG) Flexible Combined Imager (FCI) offers new opportunities for tropospheric temperature and humidity profiling, at higher spatio-temporal resolutions and expanded spectral coverage relative to its predecessor. Vertically resolved retrievals from broadband imagers are inherently challenging, and operational retrieval algorithms typically rely on numerical weather prediction (NWP) background fields to compensate for limited infrared spectral resolution, reducing the retrievals' independence. We develop a spatially aware deep learning framework to retrieve all-sky tropospheric temperature and humidity profiles from FCI, without forecast profiles as input. A Residual U-Net that exploits spatial context across all 16 FCI channels was trained on 14 months of collocated FCI observations and CERRA reanalysis targets over Europe. Validated against independent radiosondes, retrieved temperatures show biases below 0.4 K and standard deviations of 1.5-1.9 K. Retrieved relative humidity standard deviations range from 12-20 %, compared to 9-19 % for CERRA. Performance degrades modestly under clouds, with standard deviation increases below 0.4 K and 3 % RH beneath cloud tops despite limited direct radiative information. Ablation experiments show that spatial context improves retrievals, with the largest gains below cloud tops. Feature sensitivity analysis indicates broad consistency with FCI bands' established radiative transfer characteristics. Visible and near-infrared channels contribute despite not being commonly used in physics-based profile inversions. These results demonstrate that spatially aware deep learning models can extract statistically reliable tropospheric profiles from geostationary imager observations, independent of NWP forecast fields, enabling more rapid autonomous monitoring of the atmosphere.

AI.tldr: A deep learning framework (Residual U-Net) retrieves all-sky tropospheric temperature and humidity profiles from MTG FCI satellite observations without NWP background fields, achieving temperature biases < 0.4 K and standard deviations of 1.5-1.9 K when validated against radiosondes.
AI.motivation: Operational retrieval algorithms for tropospheric profiling from broadband imagers rely on NWP background fields due to limited infrared spectral resolution, reducing independence. The MTG FCI offers higher spatio-temporal resolution and expanded spectral coverage, but vertically resolved retrievals remain challenging. This work aims to develop an NWP-independent retrieval method using deep learning.
AI.method: A spatially aware Residual U-Net was trained on 14 months of collocated FCI observations (16 channels) and CERRA reanalysis targets over Europe. The model exploits spatial context across all channels without forecast profiles as input. Validation was performed against independent radiosondes, with ablation experiments to assess spatial context benefits and feature sensitivity analysis.
AI.result: Temperature retrievals show biases < 0.4 K and standard deviations of 1.5-1.9 K. Retrieved relative humidity standard deviations range 12-20%, versus 9-19% for CERRA. Performance degrades modestly under clouds (SD increases < 0.4 K and < 3% RH). Ablation experiments confirm spatial context improves retrievals, especially below cloud tops. Visible and near-infrared channels contribute despite not being commonly used in physics-based inversions.
AI.conclusion: Spatially aware deep learning models can extract statistically reliable tropospheric profiles from geostationary imager observations without NWP forecast fields, enabling more rapid autonomous atmospheric monitoring. The approach demonstrates independence from numerical weather prediction while maintaining accuracy, with potential for operational applications in tropospheric temperature and humidity profiling.

title: Visual General Intelligence: A White Paper
summary: This paper reconsiders intelligence from a vision-centered perspective and examines whether intelligence emerging from visual experience and learning may provide a pathway toward AGI. In the language domain, beginning with the introduction of the Transformer architecture, the GPT series has demonstrated transfer to unseen tasks through autoregressive language modeling on web-scale text combined with aggressive scaling. This raises a natural question, namely, what capabilities and forms of intelligence can emerge from visual modalities such as images, videos, and geometry? In this paper, we discuss whether visual intelligence can serve as a pathway toward AGI, referred to in this paper as visual general intelligence (VGI), by bringing together contributors from diverse standpoints and affiliations. Our aim is not to offer a single definition of visual intelligence, but to clarify the principles that computer vision should pursue in the AGI era, the visual input modalities, the benchmarks, the learning paradigms, and the relationship between vision, when taken as the core, and other modalities such as language.

AI.tldr: This paper explores whether visual intelligence can serve as a pathway toward Artificial General Intelligence (AGI), termed Visual General Intelligence (VGI). It draws parallels with the success of GPT series in language, asking what visual modalities (images, videos, geometry) can achieve. The work aims to clarify principles, benchmarks, learning paradigms, and the relationship between vision and other modalities.
AI.motivation: The GPT series has shown impressive transfer capabilities through autoregressive language modeling on web-scale data with scaling. This success raises the question of whether similar approaches in visual modalities could lead to general intelligence. The authors seek to determine if visual intelligence could be a pathway to AGI.
AI.method: The paper takes a multi-perspective approach, bringing together contributors from diverse standpoints and affiliations to discuss VGI. It examines visual input modalities, potential benchmarks, learning paradigms, and the relationship between vision and other modalities like language.
AI.result: The abstract does not present specific results; it is a position/discussion paper that aims to clarify the principles and framework for pursuing visual intelligence in the AGI era rather than providing empirical findings.
AI.conclusion: The paper does not offer a single definition of visual intelligence but aims to clarify what computer vision should pursue in the AGI era, including the visual input modalities, benchmarks, learning paradigms, and the relationship between vision and other modalities.

title: Fairness-Aware Test-Time Prompt Tuning
summary: Vision-language models have displayed remarkable capabilities in multi-modal understanding and are increasingly used in critical applications where economic and practical deployment constraints prohibit re-training or fine-tuning. However, these models can also exhibit systematic biases that disproportionately affect protected demographic groups and existing approaches to addressing these biases require extensive model retraining and access to demographic attributes. There is a clear need to develop test-time adaptation (TTA) approaches that improve the fairness characteristics of pretrained models under distributional shift. In this paper, we evaluate how episodic TTA affects fairness in CLIP classification under subpopulation shifts and develop FairTPT, a novel fairness-aware episodic TTA method that jointly minimizes target marginal entropy while maximizing spurious marginal entropy through soft-prompt tuning. We find that standard episodic TTA generally exacerbates disparities between majority and minority groups, that blinding a model to spurious attributes without degrading target performance is inherently challenging, and that excessive blinding can lead to catastrophic forgetting. This model collapse can be prevented by monitoring test-time changes in target loss within the linear regime, while still achieving fairness improvements on reactive data and preserving overall performance. FairTPT outperforms all state-of-the-art episodic test-time debiasing methods and establishes a foundation for robust TTA, which is essential for achieving fairness in practice.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses fairness in vision-language models (CLIP) under test-time adaptation (TTA) by proposing FairTPT, a method that jointly minimizes target marginal entropy while maximizing spurious marginal entropy through soft-prompt tuning. The study reveals that standard episodic TTA exacerbates disparities between demographic groups, and proposes monitoring test-time changes in target loss within the linear regime to prevent catastrophic forgetting while achieving fairness improvements.
AI.motivation: Vision-language models like CLIP exhibit systematic biases affecting protected demographic groups, but existing debiasing approaches require extensive retraining and demographic attribute access. There is a need for test-time adaptation (TTA) methods that improve fairness without retraining, especially under distributional shifts.
AI.method: The paper develops FairTPT, a fairness-aware episodic TTA method that uses soft-prompt tuning to jointly minimize target marginal entropy while maximizing spurious marginal entropy. The approach monitors test-time changes in target loss within the linear regime to prevent catastrophic forgetting (model collapse).
AI.result: Standard episodic TTA exacerbates disparities between majority and minority groups. Blinding a model to spurious attributes without degrading target performance is inherently challenging. Excessive blinding leads to catastrophic forgetting. FairTPT outperforms all state-of-the-art episodic test-time debiasing methods.
AI.conclusion: FairTPT establishes a foundation for robust TTA essential for achieving fairness in practice. Monitoring test-time changes in target loss within the linear regime can prevent model collapse while still achieving fairness improvements on reactive data and preserving overall performance.

title: Code World Model: Coding Agent as World Brain
summary: World models aim to simulate how complex environments evolve under actions and events, yet existing video-based world models primarily learn dynamics from visual observations, which reveal outcomes rather than the underlying knowledge, rules, and mechanisms governing world evolution. This makes it difficult to maintain persistent consequences and support coherent, open-ended evolution. We introduce Code World Model, a framework that separates world evolution from visual realization by combining the reasoning and coding capabilities of language models with the generative priors of video models. A coding agent serves as the world brain, reasoning about events and their consequences and generating executable code to maintain persistent world state and perform rule-consistent evolution. To connect executable state with visual generation, we introduce a proxy representation that encodes frame-wise spatiotemporal constraints and is compiled into a proxy video, which conditions a video model to render high-fidelity visual observations. We further develop data pipelines for constructing aligned proxy-observation pairs from gameplay and real-world videos. After fine-tuning on paired gameplay data, MiniMax-H3 follows proxy-based spatiotemporal specifications from simple interactive worlds built by the coding agent while preserving rich visual details and dynamics. These results demonstrate the potential of combining code for persistent world evolution with video models for flexible visual realization, providing a new path toward open-ended world models.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Code World Model, a framework that separates world evolution from visual realization by combining language models (for reasoning/coding) with video models (for visual generation). A coding agent acts as the world brain maintaining persistent world state through executable code, while a proxy representation bridges this to a video model for high-fidelity visual rendering.
AI.motivation: Existing video-based world models only learn dynamics from visual outcomes but fail to capture underlying knowledge, rules, and mechanisms governing world evolution. This limits their ability to maintain persistent consequences and support coherent, open-ended evolution.
AI.method: The framework uses: (1) A coding agent that reasons about events and generates executable code to maintain persistent world state and perform rule-consistent evolution; (2) A proxy representation encoding frame-wise spatiotemporal constraints, compiled into proxy video that conditions a video model; (3) Data pipelines for constructing aligned proxy-observation pairs from gameplay and real-world videos; (4) Fine-tuning MiniMax-H3 on paired gameplay data.
AI.result: After fine-tuning, MiniMax-H3 follows proxy-based spatiotemporal specifications from simple interactive worlds built by the coding agent while preserving rich visual details and dynamics.
AI.conclusion: Combining code for persistent world evolution with video models for flexible visual realization provides a new path toward open-ended world models, demonstrating the potential to achieve coherent, rule-consistent world simulation.

title: It's a matter of timescale: non-linear utility in successor features and multi-objective planning and learning
summary: Time is of the essence when dealing with multiple reward signals and non-linear utility. In this paper we argue that the current main approaches in multi-objectiveRL (SER and ESR), and successor features, are insufficient. While each approach deals with non-linear effects on user utility on different timescales, none of them take into account that different effects happening on different timescales can happen within the same decision problem. We motivate that this can indeed be the case by an example, both intuitively and numerically, leading to a new perspective, and a significant and non-trivial gap in the literature.

title: When Composition Doesn't Add Up: Humans Identifying Defects in AI-Generated Images
summary:
*Chulin Zhao and Ruoqi Hu contributed equally to this work.
  State-of-the-art text-to-image (T2I) models exhibit pronounced and systematic defects when prompts involve intricate compositional factors such as multiple entities and multiple attributes. In this paper, we investigate how humans identify such defects. Specifically, we manually select 651 reference images from the four categories of people, hand, object, and scene that exhibit complex compositional characteristics, from which prompts emphasizing compositional factors are derived by manually editing ChatGPT-generated prompts. We then feed the prompts into three selected T2I models to generate AI images and conduct a comprehensive subjective study to identify their defects. For each image, 29 participants provide multi-label assessments specifying defect types and locations. The study yields the compositional AI-generated image defect (CO-AID) dataset, including reference images, prompts, AI-generated images, and information on defect locations and types. Experimental results show that training a deep model on CO-AID can both predict defects in AI-generated images and optimize AI image generation, demonstrating its usability and effectiveness. The database and supplementary materials are available at: https://github.com/Future-IQA/CO-AID .

title: Are LLM-Enhanced GNNs Privacy-Safe?
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have recently advanced graph neural networks (GNNs) by enriching node representations with semantic information, giving rise to LLM-enhanced GNNs that achieve substantial performance gains. However, their vulnerability to privacy attacks, in which adversaries infer sensitive information from model outputs, remains largely underexplored. To bridge this gap, we present a systematic evaluation of privacy risks in LLM-enhanced GNNs through a unified framework consisting of five stages: (1) dataset preparation, (2) victim model training, (3) privacy attack, (4) risk assessment, and (5) defense analysis. Specifically, we conduct experiments on six real-world text-attributed graph datasets covering diverse domains. We consider six representative privacy attack methods targeting three fundamental threats, namely link, label, and membership inference, and construct 42 victim model configurations by combining multiple LLM-based feature enhancers with representative GNN backbones. Extensive experiments show that, despite their utility improvements, LLM-enhanced GNNs consistently exhibit increased vulnerability to privacy attacks compared to shallow text representation baselines. Further analysis reveals that semantic enrichment amplifies link-, label-, and membership-related signals in the embedding space, making them more exploitable by inference attacks. Finally, we evaluate differential privacy as a defense strategy and show that, while it can partially mitigate privacy risks, it introduces significant utility degradation, highlighting a fundamental privacy-utility trade-off in LLM-enhanced graph learning. Overall, this work provides a comprehensive understanding of privacy risks in LLM-enhanced GNNs and offers practical insights for developing more secure and trustworthy graph learning systems.
